RU.issue.letter.body: Дверь никогда не просто дверь — это мембрана между состояниями, между теплом, которое вы оставили, и холодом, в который собираетесь войти. В этом выпуске прослеживается, что пространства держат в нас, когда нас нет в них.

DE.hero.quote: "Epris journal ist nicht nur eine Veröffentlichung; es ist ein lebendiges Archiv der Dinge, die das Leben schmackhaft machen. Geboren aus dem Wunsch, langsamer zu werden und die flüchtige Schönheit unserer Existenz zu dokumentieren, dient dieses Journal als Zufluchtsort für Nachdenkliche, Neugierige und Ästhetische."
DE.about.quote1: "Epris journal ist nicht nur eine Veröffentlichung; es ist ein lebendiges Archiv der Dinge, die das Leben schmackhaft machen. Geboren aus dem Wunsch, langsamer zu werden und die flüchtige Schönheit unserer Existenz zu dokumentieren, dient dieses Journal als Zufluchtsort für Nachdenkliche, Neugierige und Ästhetische."
DE.about.bio: Mit einem Hintergrund in Kunstgeschichte und einer Leidenschaft für langsames Reisen gründete Mariia Epris Journal am 5. Juni 2024. Ihre Vision war ein digitaler Raum, der sich so greifbar und zeitlos anfühlt wie ein gedruckter Band aus einer alten Bibliothek.

FR.about.techDirector.bio: Viacheslav Munister est un auteur, chercheur, et spécialiste du patrimoine numérique. Il est membre des associations patrimoniales En Quête de Patrimoine et Histoire d’en Parler. Son travail se concentre sur l'architecture, la culture urbaine, la mémoire collective, et la préservation et la réinterprétation du patrimoine culturel à travers les technologies numériques.

FR.about.team.author-1788563282904-7a43p.bi: Edward Nesterov est le Directeur de la communication du journal EPRIS et le représentant du magazine pour les États-Unis et l'Europe de l'Ouest. Il établit des relations avec des partenaires, des institutions et des contributeurs dans ces régions, connectant EPRIS aux personnes et aux histoires qui façonnent sa voix internationale.

items.title: Oval with Points
items.subtitle: Henry Moore · 1968–70 · bronze
items.description: Two voids turn a bronze oval into a shifting horizon: Henry Moore makes weight, landscape and the human body feel inseparable.
items.homeTitle: SWEDISH FISH WATER BAG NO 94 • DYLAN MARTINAZ • 2026
items.homeDescription: A playful study of illusion, fragility, and everyday objects. Dylan Martinez transforms hand-blown glass into an uncanny water bag, complete with a bright red fish suspended inside — turning a familiar image into something quietly surreal.

items.title: The Ten Largest, No. 9, Old Age
items.subtitle: Hilma af Klint · 1907 · tempera on paper
items.description: Hilma af Klint gives old age a vivid, floating language: lilac fields, loops and dark seeds make the canvas feel grown rather than painted.
items.homeDescription: Molly Brocklehurst is a British painter known for her dreamlike oil paintings based on found photographs. Her work explores memory, nostalgia, and the blurred line between reality and fiction, creating scenes that feel like fragments of a forgotten past.

items.title: Salk Institute
items.subtitle: Louis I. Kahn · 1965 · La Jolla
items.description: At the Salk Institute, concrete is not a backdrop but a precise instrument for light, sea air and silence.
items.homeDescription: A dialogue between architectural history and contemporary living. Rich timber interiors frame a quieter arrangement of modern furniture, creating a sequence of spaces where material, proportion, and carefully controlled views become part of the experience.

items.title: Panton Chair
items.subtitle: Verner Panton · 1960 · moulded plastic
items.description: One continuous red line becomes a chair: Verner Panton reduces a familiar object to colour, curve and a single unapologetic gesture.
items.homeDescription: A sculptural object built around the tension between permanence and ephemerality. Three cast-glass elements are stacked into a monolithic form, while a small flame within introduces warmth, movement, and a sense of ritual to an otherwise solid object.

items.title: Co-op Grain Elevator, Caldwell
items.subtitle: Russell Lee · 1940 · Caldwell, Idaho
items.description: Russell Lee turns storage towers and a parked tractor into a quiet, almost abstract portrait of American infrastructure.
items.homeDescription: French photographer Guy Bourdin transformed fashion photography through surreal compositions, bold colour and enigmatic narratives. His highly staged images blurred the line between fashion, cinema and fine art, creating mysterious worlds that often feel more like fragments of an unfinished story than advertisements.

items.title: Sandra Kantanen: Beyond the Lens of Traditional Photography
items.subtitle: Photography
items.description: A photograph can be a threshold rather than a record — Sandra Kantanen turns landscape into a space between memory, myth and optical distortion.
items.homeLabel: Fedora E. D. Brown · c. 1908 · silver gelatin print
items.homeSubtitle: Fedora E. D. Brown · c. 1908 · silver gelatin print
items.homeDescription: A path dissolves into haze and trees, making the landscape feel like a memory still finding its focus.
items.homeCredit: Fedora E. D. Brown · public-domain photograph / Wikimedia Commons

items.subtitle: Contemporary Art

items.homeLabel: Hilma af Klint · 1907 · tempera on paper

items.homeDescription: Lilac fields, solar diagrams and a dark central seed make the canvas feel less painted than grown from an invisible cosmos.

items.title: Against the Right Angle
items.subtitle: Architecture
items.description: Five buildings that talked their way out of the grid — and the software, the metal, the money and the sheer nerve it took to build them.
items.homeLabel: Lekeboy54 · 2025 · architectural photograph
items.homeDescription: A quiet concrete frame turns weather, repetition and a low horizon into one measured composition.

items.title: Polish Design: Woven From Memory
items.subtitle: Design
items.description: Contemporary Polish design has arrived at a moment of profound, quiet maturity. To walk through the studios of today’s leading architects and furniture designers is to encounter a language of rigorous minimalism, tactile raw materials, and a deliberate structural honesty. Yet, this modern clarity is not a rejection of the past - it is the culmination of a century-long dialogue regarding what it means to create with a national soul.
items.homeLabel: Frank Gehry · 1972 · corrugated cardboard
items.homeDescription: A simple sheet becomes a sinuous seat: an everyday material pushed into a sculptural, surprisingly generous form.
items.homeCredit: Frank Gehry · photo CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Tadao Ando: Decoding the Philosophy of Pure Design
items.subtitle: Architecture
items.description: Tadao Ando is one of the most influential architects of 21st century, who challenges the conventional definition and boarders of architecture. His unique approach showcased the rethinking of traditional Japanese principles through bold shapes, materials and spatial organizations. In this article we are going to reveal the core principles of his philosophy and its cues.

items.title: Art that makes you smile
items.subtitle: ART & DESIGN
items.description: I believe that when you introduce playful objects into an environment, it expands the boundaries of the mind. It gives you non-verbal permission to think freely - not just to push against conventional frames, but to forget they even exist.
items.homeLabel: Umberto Boccioni · 1913 · bronze
items.homeTitle: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space
items.homeDescription: A body becomes velocity: Boccioni turns the figure into a single aerodynamic gesture, caught between sculpture and flight.
items.homeCredit: Umberto Boccioni · public-domain work / Wikimedia Commons

items.title: The Sacred Spring: A Portrait of the Vienna Secession
items.subtitle: Art History
items.description: Imagine Vienna in the last years of the nineteenth century: a city drunk on its own reflection. The Ringstrasse glittered with palaces dressed in borrowed history – a Greek parliament here, a Gothic city hall there, a Renaissance opera in between. It was magnificent, and it was exhausted. Behind the gilt, an entire generation of young painters and architects had begun to suspect that their city was building museums to a past that had never quite belonged to it, while the present – electric, anxious, alive – went unpainted.

items.title: Five Rooms, One Signature
items.subtitle: Interior Design
items.description: A dalmatian dot, a slab of burl, three portraits of the same painted dog, and one small cone that keeps reappearing where you least expect it — the disciplined vocabulary one apartment uses five different ways...

items.title: The Threshold of Time
items.subtitle: Restoration
items.description: Door restoration is an act of archaeological tenderness. From the carved portals of Tbilisi to Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise — a journey through the cities that refuse to let their thresholds disappear.

items.title: Home Away From Home
items.subtitle: Design & Travel
items.description: Choosing a place to stay in a new destination means entrusting it with the significant moments of your life. Falling into bed after a long walk through unfamiliar streets, late-night talks filled with the thoughts and emotions of the day, planning the next breakfast at your newly favorite nearby boulangerie, sharing genuine smiles and the pure excitement of exploration.

items.title: The Heart of EPRIS: Maria Is Now a Bachelor of Architecture
items.subtitle: Culture
items.description: On July 7th, Mariia Ivanova, EPRIS's editor-in-chief, officially became a Bachelor of Architecture. To mark the day – a heart built from the architecture and art that inspire her.

items.title: Rooms That Watch You Back
items.subtitle: Architecture
items.description: Glass once promised freedom, honesty and light. Then the walls learned to collect data. An essay on transparent architecture, controlled visibility and the radical luxury of being allowed to disappear.

items.title: In Conversation with Chora Practice
items.subtitle: Interview
items.description: Founders of a Lisbon-based decor studio on the art of listening to your inner self, importance of resilience and favorite places in the city

items.title: Museo Nivola: A Museum, a Village and the Memory They Share
items.subtitle: Interview
items.description: Costantino Nivola left a Sardinian village of masons for New York, worked with Le Corbusier, Sert and Saarinen, and never stopped coming back. The team of his museum, on the hill above Orani, on where a museum ends and a village begins, on the method he left behind, and on what a monographic museum can still become.

items.title: Souv: The Souvenir That Doesn't Forget
items.subtitle: Interview
items.description: Matej Petrić and Antonio Šeparović on turning an ordinary fridge magnet into the entrance to a traveler's own photos, why nobody actually wants to buy NFC technology, and what it took to put a laser engraver in a startup that started as two friends and a third coffee in Zagreb.

articles.title: Where Wisdom Takes Form: Inside the New CCA Tashkent
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: In a transformed 1912 power station, HIKMAH asks whether clay, brick, thread and collective use can give Central Asia’s newest art institution a language of its own.

content.content: A new art centre rarely opens with a question as old as wisdom. Institutions normally announce themselves through scale, novelty or civic ambition. CCA Tashkent begins differently. Its inaugural exhibition, HIKMAH, asks what knowledge can reside in clay, brick, thread, copper, gesture and repetition—and whether a building marked by empire, industry and technological change can become an instrument for thinking rather than a neutral container for display.

The Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent opened on 6 September 2026 in a former tram depot and diesel power station built in 1912. Reworked by the Paris-based practice Studio KO, it is presented as the first permanent centre of its kind in Tashkent and the wider region: not a museum with a historical collection, but a producing institution for exhibitions, performance, film, music, education and research. That distinction matters. A collection stabilises a narrative. A kunsthalle-like centre must continually invent one—and persuade a public that the invention belongs to them.
CCA Tashkent is most convincing when architecture, artwork and public use are allowed to alter one another.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/news/2026/09/01M36CY767TPGVRP48AYCT0E4H.jpg
content.caption: Opening day at CCA Tashkent, 6 September 2026. The circular stair became both circulation and an informal auditorium for the Centre’s first public. Official photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Visitors gathering around the circular staircase during the opening of CCA Tashkent.

content.content: A power station learns a different form of energy

The building stands close to Amir Temur Square, within the composite urban fabric of central Tashkent. The city around it is already an archive of competing projects: late-imperial brick construction, Soviet monumental planning, post-independence symbols and the accelerated development of the present. The 1912 complex belongs to an early infrastructural layer. Designed for trams and diesel generation, it organised movement and power before it organised culture.

That history gives the conversion more than picturesque industrial character. Electricity and transport were technologies through which the modern city reordered time, distance and labour. The new centre inherits those histories while changing the type of energy being distributed. Its raw material is now attention: who receives it, whose work is amplified, what histories can be made visible, and how long a visitor is invited to remain.

Adaptive reuse is frequently praised as if the mere retention of old walls guaranteed cultural memory. It does not. Industrial architecture can become a luxury surface, stripped of the labour that produced its scars. Studio KO’s stronger decision was to treat the surviving fabric as an active constraint. The old power hall keeps its long basilica-like volume, brick walls, arched openings and exposed roof structure. New interventions do not imitate that language. They arrive as terrazzo planes, curved circulation and dark insertions whose difference is legible.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/gallery/2026/05/01KQJ67B4Y6M3PMBTJRQCZDXKR.jpg
content.caption: The former diesel hall after Studio KO’s intervention. Brick, steel trusses and a suspended contemporary volume remain visibly distinct. Official architectural photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: The restored brick diesel hall of CCA Tashkent with steel roof trusses and a suspended white volume.

content.content: Architecture by subtraction

Studio KO co-founder Olivier Marty has described the first phase as a kind of archaeology: deciding what later additions could be removed so the 1912 composition could be read again. This is the project’s central architectural intelligence. Instead of filling the plot with programme, the architects restored the value of the void. The courtyard separates the principal volumes, admits daylight and gives events somewhere to exceed the galleries. Emptiness becomes part of the institution’s capacity.

Inside, circulation is unusually physical. A broad spiral stair curls around a central opening rather than disappearing into a service core. Ramps and curved walls slow the transition between levels. Terrazzo covers floors, counters and balustrades until circulation appears carved from a continuous mineral body. The effect is sensuous, perhaps almost too complete: an immaculate contemporary interior nested inside an industrial shell. Yet the generous dimensions keep the material finish from becoming merely decorative.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/content-blocks/2026/09/01M33TKA45GF5SPSSC51H9YDFA.jpg
content.caption: The terrazzo stair is conceived as a continuous public landscape rather than a concealed circulation element. Official architectural photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: A sculptural spiral staircase in terrazzo beneath a circular skylight at CCA Tashkent.

content.content: The restoration also draws on materials and fabrication associated with different parts of Uzbekistan. This can easily become a familiar institutional gesture: local craft applied as a badge of authenticity to an internationally authored building. At CCA, the more productive moments occur when craft is treated as technical knowledge rather than ornamental quotation. Brick bond, aggregate, perforation, joinery and filtered light become systems of environmental and spatial intelligence. The building does not need to look folkloric to be locally made.
A centre inside a city of ruptures

To read the project only as an accomplished conversion would miss the pressure exerted by Tashkent itself. The city has repeatedly been rebuilt through rupture. The Russian imperial city developed beside the older urban fabric rather than within it. Soviet planning introduced broad avenues, monumental institutions and new systems of collective life. The 1966 earthquake accelerated another reconstruction, while the decades after independence produced a further layer of ceremonial spaces, commercial development and infrastructural change. Tashkent is therefore not a city with one stable architectural identity waiting to be protected. It is a city in which different political ideas of modernity remain physically adjacent.

The CCA occupies a useful position within that condition. It is neither an isolated cultural object on an empty site nor a museum inserted into a purpose-built civic precinct. It reactivates infrastructure that already belonged to the city’s modernisation. The choice creates continuity, but not innocence. A power station speaks of collective provision and technological ambition; it also speaks of administrative control, extraction and the unequal distribution of energy. To convert such a building into a cultural institution is to inherit those contradictions rather than erase them.

This makes the Centre’s threshold especially important. Many contemporary art buildings announce difference through an intimidating façade or a plaza that must be crossed before entry. Here, the sequence is more compressed. Brick walls establish historical weight, but the courtyard and multiple programmes soften the transition from street to exhibition. The success of this arrangement will eventually be measured less by architectural photographs than by habits: whether people use the courtyard without an event, whether students treat the library as working infrastructure, whether a visitor can enter for twenty minutes without feeling that specialist knowledge is required.

The surrounding centre of Tashkent already contains museums, theatres, government buildings, hotels and heavily managed public spaces. CCA adds another cultural destination, but destination status alone is not enough. A serious urban institution must also operate as a connector. It should allow routes through the city to cross it, make room for unplanned encounters and create reasons for return that do not depend on the novelty of an opening. In that sense, free admission is spatial policy as much as cultural policy. It removes one barrier, while architecture and programming must address the others.
HIKMAH is a method, not a theme

Chief curator Sara Raza defines hikmah through wisdom, material intelligence and higher consciousness. The term carries philosophical and spiritual weight across Arabic, Persianate and Islamic intellectual traditions, but the exhibition avoids reducing it to a stable definition. It uses hikmah as a curatorial method: knowledge is approached through making, bodily repetition, inherited technique and the transformations materials undergo.
“Hikmah can be reframed as an exhibition method.” — Dr Sara Raza

That formulation is important because exhibitions about spirituality often drift toward atmospheric vagueness. HIKMAH is strongest when it remains materially exact. Steel is suspended according to measured outlines. Clay records pressure from thousands of hands. Found copper is allowed to oxidise. Thread, dust, resin and fibreglass hold evidence of labour and displacement. Wisdom is not illustrated; it is tested against matter.

The artist list deliberately crosses geographies: Ali Cherri, Nadia Kaabi-Linke, Kimsooja, Tarik Kiswanson, Muhannad Shono and Nari Ward appear alongside Shokhrukh Rakhimov and works by Vladimir Pan, Bakhtiyar Saipov and Daribay Saipov from the collection of the Savitsky Museum in Karakalpakstan. The juxtaposition refuses a simple division between an international contemporary present and a regional historical background. Whether it creates equality among those positions is the exhibition’s more difficult question.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/content-blocks/2026/09/01M33TNF8Q4XPH31QS925PKTYX.jpg
content.caption: The restored power hall during HIKMAH. The industrial volume is used as part of the exhibition’s argument rather than hidden behind a neutral white box. Official photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Long brick exhibition hall with exposed roof structure and a suspended installation at CCA Tashkent.

content.content: Kimsooja: knowledge made by many hands

Kimsooja’s participatory Archive of Mind provides the exhibition with its clearest image of collective knowledge. Visitors sit around an immense wooden table and roll pieces of clay between their palms. Each small sphere is elementary and distinct. Accumulated by the hundred and then the thousand, they become a field whose visual order is produced without central authorship.

The work changes the visitor’s position. Looking is no longer the only sanctioned activity; touch becomes a form of contribution. The sphere records time, pressure, moisture and the slight asymmetry of a particular pair of hands. Nothing about the result is spectacular in isolation. Its force arrives through duration and multiplicity—the recognition that an archive may be made from anonymous gestures rather than official documents.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/gallery/2026/05/01KQJ9DBBAJMMT3F8D7DZ9W31D.jpg
content.caption: Visitors forming clay spheres for Kimsooja’s Archive of Mind. The work turns repetitive touch into a collectively authored field. Official installation photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Visitors seated around a large wooden table covered with handmade clay spheres.

content.content: In Tashkent, the work acquires additional resonance. Clay is not an abstract universal substance here; it belongs to long architectural and ceramic histories across the region. HIKMAH does not claim that every rolled sphere transmits those histories, but it allows the material to carry more than one scale of memory: the intimacy of touch, the sociality of the table and the geological duration of earth.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/gallery/2026/05/01KQJ9DBBESEZ3VXND98N454W8.jpg
content.caption: Archive of Mind extends into the older brick volume, allowing the accumulated clay forms to register against the building’s industrial memory. Official installation photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Thousands of clay spheres spread across a surface inside the historic brick hall.

content.content: Nadia Kaabi-Linke: freedom suspended

Nadia Kaabi-Linke’s Flying Carpets is visually lighter and politically sharper. The installation derives its suspended steel forms from the rugs used by migrant street vendors in Venice to display counterfeit goods. Those rugs promise the fantasy of unrestricted flight while serving, in daily life, as devices that allow precarious workers to gather their merchandise and flee the police.

Kaabi-Linke transforms the measured outlines into a hovering structure held by descending threads. From a distance it is almost architectural: bridge, canopy, cage and drawing occupy the same air. As one walks around it, the work refuses a single image. The elegance of the suspension cannot be separated from the restricted movement it describes. Mobility, one of contemporary culture’s most celebrated freedoms, is shown to be radically unequal.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/gallery/2026/05/01KQJ9DBBJXVFC5EXT62375YHB.jpg
content.caption: Nadia Kaabi-Linke, Flying Carpets, 2011, installed in HIKMAH. Suspended metal outlines translate the improvised rugs of migrant street vendors into a floating cage. Official installation photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Suspended metal frames and dense vertical threads forming Nadia Kaabi-Linke’s Flying Carpets.

content.content: Installed within a centre created to connect Tashkent to international cultural networks, Flying Carpets also complicates the language of circulation surrounding the institution itself. Artists, curators and artworks travel through systems of visas, capital and professional recognition that remain far less open than the rhetoric of global exchange suggests. The work quietly asks who is permitted to move as a cultural agent and who is treated as a problem to be managed.
Found matter and local technique

Nari Ward’s site-specific Tashkent Groundin was developed in dialogue with local craft traditions and the building’s industrial past. Ward’s wider practice has long used found material to trace migration, value and urban memory. Here, copper and patina connect material weathering with the marks left by work. The title’s insistence on grounding counters the frictionless globalism that new cultural institutions are often asked to perform.

The exhibition’s attention to Uzbek ceramic practice deepens this question of location. Shokhrukh Rakhimov’s work, and the presence of Bakhtiyar and Daribay Saipov, position ceramics as contemporary thought rather than inherited décor. Technique becomes an argument: knowledge survives because it is repeatedly embodied, corrected and transmitted. The hand is not opposed to the conceptual; it is where the concept acquires consequence.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/gallery/2026/05/01KQJ9DBBG45G6BNYKTRQ0W5QY.jpg
content.caption: An installation view of HIKMAH, where floor-based material work and wall drawing resist the conventions of isolated display. Official photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Contemporary installation using a line of material on the floor and red drawing on a white gallery wall.

content.content: Tarik Kiswanson’s newly commissioned Nest, made from steel, resin and fibreglass, approaches belonging from another direction. Its inward-growing form holds protection and entrapment in suspension. A nest is built to make vulnerable life possible, but it is also temporary: a structure organised around eventual departure. Within a new institution defining its place in the region, that ambiguity is particularly apt.

Muhannad Shono and Ali Cherri extend the exhibition toward erasure, archaeology and speculative memory. Cherri’s moving-image work The Digger follows a caretaker guarding ancient ruins in Sharjah, refusing the heroic tempo through which archaeology is usually narrated. The patient labour of watching over fragments becomes an ethical counterpoint to institutions that treat the past as material to be rapidly packaged for a contemporary audience.
An exhibition assembled through different speeds

HIKMAH does not reveal itself through a single panoramic view. Its works ask for incompatible durations. Archive of Mind develops through repeated participation; Flying Carpets changes as the body moves beneath and around it; film requires surrender to another temporal order; ceramics may initially appear still but condense years of technical learning. The exhibition’s intelligence lies partly in refusing to synchronise these speeds. Visitors cannot consume every work through the same rhythm of recognition.

This is also where the architecture performs a curatorial role. The long industrial hall creates distant sightlines, but its brick surfaces prevent the optical neutrality of the white cube. Smaller rooms contract attention. The stair turns the movement between works into a public spectacle: visitors see one another arriving, pausing and returning. The Centre’s architecture continuously reminds the solitary viewer that interpretation is taking place among other bodies.

The historical works associated with the Savitsky Museum introduce another temporal complication. Their presence avoids presenting contemporary art in Central Asia as something that began with new international institutions. Yet historical inclusion carries responsibility. A small number of earlier works can become ancestry on demand, enlisted to legitimise a contemporary programme without being granted enough space to disturb it. HIKMAH points toward a richer genealogy; future exhibitions will need to expand it through sustained research, loans, translation and publication.

The same applies to the category of craft. In global exhibition culture, craft is frequently welcomed at the moment it can be described as embodied knowledge, ecological intelligence or decolonial practice. Those frameworks can be productive, but they can also convert living economies into curatorial metaphor. HIKMAH is strongest when technique retains specificity—when clay, copper or textile is connected to particular forms of labour and transmission—and weaker whenever materiality is allowed to stand in for an undifferentiated spiritual depth.
The institution beyond the exhibition

CCA Tashkent’s most consequential spaces may not be its galleries. The library, workshop, cinema, courtyard, restaurant and shop establish different reasons to enter and different durations of stay. The Centre is open six days a week and admission to HIKMAH is free. On opening day, curatorial tours were joined by poetry, children’s workshops, film, live performance and Shashmaqom music. This was not supplementary entertainment; it was an early statement about the kind of public the institution hopes to produce.
https://ccat.uz/storage/uploads/content-blocks/2026/09/01M33TKA493ZDX645PA1R7VHDC.jpg
content.caption: The CCA library and reading room. Research infrastructure is essential if the Centre is to become more than a sequence of temporary exhibitions. Official architectural photograph courtesy CCA Tashkent.
content.alt: Library with long reading table, bookshelves and upholstered chairs at CCA Tashkent.

content.content: A non-collecting institution can be unusually responsive, commissioning new work and changing direction without the weight of a permanent display. It can also be fragile. Its memory must be constructed through archives, publications, education, repeated relationships with artists and the knowledge retained by staff and audiences. The residency programme, operating since 2024, is therefore not peripheral. It offers the possibility that international attention might support sustained production rather than a succession of imported events.
The difficult politics of a new cultural landmark

No major institution arrives outside politics. CCA Tashkent is a flagship project of the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation, and its opening participates in a broader effort to place the country within international circuits of biennials, architecture, tourism and cultural diplomacy. The quality of the building and programme should not make that framework invisible. Public cultural investment can create genuine infrastructure while also producing an image of openness for external consumption.

The test will be what happens after the inaugural visibility subsides. How much curatorial authority will be available to artists and researchers based in Uzbekistan? Can difficult work remain difficult when it conflicts with an official narrative of cultural renewal? Will regional practitioners appear as intellectual partners rather than providers of craft knowledge and historical texture? Can a free institution remain accessible to publics beyond the internationally mobile cultural class?

HIKMAH begins to address these questions by refusing a simple showcase of national identity. Yet the balance remains delicate. An internationally legible roster and a globally recognised architecture practice bring attention; they can also establish the terms through which local practice becomes visible. The Centre’s future significance will depend on whether it can reverse that direction—allowing knowledge generated in Tashkent, Nukus and across Central Asia to alter the international conversation rather than merely enter it.
What kind of public can a new institution make?

Museums often speak of attracting an existing public, as if audiences waited outside in completed form. In reality, institutions produce publics through repetition. Opening hours determine who can attend. Language determines who can interpret. Seating determines who may linger. Security determines who feels watched. Programming determines whether children, artists, students, neighbours and occasional visitors recognise the building as available to them. A public is not a demographic reached by marketing; it is a relationship built through many small institutional decisions.

CCA’s opening programme understood this multiplicity. Film, workshops, poetry, performance, music and tours offered more than parallel attractions. They created several legitimate ways of being present. This matters in a context where contemporary art may still be perceived as a specialised or imported domain. The institution does not need to simplify art to broaden its audience. It needs to multiply the forms of entry while preserving the complexity of what is encountered inside.

Language will be decisive. Uzbek, Russian and English do not simply translate the same cultural field; they connect different generations, educational histories and international networks. A centre that works across those languages can become an unusually valuable site of intellectual exchange. A centre that privileges English at the level of research and global communication while treating local-language mediation as a service risks reproducing the hierarchy it claims to overcome. Translation must therefore be part of curatorial authorship, not an administrative final step.

Digital access poses a related question. Strong documentation can carry exhibitions beyond the period of display and beyond Tashkent, but an online archive should offer more than polished installation views. Commissioned essays, transcripts, artist conversations, bibliographies and records of public disagreement would allow the Centre to accumulate knowledge despite not accumulating objects. For a non-collecting institution, publishing is one of the principal ways memory becomes durable.

The Centre’s urban promise finally depends on recurrence. A landmark can draw a crowd once. An institution becomes civic when the same person returns for unrelated reasons: to read, meet, disagree, see a film, attend a workshop or simply cross the courtyard. The most persuasive photograph of CCA Tashkent will not be an empty hall but an image, years from now, in which use has left visible traces on Studio KO’s carefully completed surfaces.
A promising first proposition

CCA Tashkent is not important because it resolves the relationship between heritage and contemporaneity. It is important because its opening makes that relationship newly contestable. The building preserves evidence without freezing it. HIKMAH places spiritual and material knowledge in proximity without pretending they are interchangeable. The public programme treats the institution as a place for making, listening and gathering as well as viewing.

There are moments when the architecture’s polish risks overpowering the provisional character on which contemporary art depends. There are moments when the exhibition’s language of wisdom threatens to become too capacious, able to hold every work without sufficient friction. But the strongest installations push back. Clay accumulates irregularly. Suspended steel turns elegance into constraint. Found matter discolours. The old hall refuses to become silent.
The real achievement is not a finished cultural monument, but an institution that still appears capable of being changed by use.

For a centre opening without a permanent collection, this is the correct beginning. CCA Tashkent has created a compelling architectural and curatorial proposition. Its task now is slower and less photogenic: to build trust, critical independence, institutional memory and a public that does not experience contemporary art as an imported language. Wisdom, HIKMAH suggests, is not possessed at the moment of opening. It is produced through what a place learns to hold.
Visitor information

HIKMAH is on view at CCA Tashkent, Building B, 6 Amir Temur Street, Tashkent, through 31 January 2027. Admission is free. Visitors should consult the Centre’s official website for current opening hours, registration requirements and public events.

articles.title: Who Needs a Museum? The Urban Design of Invitation
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: A museum does not find its public at the ticket desk. It finds—or loses—it through transport, pavements, thresholds and the civic life of the street.

content.content: A museum visit rarely begins with art. It begins with a calculation: how long the trip will take, whether the route is legible, whether the entrance looks public, whether there is somewhere to pause, whether the building seems intended for people like us. The institution may own a major collection and charge nothing, yet still remain socially and spatially expensive. A free door at the end of an uncertain journey is not the same thing as access.

This is the central urban problem of mass culture. Museums are asked to serve a broad public, but they are often planned as singular objects: a landmark placed on a site, photographed from across a plaza and judged by what happens inside. Visitors experience something else. They encounter a chain of thresholds stretching from the timetable to the pavement, from the pavement to the forecourt, from the forecourt to security, and from security to the first room. Every threshold can convert a passer-by into a visitor—or quietly send them away.
The museum does not find its public at the ticket desk. It finds—or loses—it along the route through the city.
Who actually needs the museum?

The conventional answer is universal: everyone. It is morally attractive and operationally weak. Different publics need different things from the same institution. A tourist may need a recognisable destination and a predictable two-hour visit. A local resident may need a place that remains useful after the temporary exhibition closes. A parent needs toilets, seating and a route that works with a buggy. A teenager may need permission to enter without already knowing how to behave. A disabled visitor needs reliable information before leaving home, not an improvised solution at the door.

Participation data makes the limits of universality visible. England’s 2019–20 Taking Part survey found that 51 per cent of adults had visited a museum or gallery in the previous year; nearly half had not. Later Participation Survey data continued to show strong differences by education, occupation and deprivation. Free admission can increase total attendance without automatically changing who feels entitled, informed or able to attend. The museum’s public is not simply waiting outside. It is produced by transport, time, habit, social confidence and the design of the invitation.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3d/Tate_Modern_Turbine_Hall_2026-08-10.jpg
content.caption: Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, London, 2026. The monumental interior functions as a free civic room before it functions as gallery circulation. Photograph by Brett Jordan, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.alt: Visitors moving through the monumental Turbine Hall at Tate Modern.

content.content: Access is a sequence, not a radius

Urban plans often describe cultural access with circles: a museum lies within a ten-minute walk, or within a transit catchment. Distance matters, but the circle hides the journey. Recent research on perceived museum accessibility proposes a more useful sequence: pre-trip feasibility, comfort and predictability in transit, and usability on arrival. Two museums can be equally close in metres and radically different in practice. One route crosses active shopfronts and a shaded square; the other follows a blank wall, crosses six traffic lanes and ends at an entrance visible only after a security barrier.

The sequence suggests six forms of friction. Informational friction asks whether opening hours, price and access conditions are clear. Temporal friction measures the real time cost, including transfers and queues. Mobility friction includes broken pavements, unsafe crossings and missing step-free routes. Visual friction concerns whether the destination and door can be found. Social friction asks whether the approach signals welcome or surveillance. Procedural friction begins at the threshold: bag rules, ticketing, security and the uncertainty of where to go next.

No single architectural gesture removes all six. A spectacular canopy cannot repair an unreliable bus; free admission cannot make a hostile underpass comfortable; a transparent lobby cannot help if the only approach is a service road. The effective unit of museum design is therefore not the building but the complete visitor journey.
How to find a visitor in the street

The passer-by is not an empty category. Most people on a street already have a destination, a schedule and a reason for being there. To attract them, a museum must offer a low-risk interruption. The first requirement is visibility, but visibility is not the same as monumentality. A façade can be unmistakable and still conceal what entry involves. Useful visibility reveals activity: a foyer, a free installation, a café, people sitting, a route continuing through rather than terminating at the institution.

The second requirement is a reversible commitment. A person should be able to approach, look and leave without embarrassment or cost. Steps, forecourts, arcades, gardens and free halls can create this intermediate condition. The Metropolitan Museum’s steps are successful not because they funnel everyone efficiently through the doors but because they also operate as seating, meeting place and urban theatre. Their civic use allows the museum to enter ordinary routines before a ticket is considered.

The third requirement is information at the speed of walking. A street-facing message has seconds, not minutes. It should answer three questions: what can I see now, can I enter without booking, and how much time or money will it require? Institutional slogans answer none of them. A programme board, a visible free zone and a clear door do more work than a campaign about openness.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6e/Design_Museum%2C_Kensington_-_London_-_DSC01548.jpg
content.caption: The Design Museum in Kensington: a museum threshold situated between the high street, housing and Holland Park. Photograph by Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.alt: High-resolution architectural view of the Design Museum in Kensington, London.

content.content: Not every street can do the same job

The ideal museum street is often imagined as busy, central and mixed-use. That is only one model. A high street supplies continuous footfall, public transport and reasons to combine a visit with other errands. A park edge supplies slower movement, family use and room for outdoor work. A waterfront supplies visibility and promenade traffic but may become empty in poor weather or after dark. A campus offers repeated local users but can feel territorial to outsiders. An industrial fringe provides scale and affordability while making spontaneous attendance harder.

The question is not whether a street is universally suitable. It is whether its existing movement patterns match the museum’s public mission. A venue dependent on school groups needs coach access and safe group assembly. A contemporary art hall seeking young local audiences needs evening transit, ordinary food nearby and a threshold that does not read as ceremonial. A sculpture museum can use a park as an open collection, while a fragile archive may require a more controlled edge. The programme and the street must be designed as one system.

Four street conditions are consistently valuable: a continuous pedestrian route, enough dwell space near the entrance, active uses that extend beyond museum hours, and more than one reason to be there. Footfall alone is not enough. Commuters moving through a narrow interchange may be numerous but unavailable. A smaller flow that already slows down—to sit, meet, eat, watch or cross a park—can be more convertible.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Berlin_Neue_Nationalgalerie_asv2021-11_img1.jpg
content.caption: Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin: the museum begins on an elevated civic platform before the glass hall. Photograph by A. Savin, Free Art License, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.alt: Neue Nationalgalerie and its open public platform in Berlin.

content.content: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/HK_YTM_%E8%A5%BF%E4%B9%9D%E9%BE%8D%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E5%8D%80_West_Kowloon_Cultural_District_M%2B_Plus_Museum_%E5%A4%A9%E5%8F%B0%E8%8A%B1%E5%9C%92_roof_garden_view_Victoria_Harbour_%E9%BB%83%E6%98%8F_%E6%97%A5%E8%90%BD_sunset_at_%E9%A6%99%E6%B8%AF%E6%95%85%E5%AE%AE%E5%8D%9A%E7%89%A9%E9%A4%A8_HK_Palace_Museum_July_2022_Px3_01.jpg
content.caption: M+ and the West Kowloon waterfront at sunset. Museum, roof garden, park and harbour form one continuous cultural landscape. Photograph by Bkemaoe HOMA, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.alt: Sunset view across the M+ roof garden and Victoria Harbour in Hong Kong.

content.content: Public art is not automatically public

Large sculpture and murals are frequently asked to solve the relationship between museum and city. They can establish orientation, make a route memorable and allow contact with art without admission. But scale and outdoor location do not guarantee publicness. A work on a fenced plaza, surrounded by traffic or presented without shade, seating or a safe crossing, remains formally public and practically remote.

Public art becomes urban infrastructure when it changes what a place permits. It may create a meeting point, mark an accessible route, provide shelter, hold a memory that commercial development would erase, or connect neighbourhoods across a barrier. This is a higher standard than visual impact. It asks who can approach the work, at what hours, under whose rules, and whether lingering is treated as legitimate.

The distinction also protects art from being reduced to placemaking equipment. Not every work must produce sociability or economic uplift. Critical, difficult and even obstructive art has a public role. The urban obligation lies with the setting: the city must provide the physical and civic conditions in which disagreement, curiosity and indifference can occur without purchase.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Mobile_M%2B_Inflation_temporary_Sculpture_Park_201305.jpg
content.caption: Mobile M+ Inflation in West Kowloon, 2013: temporary sculpture used the open park as exhibition space before the permanent museum opened. Photograph by See-ming Lee, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.alt: Visitors moving through a temporary outdoor sculpture park by M+ in Hong Kong.

content.content: The Bilbao problem
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/31/Guggenheim_-_Bilbao.jpg
content.caption: Guggenheim Bilbao at sunset, seen as part of the river landscape rather than as an isolated icon. Photograph by Thomas Fabian, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.alt: Wide sunset view of the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and the Nervión riverfront.

content.content: The Guggenheim Bilbao remains the unavoidable case because it turned a museum into a global image of urban change. The ‘Bilbao effect’ is commonly narrated as architectural causation: commission an extraordinary building and visitors, investment and confidence will follow. The account is incomplete. The museum belonged to a broader programme of riverfront remediation, transport investment, new public space and economic restructuring. The icon was powerful because the city had altered the systems around it.

Copying the object without those systems produces cultural isolation: a destination reached by visitors but weakly connected to local life. Regeneration can also redistribute value unevenly. Rising land prices, tourist retail and the branding of former industrial districts may displace the communities whose history supplied the area’s identity. A museum can be economically successful while narrowing the social meaning of its surroundings.

The relevant question is therefore not whether a museum increases visitor numbers, but how value circulates. Do local routes improve? Can residents use the landscape without buying admission? Are small businesses connected to the new footfall? Does the institution commission locally and provide routes into employment? Does the public realm remain public when the museum is closed? These questions turn impact from a headline into an urban account.
The free room before the collection

A museum can lower the institutional threshold by placing useful public rooms before the controlled galleries: foyer, library, toilets, café, seating, project space, education room or covered passage. Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall demonstrates the force of such a room. It is monumental, but its practical achievement is simpler: a visitor can enter an unmistakably cultural interior without first choosing an exhibition or demonstrating expertise.

This front room should not be confused with a retail lobby. Its success depends on non-commercial permission. If every chair belongs to a café, if security challenges people who are waiting, or if the free route is visually subordinate to the ticketed one, the promise collapses. The best threshold spaces support several durations: two minutes to orient oneself, twenty minutes to meet someone, an hour to work, or an afternoon that gradually becomes a museum visit.
Inside, the city continues

Crossing the door does not end the urban problem. Museum circulation distributes attention much as streets distribute movement. Visitors follow visible openings, other people, landmarks and perceived shortcuts. A century of visitor studies shows that path choice cannot be reduced to a universal rule such as always turning right. Layout, attraction, prior knowledge, crowding and individual purpose interact.

Good wayfinding is not the multiplication of signs. It begins with an intelligible spatial structure: a visible next destination, distinguishable routes, places to stop without blocking movement and a reliable way back. Digital navigation can assist, but it cannot repair a plan in which every threshold looks identical or the main stair is hidden. The museum should allow both a concise route for a first-time visitor and lateral choices for return visits.

The deepest connection between museum and city is therefore behavioural. Both should permit orientation without demanding obedience. A successful museum route offers enough structure to reduce anxiety and enough choice to sustain discovery. That balance is especially important for visitors who do not arrive with a learned museum habit.
Three tests for the museum edge

Three influential accounts of public life sharpen the museum’s urban obligations. They do not provide a style guide. Each offers a test: whether the edge is watched and inhabited, whether life precedes form, and whether visitors can act rather than merely receive.
The inhabited edge
“There must be eyes upon the street, eyes belonging to those we might call the natural proprietors of the street.” — Jane Jacobs

Jacobs’s “eyes upon the street” are often reduced to passive surveillance. Her larger point is about reciprocal confidence produced by ordinary activity. Applied to a museum, it asks whether the ground floor contributes doors, windows, work, seating and repeated local presence—or only a guarded façade. The museum edge becomes safer and more public when people have reasons to inhabit it that are not limited to exhibition attendance.
Life before form
“First life, then spaces, then buildings—the other way around never works.” — Jan Gehl

Gehl reverses the usual museum competition, in which a building is commissioned first and public behaviour is expected to follow. His sequence begins with observation: who already walks, waits, plays, works and meets here; at what hours; in what weather; and with what physical constraints? Space can then support those patterns and create new ones. The building comes last as a participant in public life, not its substitute.
From audience to participant
“A place where visitors can create, share, and connect with each other around content.” — Nina Simon

Simon’s participatory museum shifts the public from demographic target to cultural actor. Urbanistically, participation begins before a workshop or comment wall. Can people appropriate the steps, hall or garden for meeting and informal use? Can local knowledge enter the institution’s programme? A threshold that tolerates only the behaviour designed by the museum contradicts participation even when the exhibition invites feedback.

Together, the three tests form a demanding sequence. Jacobs asks whether everyday life makes the edge trustworthy. Gehl asks whether observed human activity shaped the space. Simon asks whether the institution gives visitors meaningful agency. A museum can pass one and fail the others: it may be busy but non-participatory, beautifully scaled but socially controlled, or participatory inside while remaining forbidding from the street.
A practical test for the museum street

Before approving a cultural building, planners and institutions should walk the complete route with several users and record the points of uncertainty. Can the entrance be identified from the nearest stop? Is every crossing legal, direct and step-free? Can a person pause near the door without buying anything? Is the current programme legible from the pavement? Are opening hours and prices visible before the security line? Does the ground floor reveal a public use? Is there a reason to remain when the galleries are closed?

They should also measure what conventional attendance figures miss: how many people use the forecourt without entering, which approaches are avoided, where groups wait, when the edge becomes empty, how often passers-by ask security for directions, and whether local residents return for non-exhibition uses. These observations reveal whether the institution is a public place or merely a publicised object.
A museum becomes civic when the city can use it before deciding to visit it.
The museum as an agreement with the street

Mass art does not mean art simplified for the largest possible audience. It means the possibility of encounter is distributed broadly enough that knowledge, confidence and money are not prerequisites for crossing the threshold. Architecture cannot accomplish this alone, but it can make exclusion easier or harder. So can the bus timetable, the crossing signal, the bench, the programme board, the guard’s instructions and the price of an hour.

The museum’s urban task is not to capture every passer-by. It is to make approach understandable, entry reversible and return plausible. Some people will use the steps and never see the collection. Some will come for the café, the view, the toilet, the library or the shelter. This is not leakage from the institution’s purpose. It is the process by which an institution becomes part of ordinary civic life—and by which a passer-by may eventually become a visitor on their own terms.
