The Southern solution was the most expensive and the most colossal: to dig an entirely new river across the Horta, from Quart de Poblet to the sea near Pinedo. The Council of Ministers chose it on 22 July 1958, and a law of 1961 set out how it would be paid for, including a detail every Valencian of that generation remembers: for as long as the works lasted, every letter and parcel posted in Valencia carried an extra 25-céntimo stamp for the river.

Work under the Júcar River Basin Authority began in the mid-1960s. Franco inspected the finished channel on 22 December 1969, and by around 1973 the Turia no longer ran through the city. The new course is 11,868 metres long, 175 metres wide for most of its length and 200 metres near the sea, and was designed to carry 5,000 cubic metres of water a second. Its banks became a ring road, today's V-30. And in the middle of Valencia it left a long, dry, empty space, which the plans of the 1960s had already assigned to motorways and a transport axis linking the port and the airport.
The riverbed is ours

The motorway was never built, for two reasons that reinforced each other. The ring road along the new channel made a highway through the centre less necessary. And the city began to argue. From 1973 Las Provincias ran campaigns defending the riverbed, its five-hundred-year-old parapets and its bridges as heritage. Neighbourhood associations, in one of the first examples of organised citizen participation in Francoist Valencia, took up a slogan that is still painted into Valencian memory: El llit del Túria és nostre i el volem verd, the Turia riverbed is ours and we want it green. In 1976, a year after Franco's death, a decree signed by King Juan Carlos transferred the old bed to the city. In 1979 it was formally designated as green space and a public park.

What to plant there was another question. In 1981 the city commissioned a plan from Ricardo Bofill's Taller de Arquitectura, but only part of it was built; the final scheme approved in 1984 divided the riverbed into eighteen numbered sections, from Mislata to Natzaret, and gave them to different teams. Work began in 1985, and the first sections opened to the public in 1986 and 1987.

Bofill's own section is the most monumental: orange trees, palms, water and white neoclassical colonnades in front of the Palau de la Música. The concert hall was built under a national plan of 1983 to give every Spanish region an auditorium, and the site chosen for it, beside sections X and XI of the future garden, was a derelict industrial plot known as la Azufrera, the sulphur works. José María García de Paredes designed a glass-vaulted building that opened in 1987 and sits in the riverbed like a winter garden; Eduardo de Miguel extended it in 2003.

content.credit: Wikimedia Commons: Dorieo, CC BY-SA 4.0; Joanbanjo, CC BY-SA 3.0
content.caption: Colonnades and water in front of the Palau de la Música.

content.content: The rest of the garden changes character every few hundred metres, because it was designed by many hands. Vetges Tu i Mediterrània laid out sports pitches, meadows and fountains between the Casa del Agua and Nuevo Centro; the regional agriculture department planted an urban forest of thousands of pines between Nuevo Centro and Serranos; the architects Otegui, Gisbert and Noguera and the landscape architect Ángel Zurilla shaped further stretches. What holds it together is the one thing no designer invented, the line of the old river. Today the garden covers about 136 hectares, with an average width of 160 metres; the last sections towards the port, where groundwater still seeps into the old bed, are unfinished, and when they are done the park will be almost ten kilometres long and 160 hectares in size.

content.credit: Wikimedia Commons: Dorieo, CC BY-SA 4.0; Dorieo, CC BY-SA 3.0; Dorieo, CC BY-SA 4.0
content.caption: Sports pitches, pines and palms: different sections of the same riverbed.

content.content: A giant for the Lilliputians

In 1986 the city and the regional government commissioned a playground under a programme called Un riu de xiquets, a river of children. The architect Rafael Rivera and Manolo Martín, an artist who built falles, the enormous satirical figures Valencia burns every March, produced a design by Sento Llobell: Lemuel Gulliver, seventy metres long, tied to the ground at the moment he wakes in Lilliput. Children become the Lilliputians, climbing his coat, sliding down his hair and hiding in his pockets. It cost 220 million pesetas, entry is free, and after a renovation it reopened in November 2022. It is a playground, and also a quiet joke about the whole project: a city discovering what to do with a space that had suddenly become far larger than itself.

content.credit: Wikimedia Commons: Joanbanjo, CC BY-SA 4.0; Steven Lek, CC BY-SA 4.0
content.caption: The Gulliver playground, seen from a bridge and from the ground.

content.content: Crossing a river that isn't there

Because the garden is still a river in the city's mind, Valencia crosses it on bridges, more than twenty of them. The Pont del Mar, with ten pointed arches and 160 metres long, was for centuries the road to the port; in 1933 it became a footbridge, with stairs by the architect Javier Goerlich, and when the garden was made a round pool was placed beneath its arches. The Serranos bridge leads to the medieval city gate. Santiago Calatrava, born in Valencia, built his first bridge here, the Nou d'Octubre in 1989, and later the Pont de l'Exposició above the Alameda metro station, which locals call la peineta, the comb, and the Assut de l'Or, known as el jamonero after the stand used to slice ham.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu5turia-12.jpg
content.caption: One of Santiago Calatrava's bridges over the garden.

content.content: The eastern end belongs to Calatrava's City of Arts and Sciences, raised in the riverbed from the 1990s: L'Hemisfèric opened in 1998, the science museum in 2000, L'Umbracle in 2001, L'Oceanogràfic, with thin concrete shells by Félix Candela, in 2003, the Palau de les Arts in 2005 and L'Àgora in 2009. It became Valencia's postcard and one of its most argued-over projects: budgeted at around 300 million euros in 1991, it ended up costing about 1.2 billion. Seen from the garden, it reads as the loudest chapter of a story that began with mud in the streets.

content.credit: Wikimedia Commons: Javier Boadella, CC BY-SA 3.0; Esniom, CC BY-SA 4.0; José Luis Filpo Cabana, CC BY 3.0
content.caption: L'Hemisfèric and the Palau de les Arts; L'Àgora and the Assut de l'Or bridge; the garden near the Palau de les Arts.

content.content: October 2024

On 29 October 2024 another gota fría stalled over the region. The new channel of the Turia, dug after 1957, carried the flood past Valencia and the city centre stayed dry. South of it, the Poyo ravine, normally a dry bed running parallel to the river, rose past the maximum alert threshold of its single flow sensor; at 18:05 it registered almost 994 cubic metres a second, and the water poured through the towns of l'Horta Sud. More than two hundred people died in the province. In the following days thousands of volunteers walked from Valencia to the flooded towns across a footbridge over the new channel; it has since been named the Pont de la Solidaritat. Some experts point out that the channel protected the capital but not the wider plain around it, and that the lesson of 1957 was learned for one river rather than for the whole landscape.
What the garden teaches

The Turia Garden is usually described as a park. It is closer to an argument about what a city owes the people who live in it. The same empty bed could have become a fast road between the edges of Valencia; instead it became a slow line joining its neighbourhoods, where people walk, run and cycle from one end of the city to the other without meeting a car, and where the old bridges still frame views of a river that is no longer there.

Many cities now try to uncover buried rivers, tear down urban motorways or turn railway lines into parks. Valencia did something similar half a century ago, before it was fashionable, and for a reason that 2024 made painfully clear: people who had lived through a flood asked that the place of the disaster be given back to them green. The water was sent elsewhere. The memory stayed in the riverbed, and the city chose to walk through it every day.

Text: Viacheslav Munister for EPRIS Journal. Sources include the Spanish Wikipedia entries on the Plan Sur, the Jardín del Turia, the Parque Gulliver, the Palau de la Música and the October 2024 floods, and the Colegio Territorial de Arquitectos de Valencia. Photographs: Wikimedia Commons, authors and licences are given with each image.

articles.title: Inside the Victoria Museum
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Ukraine's first museum of costume, founded in a restored Kyiv mansion in 2017: over 1,500 objects across seven rooms, corseted silk gowns, a gold-braided court coat, cameos cut from shell, and the small objects, lockets, scent bottles, enamel boxes, that a life actually held.

content.content: The Victoria Museum sits behind an arched doorway a few steps off Khreshchatyk, in a nineteenth-century apartment building whose stucco cornices and rusticated ground floor give away nothing of what is inside. A small plaque by the entrance reads Victoria Museum — Музей костюма та стилю, the Museum of Costume and Style, open Thursday to Sunday. I went on a whim after a walk through the city centre, and stayed for most of the afternoon.

It's a younger institution than it feels. The collector Victoria Lysenko opened it on 30 May 2017, after nine months of preparation, as the first museum in Ukraine built entirely around historical dress. The building itself is older: a mansion raised in the late nineteenth century, left derelict from around 2000, and extensively restored in 2009, with the original balcony railings on the second and third floors kept rather than replaced. What Lysenko assembled inside now runs to more than 1,500 objects across seven rooms on two floors, over two hundred of them complete garments, alongside what the museum counts as the largest collection of fans in Ukraine, more than eighty of them. In 2022 it was presented at the European Museum of the Year Award; that same spring, on the forty-fifth day of the full-scale invasion, it reopened rather than stay closed.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/victoria-museum-17-facade-wide.jpg
content.caption: The museum's building, a restored nineteenth-century mansion off Khreshchatyk.

content.content: A wardrobe from another century

Room by room, the museum is built around clothing: dozens of women's gowns from the second half of the nineteenth century into the 1900s, most of them shown on mannequins inside glass cases, lit like the jewellery beside them. A deep purple velvet bodice trimmed with tatted lace stands beside a slate-blue silk skirt; a few steps on, a crinoline gown in a rust-red floral print from the 1860s balloons out under its own weight, the pattern of small roses running unbroken from waist to hem. One label, in Ukrainian and English, catalogues a dark chocolate-coloured dress with floral ornaments and buttons from the 1880s in the plain language of a museum inventory, cotton, velvet, that undersells how much handwork sits inside a single sleeve.

content.caption: A velvet bodice, an 1860s crinoline gown, and a chocolate-coloured dress from the 1880s, shown beside a period portrait and a gentleman's uniform coat.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/victoria-museum-18-gallery-row.jpg
content.caption: A full case of crinoline gowns from the 1850s–60s, each shown with its own shoes, fan or parasol and a matching portrait.

content.content: Further in, the colour gets bolder. A cropped coat cut from a brown, orange and cream paisley weave, lined in dark velvet, sits under a framed photograph of the woman it may have been made for, an unusual survival: paisley was for shawls and interiors more often than outerwear, and seeing the whole pattern wrap around a body rather than lie flat changes how you read it. Two cases along, an ivory gown drops its sleeves off the shoulder into a froth of tulle roses and pearl trim, the bodice hand-embroidered with sprays of leaves in a pattern that repeats down the full length of the train, evening dress built for a room with better lighting than daylight.

content.caption: A paisley coat lined in velvet, and an ivory evening gown embroidered with leaves and tulle roses.

content.content: Some pieces are display-cased tableaux rather than single garments. In one corner, a mourning dress hung with small framed photographs down its bodice stands beneath sepia portraits of the women who might have worn it, next to a folded parasol and a pale silk dress with a deep lace collar, a whole small theatre of a nineteenth-century household, assembled inside a single vitrine.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/victoria-museum-02-room.jpg
content.caption: A mourning gown hung with framed photographs, beside sepia portraits and a folded parasol.

content.content: Silk, braid, and a court coat

The collection isn't only for women's dress. A single red wool coat, cut like a courtier's or a footman's livery, is trimmed the length of both lapels and cuffs in wide gold metallic braid, closed with a column of domed brass buttons, the kind of formal coat that would have been made to a household's own pattern, not bought off a rail. Nearby, a cream silk bodice with a high boned collar carries the same embroidered lyre-and-scroll motif repeated at the shoulders, throat and hem, the sort of detail that only shows itself under a display light.

content.caption: A gold-braided court coat, and the repeated lyre motif on a cream silk bodice.

content.content: A case of men's accessories does the same close-looking trick from a different angle: a row of walking canes, their handles carved from bone and ivory into a bird's head, a lion, a laughing face, stand beside a white double-breasted summer coat with a black velvet collar, an old leather travelling bag and a single pair of high-buttoned boots, worn enough to have belonged to somebody. Two more gowns, one in dusty pink chiffon with a lace-trimmed train, one in pale cream silk with a beaded high collar, are shown against period portraits of women dressed almost identically, so the wall reads as evidence rather than decoration.

content.caption: Carved cane handles and a gentleman's summer coat; a pink chiffon gown and a cream silk dress, each shown beside its period portrait.

content.content: Cameos, lockets, and small boxes

A side room is given over to what would have sat on a dressing table or travelled in a pocket: rings and brooches set with painted miniature portraits, enamelled trinket boxes in cobalt blue and gold, a scent bottle on a chatelaine chain. On one wall, more than a dozen cameos, carved from shell, onyx and sardonyx, English and Italian, mostly nineteenth-century, are mounted in a single gilt frame like a cabinet of miniature paintings: a saint on horseback, a scroll of acanthus leaves, a woman's profile turned three-quarter to the light. The museum's fan collection, the largest in Ukraine by its own count, keeps company with the same cases: a hand-painted court scene on silk, its sticks carved and gilded, folds open beside a stack of enamelled boxes on a single glass shelf.

content.caption: Cameo brooches, rings and enamel boxes from the museum's jewellery cases.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/victoria-museum-19-fan.jpg
content.caption: A hand-painted, gilded fan from the museum's collection, the largest of its kind in Ukraine.

content.content: Paintings and a bronze figure, for context

The clothes are hung against a backdrop of paintings and objects from the same decades: a French Madonna and Child with John the Baptist from the early nineteenth century, gilt-framed portraits of women in the same silhouettes the mannequins wear, a bronze figurine of a woman in a plumed hat holding a fan halfway to her face. None of it is didactic. There's no long wall text explaining the history of the corset or the politics of mourning dress; the museum mostly lets the objects sit close enough together to make their own argument about a period that dressed itself with tremendous, specific care.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/victoria-museum-11-bronze-madonna.jpg
content.caption: A bronze figure and a French Madonna and Child, both nineteenth century.

content.content: The Victoria Museum is open Thursday to Sunday, 11:00–18:00, a short walk from Khreshchatyk. It's a small museum and an easy one to see in an hour, but I'd allow longer, the glass cases reward the kind of slow looking that a phone camera keeps interrupting.

articles.title: Two Ways of Looking at the Same Building - interview with Manuel Heywinkel
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Architect and photographer Manuel Heywinkel on photographing a building he spent years supervising into existence, why colour and black-and-white were never separate chapters for him, and a black-and-white show on a raw construction site that had to be called off days before it opened.

content.content: Manuel Heywinkel was photographing buildings before he was trained to design them. There was no year when the camera turned professional and no clean break between the two – architecture school and, later, work as a construction-supervising architect simply sharpened a habit that was already there, teaching him to notice geometry, sightlines and proportion almost without deciding to. Colour came first, for the ordinary reason that it came before digital did; black-and-white arrived later, once post-processing and then Instagram gave it somewhere to live. He treats the two as equally valid today, decided case by case, image by image.

The clearest instance of both roles meeting in one place is the LernWerk in Bocholt – the conversion of the former Herding spinning mill, where Heywinkel spent years as project lead for ACMS and photographed the building throughout construction, not after it. Cast-iron columns from the original mill were kept and picked out in colour; a new, contemporary volume was inserted in a fibreglass-mesh cladding that quietly echoes the site's textile past. Old and new, as he puts it, stay legible as distinct layers of time and still stand in relation to each other.

His exhibition record runs in both registers too. FARBRAUM, running through 30 September at Galerie im Turm in Wuppertal with guest photographer Andreas Kretzschmar, extends colour photography into the room itself with passe-partouts and backing fabrics matched to each image – a deliberate answer to 2025's all-black-and-white show at the same venue. A third show, Black & White in Unfinished Core, was planned for a raw, unheated construction shell on Moltkestrasse in Essen – fine-art prints on acrylic glass staged inside bare concrete and unfinished masonry, admission by invitation only – and had to be called off at short notice, when days of bad weather made the site too risky for visitors. The idea itself, he says, is far from finished, and he hopes to find a suitable location for it one day. Two of his staircase images independently made the jury's Top 50 at the SPC competitions – Treppe im Kunstpalast Düsseldorf in Berlin, Treppe im Museum Küppersmühle in Duisburg in Cologne – while a third, of a ceiling light in his mother's living room, took fourth place in Cologne's public vote. Docu Magazine has run two issues of his work, and one image – Tiger & Turtle, the public sculpture in Duisburg – was shown at the Black & White International Photography Awards Exhibition at One Art Space, New York, in June 2026.
We spoke with Manuel about photographing a building he was also professionally responsible for, why staircases keep pulling him back, and what a jury looks for that a public vote doesn't.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mudny8penqaccw.jpg
content.caption: LernWerk, Bocholt – completed. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: 01 · Two ways of seeing

Viacheslav Munister [VM]: You work on architecture both as an architect and, since long before that was your job, as a photographer. Has your eye for architecture changed in any way you can point to – and where do colour and black-and-white each come in?

Manuel Heywinkel [MH]: I've been photographing since I was very young, and architecture was one of my subjects almost from the start, so I can't name a moment when my eye for it changed fundamentally. When I was younger I also spent a good deal of time on film and video, making animated films among other things, before photography moved back to the centre.

Studying architecture, and later working as an architect, sharpened that eye considerably. You start paying much closer attention to geometry, line, vanishing points, proportion, spatial relationships – a lot of it happens automatically by now. Interestingly, before digital photography I shot almost exclusively in colour. Black-and-white came later, mainly once digital editing made it easier and then once I started posting on Instagram. Today the two are equal for me as forms of expression – I decide per image which one actually works for it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjdvd3mpagd.jpg
content.caption: DZ BANK, Frankfurt am Main, 1996. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: Was there a specific photograph or moment where documentation stopped being enough and it became a more deliberate, composed way of looking at architecture – or were the two always tied together for you?

MH: I can't name a specific moment – the more deliberate way of seeing developed continuously rather than arriving all at once. Today I notice details much more consciously, but also the sightlines between parts of a building, or between different buildings, and the urban context around them: how a building sits in its surroundings, how it responds to them, what perspectives that creates. It's exactly out of those relationships that interesting lines, vanishing points and perspectives tend to emerge for me – and years of close engagement with architecture have made that way of looking steadily more conscious.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjem8t5dujd.jpg
content.caption: Potsdamer Platz, Berlin, 2024. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: 02 · The LernWerk

VM: The LernWerk in Bocholt is a building you supervised as an architect over years and photographed throughout that same time, not after the fact. Does watching a building you're also professionally responsible for change what you see in it – do things show up that the strictly professional view might miss?

MH: It isn't always easy in the middle of a construction site. As the architect supervising the build, you're deeply embedded in the daily process – coordinating contractors, sorting out agreements, and above all quality-checking the work that's been done. That inevitably narrows your focus to individual details and immediate tasks a lot of the time.

Which is exactly why it matters to step back periodically and see the emerging building as a whole again. My photographic eye helps with that, I think – I keep trying to take a step back and not just see the detail or the current problem, but the space, the architecture, what's actually taking shape there. On a project you're following over a long stretch of time, it's easy to otherwise lose sight of how the building is developing as a whole.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjfbjjfgda9.jpg
content.caption: LernWerk under construction, Bocholt, 2022. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: Is there one image in the series where the coexistence of the old mill and the new building reads most clearly to you?

MH: That depends a great deal on the design itself first. At the LernWerk, a central idea was developing the historic fabric for a new, contemporary use and reinforcing it technically without covering over the building's history. You can see that, for instance, in the original cast-iron columns – they were largely preserved and deliberately highlighted through their colour treatment. At the same time, the newly inserted cube introduces a clearly contemporary element into the existing fabric; its fibreglass-mesh cladding in turn references the building's original use as a spinning mill.
I find exactly that juxtaposition compelling: old and new stay legible as distinct layers of time, and still stand in relation to each other.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjfs9nlf4ec.jpg
content.caption: LernWerk, Bocholt, 2025. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: How do the architect's eye and the photographer's eye actually divide the work on a project like this – are there moments where one has to consciously take the lead?

MH: In the daily rhythm of a construction site, the architect's view naturally comes first – checking completed work, coordinating the process, communicating with the client and the tradespeople, and at the LernWerk, eventually with the building's future users and to some extent the public. Part of the job is also thinking ahead rather than only at the current detail: what comes next, how does one decision affect other work, how does it all come together in the end?

The shift into photographing isn't that different, actually. There too I can focus very tightly on a detail, a line, a specific situation, and then deliberately let go of it again to take in the space or the building as a whole. The two ways of seeing complement each other well for me.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjgc0dyneed.jpg
content.caption: LernWerk, Bocholt, 2025. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: 03 · Recurring motifs

VM: Staircases keep returning across your work – Schwerin Palace, Düsseldorf's Kunstpalast, the Museum Küppersmühle in Duisburg, the Ruhr Museum on the Zeche Zollverein site in Essen. What is it about a staircase that keeps pulling you back?

MH: A staircase is far more, for me, than a building component that connects a building's levels. Historically, staircases were often deliberately staged elements of representation – in palaces especially, they could be a direct expression of power, rank and importance.

Photographically I find them just as compelling. Their construction almost automatically offers interesting sightlines, vanishing points, repeating lines and perspectives – the same staircase can look completely different depending on where you stand. Maybe that's exactly the fascination: a staircase serves one unambiguous function and, at the same time, offers an almost unlimited number of ways to interpret it, architecturally and photographically.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjh1tfqbpy4.jpg
content.caption: Staircases, Aachen / Schwerin, 2026. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: Your Zeche Zollverein images show a place that was once industry and is now a monument – a coking plant, reflections, machinery nobody operates anymore. How do you approach a site with that much history without the picture becoming a mere illustration of it?

MH: What strikes me first about old industrial sites is the sheer scale of the engineering achievement. Looking at Zeche Zollverein, or other large industrial complexes, it's worth remembering these complex structures were planned and built at a time with no computers, no CAD – much of it was still drawn by hand at the drafting table, something I learned to do myself as a trained architectural draughtsman.

Walking through a site like that today, I often find myself wondering what function a given building, machine, pipe or structure originally served. Now everything stands still. You can only imagine the working life that went on there, and probably only imagine, at that, the physical effort some of that work demanded. At the same time, these sites are photographically extraordinary – the sheer range of structures, materials, pipework, technical detail and large spatial relationships offers an enormous variety of motifs and perspectives. Zeche Zollverein is a very good example of that.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjhemdnlxvv.jpg
content.caption: Zeche Zollverein, Essen, 2026. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: What draws you to exploring different cities photographically, and what decides which motifs from a city become a series?

MH: Cities don't interest me only for their architecture. I'm also drawn to their history – why certain things emerged in a particular place, how a city became what it is today. With Frankfurt, for instance, I'm interested in how it grew into a major trade-fair city, but also its history as an imperial coronation city with its Kaiserdom. Other cities raise entirely different questions. Bielefeld is my hometown; Freiburg has a completely different character; Düsseldorf another again. Every city has its own charm, its own vibe.

So I'm interested not just in the historic building stock or the modern architecture, but in the life in between: how people use their city, move through it, engage with the spaces available to them. That's what I try to capture, alongside the architectural photography, through street photography as well.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjic1o2z5ev.jpg
content.caption: Street photography, Berlin / Freiburg / Nuremberg, 2024–2025. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: 04 · Black-and-white and colour

VM: After your black-and-white show at FotoForum Wuppertal in 2025, your current exhibition FARBRAUM deliberately shows colour work. What led to that decision, and what does colour open up for you as a photographic tool that black-and-white doesn't?
MH: For FARBRAUM, still on show now, I decided on colour photography quite deliberately from the start – partly as a counterpoint to last year's show, where I showed exclusively black-and-white work.

My basic idea was not to confine the colour to the image itself, but to carry it into the room. I did that with passe-partouts matched in colour to each photograph, and for individual works, matching fabric behind the image as well. That way the image's colour continues into the space around it and shapes how it's perceived and its mood at the same time.

Colour matters to me as a design tool in architecture too, for what it's worth. Architecture can of course work very deliberately with a reduced, white palette and achieve a completely different effect that way. But deliberately applied colour can emphasise spaces, surfaces and proportions and change how they're perceived – with lighting conditions playing an important role there as well. That interplay of image, colour and space is the whole premise of FARBRAUM.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjiltv4thju.jpg
content.caption: FARBRAUM exhibition, Wuppertal, 2026. Photo: Anatolii FotoForum

content.content: VM: Why plan a black-and-white show for an unfinished space rather than a conventional white-walled gallery?

MH: The underlying idea for that show, too, was to connect architecture and photography directly. I wanted to present high-quality, precisely finished architectural photographs on acrylic glass inside a deliberately unfinished setting – a raw construction shell, exposed concrete, unplastered masonry, all the traces of an ongoing build.

That contrast was exactly what drew me: the finished image inside the unfinished room. The photographs show architecture in a resolved, completed form, while the exhibition space itself was still mid-process.

Unfortunately I had to cancel the show on short notice for safety reasons. Weather conditions in the days beforehand made the risk to visitors on an active construction site simply too high. The concept itself is by no means dead, though – it's still in the back of my mind, and since I deal with construction sites regularly through my work, I'm hoping to eventually find the right location to still make it happen.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjj18bzk894.jpg
content.caption: Construction site, Essen, 2026. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: What did putting together l'une et l'autre – your Cologne show with Monika Geisler – teach you about your own work that you wouldn't have noticed alone?

MH: What I found especially interesting about the Cologne show was that we combined photographs with quite different styles and approaches, and still found surprisingly strong connections between many of the pieces – in content or in form.

So we deliberately paired images, placing works side by side that look very different at first glance but engage with similar motifs, shapes or structures. A good example: Monika Geisler's photograph of a snail next to my photograph of the spiral staircase inside Berlin's Siegessäule – two completely different subjects, and yet the similarity in form creates an immediate connection.

Putting the show together, I was genuinely surprised how many such relationships emerged between individual works. It was exactly those different photographic perspectives on related forms and themes that ended up being the particular appeal of the show, for me.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjju43oelus.jpg
content.caption: Snail / the staircase up to the Victoria, Berlin, 2024. Photos: Monika Geisler / Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: 05 · Juries, print, a room in New York

VM: Two of your staircase images independently made the jury's Top 50 at the SPC competitions, while a third – of a ceiling light in your mother's living room – took fourth place in the public vote. What does that split tell you about the difference between what a jury looks for and what actually reaches an audience?

MH: I was of course very pleased that two of my staircase images were selected by the jury for the Top 50, even though neither placed in the actual competition. What I found even more interesting was that my image Unter der Decke – showing a ceiling light in my mother's living room – came fourth in the Cologne public vote.

A specialist jury engages with submitted work in a targeted, comparative way. Depending on the jurors' own photographic backgrounds, things like composition, technical execution, craft, or how a theme is handled can carry particular weight. With the public, the immediate personal or emotional response probably plays a stronger role – what speaks to me right away, what excites me about an image, does the motif remind me of something I've experienced or seen myself? That doesn't mean the public is blind to technical or formal qualities, of course. But a personal connection to an image can weigh more heavily in a public vote.
That's exactly why I find both forms of judgment interesting – they show how differently photographic work can be perceived.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjkbj8xyjaz.jpg
content.caption: Kunstpalast Düsseldorf / Museum Küppersmühle (MKM), Duisburg / “Unter der Decke”, 2025. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: VM: What changes about an image once you know it will be seen printed and bound, not just on a screen?

MH: I don't actually distinguish, while shooting, based on where or in what form an image will later be shown. Whether it ends up on Instagram, in a magazine, or in an exhibition is secondary at the moment of taking it – what has to work first is the subject, the composition, the way it's built.

When an image is later selected for a show or a publication, that's obviously very gratifying. I was especially pleased that my photograph of Tiger & Turtle was shown as part of an exhibition in New York – it meant something to present a piece of my own work in that kind of international setting. And I liked the thought that, with Tiger & Turtle, I was showing a motif from Duisburg – and with it, a piece of North Rhine-Westphalia and Germany.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjkpz9vxoyj.jpg
content.caption: Tiger & Turtle, Duisburg. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: 06 · Looking forward

VM: Comparing today's work to your first architectural photographs – as both architect and photographer – what's changed the most in how you look? And what are you still looking for in either role that you haven't found yet?

MH: Today I seek out and look at architecture far more deliberately than I used to. Things I might once have photographed almost in passing, as a young photographer, I now go looking for quite consciously.

I research particular buildings and places in advance and think about what might interest me photographically there. Often that's museums, but just as often other publicly accessible buildings – and, naturally, places that aren't normally accessible hold a particular appeal. My professional work sometimes opens up the chance to photograph buildings during construction, or shortly before completion – before they go into use and become accessible to the public. Photographically that's very exciting, because you get to experience spaces in a state that won't exist again once they're in use.

Next up is a joint exhibition with Petra Baumgart and Andreas Kretzschmar at the IKIGAI-Raum in Cologne, and I'll be taking part in the SPC in Cologne again. What the new year brings beyond that, we'll see. Further PhotoWalks are being planned, among other places at Zeche Zollverein and in Berlin, but for now these really are plans rather than fixed dates.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjlyxofuxlr.jpg
content.caption: Freilichtmuseum Detmold under construction, 2026. Photo: Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubhjlk5lngzr1.jpg
content.caption: Flyer for the exhibition “Daseinsräume”, IKIGAI-Raum, Cologne, 13–15 November 2026. Works: Petra Baumgart, Andreas Kretzschmar, Manuel Heywinkel

content.content: Manuel Heywinkel’s photography can be seen at manuel-heywinkel.com, his work as an architect at acms-architekten.de, on Instagram at @manuel_242neo and on 1x at 1x.com/manuelheywinkel. Images © Manuel Heywinkel unless credited otherwise; published with permission.

articles.title: The Red Thread: Veronika Chernienko on Painting What Words Can't Reach
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Veronika Chernienko
articles.excerpt: Ukrainian painter Veronika Chernienko, trained at the Kyiv academy and based on Cyprus since 2014, on why she calls herself a colourist before anything else, the recurring red thread that runs through her most personal work, and the biennial sketch about home and distance that she still can't look at without crying.

content.content: Veronika Chernienko paints the way she was trained to at the Kyiv academy she still calls home, and paints against it in the same breath. A colourist first, she says, before she is anything else – someone who works from the conviction that colour, not drawing, carries what she actually wants to say.

She left Ukraine for Cyprus in 2014, and for years her painting barely registered the move: the palette stayed hers, the subjects stayed the human figure. What changed the work was not geography but the war. Since 2022 she has painted more, and differently – not always about the war directly, but carrying its aftershock in every canvas: vulnerability, the need for shelter, a search for roots and for the people left behind. A recurring red thread, tied around a wrist or trailing into water, is not a fixed symbol for her so much as a nerve that different paintings touch for different reasons.

One of those paintings – a child curled in the exposed roots of a tree, a red thread running through the whole composition – was made for a 2023 biennial in Larnaca on the theme of a home far from home. It was not selected. She still cannot look at it without crying.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljntzt73dx1.jpg
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, untitled (a child among roots), oil on canvas – the sketch made for the 2023 Larnaca biennial, not selected

content.content: 01 · Where the training came from
Viacheslav Munister [VM]: Could you introduce yourself and outline the path that brought you from your training to your practice today, based in Cyprus?

Veronika Chernienko [VC]: I've been painting since early childhood – it was always a natural part of my life. At twelve I entered an art boarding school in Kyiv, and later graduated from the National Academy of Fine Arts and Architecture with a master's in easel painting. Toward the end of my studies I joined the National Union of Artists of Ukraine and took part in Ukrainian and international exhibitions.

When my family and children came along, I focused for a while on painting for myself. In 2014 we moved to Cyprus, where I joined the local art community, painted portraits on commission, did wall murals, and taught children – including preparing them for entrance to art school. The circumstances and forms of the work kept changing, but the daily practice never left me. I always felt painting was my profession and my calling.

With the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine, I began painting especially intensively – painting helped me live through what I had no words for. Even when a work doesn't address the war directly, it carries an echo of what I've lived through: a sense of vulnerability, a need for protection, a search for support and for connection to my roots. Through the human body and its gestures, I speak about an inner pain that isn't always visible from outside.

It was on Cyprus, among artists from many countries, that I understood more deeply the distinctiveness of the Ukrainian school of painting that shaped me – I saw the richness of our palette and the boldness of our colour and imagery with new eyes. Today it matters to me to keep developing that inheritance in my own work and to pass it on to my students, to keep a living connection to the culture that raised me and that I carry with me.
VM: Could you place your training within a specific pedagogical tradition, and how much do you see your current work as a continuation of it, or a departure from it?

VC: My education belongs to the Ukrainian academic school of painting. I studied in the workshop of Oleksandr Lopukhov – our graduating class was, sadly, his last. Composition and the genre picture were the foundation there. At the same time we worked a great deal with Ihor Yulianovych Melnychuk, whose approach is marked by decorative sensibility and a bold, saturated palette. It was the combination of the two that formed how I see a painting.

Field practice mattered enormously. We spent long stretches in the Carpathians and in Transcarpathia, painting from life, studying the local culture and customs. Ukrainian motifs became part of my personal experience. Even in those student years, when many were looking for themselves outside the academic school, I was glad to belong to the Ukrainian tradition of realism and impressionism. The human being, and the theme of Ukraine, have stayed with me since.

At the same time, I feel today that I've moved away from academicism and from the need to follow rules. In a world that keeps changing, with so much creative freedom available, I've allowed myself to do what I want – to trust my own sense of colour and form, and to follow where the work itself leads. I rely on intuition more and more, but it's an intuition that grew out of deep training and years of practice. The school became an inner foundation that gives me the freedom to experiment. And the simple joy of the process itself matters enormously to me – I get real pleasure from what I do.
02 · A colourist's worldview
VM: How would you describe your practice as a whole to someone encountering it for the first time – what should they understand before anything else?

VC: My practice begins with an attentive, enamoured look at the world. I have a weakness for admiring everything alive – I love watching nature, the movement of light, reflections and colour echoes. Seeing the world through a painter's eyes feels natural to me: I'm constantly noticing combinations of colour and barely perceptible shifts that I want to carry onto canvas.

Above all, I feel myself to be a colourist. It's through colour, more than through form, that I convey my perception and what I'm living through. Even when the world holds so much pain, I'm captivated by how everything alive around us keeps changing without pause, and I want to carry that feeling into my painting.

I want to show the viewer what I see, and what they might otherwise pass by. To invite them to stop, look closer, and feel. What matters most to me is that the colour touches a person – that it calls up a memory of their own, a feeling, a new sense of something familiar.
03 · Cyprus and what geography did not change

VM: Displacement from Ukraine to Cyprus is a fact of your biography. Is it also a fact of your painting – does geography enter as subject, as light and palette, or does it stay outside the work itself?

VC: A different culture and landscape can certainly change how an artist works. But I can't say the move to Cyprus significantly changed my palette or my range of subjects. I keep painting what is close to me, drawing on a way of seeing that formed in Ukraine.

Even when I turn to the Cypriot landscape, I see it through my own experience, and render it in my own manner and colour relationships. What interests me is what image of this place can be born from that particular gaze – I feel it will differ from the Mediterranean painting I encounter here. It's precisely on Cyprus, among artists from different countries, that I notice most clearly the differences in our painterly approaches, and recognise what the Ukrainian school gave me.

Plein-air practice never really took root for me here, though I've tried more than once to return to it. I mostly work at home, and paint a great deal of figurative work. The human being and their inner world stay at the centre of my attention.

With the start of the full-scale war I joined volunteer work at the Ukrainian House in Cyprus, where I teach Ukrainian children. Together we keep our artistic tradition alive, turn to Ukrainian imagery, work with colour. It matters to me that children growing up abroad feel a living connection to their culture and can develop it in their own work. I see this, too, as a continuation of a path that began in Ukraine.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljrtgp6kqn4.jpg
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, three women in traditional headdress, oil on canvas

content.content: 04 · Sources, and standing apart from lineage

VM: Beyond direct observation, what is your primary source of visual reference – art-historical precedent, photography, something else – and how consciously do you place your own work within a lineage of painters?

VC: My paintings are born from a combination of sources: studies, photographs, gestures I've seen, observation. Most often I turn to photography – it's convenient working material, and experience lets me reinterpret it freely. But working from life remains irreplaceable. Here on Cyprus, in our art community, we still work with a live model, and I value that greatly. When a photograph isn't enough, I go back to life, to look closer, to clarify, to feel what the image can't carry. Without that living experience, painting doesn't feel complete to me.

I often return to Ukrainian painters – Oleksandr Murashko, Viktor Zaretsky, Tetiana Holembievska, Tetiana Yablonska. My teachers had a great influence on me too. I also follow contemporary artists with interest, including those working alongside me on Cyprus. Everything I admire stays, to some degree, in my visual memory and shapes me.

At the same time, I don't place myself within any particular style, and I don't consciously try to follow a specific artist. While working I don't think about who my painting should resemble, or which tradition it continues. The knowledge, impressions and influences are already part of me – standing at the canvas, I trust my own sense of things and focus on what I want to convey.
05 · Still life and the figure – one language, not two

VM: Your still lifes pursue an almost hyperrealist finish, while the figurative work stays looser and more painterly. Are these two different languages for you, or one language used at different pressures?

VC: For me it's really one approach, in which the balance between precision and looseness shifts depending on what I want to convey. Academic training gives me an understanding of form, but photographic accuracy on its own isn't my goal. What captivates me is the chance to intensify what I've seen many times over – to sharpen colour, to underline the body's plasticity, to make felt what caught my attention.

Our everyday life is saturated with images, and I want to give the viewer a reason to let their eye linger. I take in the world through colour and plasticity, and I want to show what usually goes unnoticed. Sometimes that calls for careful modelling of form, sometimes for a large flat field of colour. The choice is often intuitive, made in the process of working.

The human figure remains an inexhaustible source of beauty and fascination for me. Through the body, its movement and gesture, I want to build an emotional connection with the viewer. At the same time, I'm captivated myself by painters who notice even finer nuances and show me things I hadn't seen before. That ongoing deepening of the eye is one of the greatest joys painting gives me.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljn4x009g9p.png
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, still life with antiquities, oil on canvas

content.content: 06 · Wall and canvas
VM: Working across mural and easel painting means moving from a public, site-specific scale to an intimate one. How does your approach change?

VC: Monumental and easel painting call for different approaches to composition, scale and the organisation of space – they're separate specialisations, and the academy has a dedicated monumental painting workshop. But I approach a wall as an easel painter: I treat it as a large canvas and carry my own way of working onto it.

It isn't natural for me to build an image out of large generalised masses and flat fills. I work with brushes, keep the painterly stroke, and build form, transitions, a sense of air through it. Even in black-and-white murals, that liveliness of the stroke matters to me. There's a particular appeal in that approach, one my clients value.

Of course, on a large surface that kind of work takes far more time, and I always warn people about that in advance. But I enjoy the process itself – I love working with a brush, watching an image slowly come alive. The scale changes; the pleasure of painting and my own approach stay with me.
07 · A turning point
VM: Looking at your practice over time, is there a specific body of work you'd identify as a turning point?

VC: There was a period of deliberate experiment in my practice. During the pandemic I became absorbed in the work of American realist painters – their restrained, dark palette, complex colour nuance, the fine handling of the painted surface. I tried to change both my colour range and my technique. A number of darker, more delicately rendered works came out of that period.

Over time I felt that manner wasn't close to me. The work found less response from viewers, and I understood, more and more clearly, that in that search I was moving away from myself. Now I'm returning to what I loved since childhood, and what captivates me in Ukrainian painting: bold, exaggerated colour, a broad stroke, freedom.

What turned out to be the real turning point was realising how important it is to trust my own nature. This is a return to myself, but with different experience and greater confidence in my own language.

My most personal works are born from a deep inner feeling. Knowledge and experience support me, but every time, something happens at the canvas that I can't fully predict or explain. Sometimes I feel it as a connection to something larger than myself – to God, to the world, to the very energy of life. What matters to me is staying open to that state and letting it guide my hand.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljmbjal4u75.jpg
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, figure on the shore, oil on canvas – the work Veronika names as her turning point

content.content: 08 · The red thread
VM: A recurring motif – a red thread bound around the wrist – punctuates an otherwise restrained body of work. What does it mean to you, and has its meaning shifted from painting to painting?
VC: I wouldn't call this motif a sign with one fixed meaning – it's born from the feeling behind each specific work.

I imagine you mean, first of all, the girl among the roots – the sketch for the 2023 Larnaca biennial on the theme 'a home far from home.' That painting still brings me to tears. In it, helplessness and a deep connection to home, to the people close to me, to Ukraine, come together. The red thread makes that invisible connection visible. Far from home it sometimes feels even stronger, even more painful – you can't embrace the people you love, but everything that happens to them passes through you. And at the same time, it's exactly that closeness that gathers us into a community, that helps us hold on to one another.
Sadly, the sketch wasn't selected. I don't know why. Perhaps the organisers didn't want to focus specifically on the Ukrainian experience of war and distance from home – but that's only my guess.

If you also mean the girl in the water, with a red ribbon in her hair – that painting is my reflection on the terrible violence in Bucha. Even now it's hard for me to talk about it: painting became a way to express a pain I had no words for.

So the meaning of the red accent shifts along with the painting itself. These images arose intuitively, from different experiences. What unites them is human vulnerability, and my own deep, personal response.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljp8gaeemeu.png
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, untitled (in the water), oil on canvas – a reflection on the violence in Bucha

content.content: VM: Certain works – like the piece addressing children's bound hands – engage directly with violence and vulnerability. Does that content change how you paint, technically?

VC: You may be thinking of the painting with the girl embracing her own shoulders, a red ribbon from her hair trailing down into the water. That work arose as my reflection on the terrible violence in Bucha.

That content certainly affects how I paint, even though my painterly vision stays recognisable. I become especially attentive to human vulnerability, and try to render it as gently and tenderly as I can. Some fragments of the figure I render more carefully, lingering longer on a gesture, on subtle value shifts and colour transitions. Through that attentiveness to the body, I try to convey an inner pain.

These shifts arise from the feeling itself, intuitively. Colour, stroke, and how far I take a form are all subordinated to what I feel in front of the canvas. I think the viewer can sense that tenderness and pain before they even learn the story behind the painting.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljqcas4meij.png
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, untitled, oil on canvas

content.content: 09 · What she cannot look at without crying
VM: Is there a work you consider technically or conceptually significant beyond its public reception?

VC: For me, that work is the girl among the roots with the red thread, which I've already mentioned. That sketch for the Larnaca biennial became a very personal statement about home, distance, and a bond that cannot be broken. In it, a person's helplessness meets the strength of their belonging – to the people close to them, to their land, to their community. I still can't look at that painting without tears.

The sketch wasn't selected, and it's painful to me that it didn't get the chance to be heard in the context it was made for. I don't know the reasons for that decision and can't explain it with any certainty. A work's personal significance doesn't always match its outside recognition.
Its value for me hasn't changed: in it I managed to convey a feeling that's still hard to put into words. I'd like that work to still have the chance to meet its viewer.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljoj26oe4d3.jpg
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, detail of the untitled roots painting

content.content: 10 · Knowing when to stop
VM: Your still-life practice pursues an almost hyperrealist finish, while the figurative work is much freer – how do you know when a painting is finished?

VC: For me a painting's completeness is decided by whether I've managed to convey what matters most. I often work alla prima, trying to capture the image at once, to keep the force of the first impression. Working fast matters to me. I used to see that impatience as something of a flaw, but over time it became a distinctive feature of my painterly language.

That's tied to my training too – we painted a great deal of studies en plein air, worked from live models outdoors, often in one or two layers. That practice taught me to focus on the essential. Long, many-layered work on a canvas isn't close to me, though commissioned still lifes, with their specific brief, sometimes demand more detail.

In my own work I stop when I feel I've said what I wanted to say. Areas of the canvas can stay unresolved, brushstrokes free, forms only suggested. For me those are spaces of the unsaid, where the viewer can feel and complete the image themselves. I don't want to overload the canvas – it matters to me that it breathes.
So what looks unfinished can, for me, be an entirely finished painting. I trust my own sense of that boundary, and I trust the viewer, too – not every detail needs explaining.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mubljr7h52mq34.jpg
content.caption: Veronika Chernienko, wedding scene, oil on canvas

content.content: Veronika Chernienko's work can be followed on Instagram at @artveronika_painting.

articles.title: Eight Years to a Home: Olha Wood on Building Across Distance, Pandemic and War
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Olha Wood
articles.excerpt: Interior architect Olha Wood works between Kyiv, Denmark and the UK, often without standing in the rooms she shapes. She talks about the Kyiv apartment that took eight years, one pandemic and a full scale war to finish, the house whose site was lost but whose concrete survived into another, and why every project she makes ends up reaching for the garden.

content.content: Olha Wood describes her practice in four lines on Instagram: interior architect, high end residential, international experience, remote collaboration with UK studios and private clients. It reads like a list of capabilities. It is closer to a description of a life. The studio began in Kyiv twenty five years ago and now works between Kyiv, Denmark and the United Kingdom, frequently without its architect standing inside the rooms she is shaping until very late in the process, if at all.

Her portfolio keeps unusually honest time. One Kyiv apartment is titled, simply, Eight Years to a Home: commissioned in 2018, moved to a different flat in the same building before construction could begin, redesigned around a terrace when the pandemic made private outdoor space essential, then carried through a full scale war its clients chose to stay in Kyiv for. A house on the Fish Island has been listed as in progress since 2020. The Bridge House carries the dates 2017 to 2026.

We wrote to her about what happens to buildings that have to wait, about designing a room around a sofa chosen years before the room existed, and about the thing she keeps returning to in every house she names: the garden, the terrace, the bridge, the way a building reaches for the ground it stands on.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojoeeixcct3.jpg
content.caption: An interior from the Kyiv practice where Olha Wood's studio began.

content.content: 01 · A practice shaped by places

Viacheslav Munister [VM]: Your Instagram bio reads “Interior Architect | High-End Residential | International Experience | Remote Collaboration with UK Studios & Private” – four lines that describe a practice built almost entirely around distance, flexibility and movement between places, rather than around one fixed studio in one fixed city. Your own portfolio bears that out: projects photographed in Kyiv, a house extension sketched for Tuscany, an island house visualised by a studio in another country entirely, clients across the UK. Was your practice always this dispersed, by temperament or by the nature of high-end residential work – or is this geography something the last several years specifically forced you to design, the way you might redesign a floor plan around a load-bearing wall that suddenly can't be moved?

Olha Wood [OW]: I was fortunate to begin my career in one of the strongest architectural studios in the city where I was born and educated. It was an unusually good place to start. At a time when many practices were concerned chiefly with the local market, they travelled to the Milan furniture fair each year, worked with Italian furniture – including Minotti – and designed interiors and penthouses of a kind that introduced me early to a world beyond my own city.
Perhaps this is why I never learned to think of architecture as something confined by geography.

A few years later, I began my own practice. My first client was a Ukrainian pop star. The beginning was almost disarmingly easy. I did not feel that I was entering an unknown profession; rather, I seemed simply to continue walking along a road I had already been travelling for years.

I entered competitions constantly. It was not only about winning, although I did take first places in several Ukrainian competitions. I wanted the work to exist outside the rooms in which it was made – to be looked at, questioned and placed beside the work of others.

In time, one of my projects was longlisted for the Dezeen Awards in 2018, and another was published on Dezeen. Those moments mattered to me not simply as distinctions, but because they allowed the work to travel further than I could.

My first international clients were a Slavic couple living in Hamburg. They had commissioned me to create an interior around Promemoria furniture, but wanted it to possess a distinctly Western European character. It was an interesting request: how does one create a sense of belonging to a place without merely reproducing its familiar images?

I was already spending considerable time in Britain then, because my future family lived in England. I travelled back and forth, and gradually absorbed something of the country – its architecture, its proportions, its restraint, its particular relationship between old and new. Much of what we absorb from a place happens without our noticing it at the time. A window, a staircase, the colour of a painted room, the way an old house has been altered rather than replaced – these things remain somewhere in the mind.
This has become one of the reasons I continue to prefer working with international clients.

Every country has its own domestic language. It lives not only in architecture, but in the way people arrange a table, choose a chair, preserve an old floor, tolerate an imperfection, or decide what deserves to remain. I find that learning these small distinctions is as important as understanding the larger architectural context.

This year I worked for a Danish couple, restructuring their bathroom and restyling the remaining rooms through decoration. It was another opportunity to look closely at a culture I had previously encountered professionally, but now from inside a private home.

I discovered more about the Danish market, but also returned to something I have always valued in Scandinavian design: objects that do not need to announce their importance. Ferm Living and House Doctor are not about the spectacle of high-end furniture. Their appeal lies elsewhere – in material, proportion, familiarity and the accumulated feeling of a domestic life.
Perhaps this is what I have been looking for throughout my twenty-five years of practice.
Not a particular style, and certainly not a particular country.
Rather, the possibility of entering someone else’s world for a while, understanding what belongs there, and making something that feels as though it could not have been made anywhere else.
02 · Eight years to a home

VM: One of your project pages narrates its own timeline with unusual honesty. A home was commissioned in 2018; the clients then discovered a different apartment in the same building, with a large terrace, and exchanged their original unit for it before construction could even begin. Then COVID arrived, and – in your words – “a garden on the terrace suddenly became more than an attractive addition to the brief... having a private outdoor space, somewhere to step outside without leaving home, became essential.” Then the full-scale war began, and your clients chose not to leave Kyiv. You call the project, simply, “Eight years to a Home.” At what specific point across those eight years – the apartment swap, the pandemic, or the war – did you notice yourself stop thinking of it as one job delayed by circumstance, and start thinking of it instead as a shared act of endurance between you and your clients?

OW: That is what I call responsibility – to the object, and to the people for whom it was made. It is painful to see a place intended for a family’s future remain silent and unfinished. A house is not simply an object that waits for completion; it waits for the life that is meant to happen within it.
So I kept reminding my clients with inspiration that the work was not finished. Perhaps there would come a moment when we would find the strength to return to it, and to finish what we had begun.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotcl9766io8.jpg
content.caption: Eight Years to a Home, Kyiv: the living and dining room, with the black Poliform cabinet by Piero Lissoni at the left.

content.content: VM: That same project's brief was, as you put it, “wonderfully specific”: your clients had always dreamed of particular pieces from Italian design houses – a Poliform cabinet, a B&B Italia sofa, an Antonio Lupi basin – items you describe as “not simply items on a shopping list, but part of the image of the home they wanted to create.” When a client arrives already attached to the exact sofa and the exact basin, sometimes years before the room around those objects even exists, how do you design that room so it reads as something more than a frame built to justify a purchase already made?
OW: Each piece of furniture has its own history – of material, place of origin, style and suitability.

The furniture selected by the clients often told me more about the future interior than a conventional brief could. My task was to bring these individual objects into a conversation with the architecture, the views from the windows and one another, so that the interior would acquire a coherent language rather than become a collection of beautiful things.

For example, the black Poliform cabinet, designed by Piero Lissoni, led me towards black-veneered wall panels of the same architectural restraint. The colour of the B&B Italia sofa became the starting point for the bespoke kitchen, whose ceramic fronts were made in a closely related shade.

The clients had a particular affection for Italy, and I wanted to acknowledge that without making the house feel as though it belonged elsewhere. The Ukrainian landscape outside the windows remained essential. I brought its yellow and brown tones inside through yellowish terrazzo, travertine and the warm grey of Little Greene’s Slaked Lime – Dark 151. The garden partly obscured the view, which I came to see not as a limitation but as something that gave the sitting room a sense of intimacy – a room held gently between the house and nature.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotdefcyl80p.jpg
content.caption: The material board for Eight Years to a Home: terrazzo, travertine and the warm grey of Little Greene's Slaked Lime Dark 151.

content.content: 03 · The projects that wait

VM: Your house on the Fish Island has been listed as “In Progress” since 2020 – a 450-square-metre concrete-and-steel structure, envisioned explicitly as a prototype for several future houses to be built on the same riverbank, built around a client's very particular list: a swimming pool, a fish pond, dedicated parking for a car collection, and three bedrooms, one for each of his children. Six years is a long time for a prototype to still be a work in progress. Has the house itself changed across those six years – in brief, in detail, in what “prototype” even means for the houses that might follow it – or has the delay simply been the ordinary friction of building something this large?
OW: This is perhaps one of the more painful questions I might be asked.

The building project was cancelled when my clients lost the plot of land. There is something particularly difficult about seeing a house that has been carefully imagined never acquire the life for which it was intended.

And yet, the work did not entirely disappear. The concrete structure and its carefully resolved junctions found a second life in another house that was later conceived for the same site and exists there today.

Perhaps this is one of the quieter truths of architectural work: an idea does not always arrive at its first destination. Sometimes part of it survives, altered by circumstance, and continues its life somewhere else.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotdvmmcdg5v.jpg
content.caption: House on the Fish Island: the section cut through pool and terrace, the structure set into the hill.

content.content: VM: The Bridge House has the longest visible timeline in your entire portfolio – 2017 to 2026, described on your own site as an “evolution of the architectural concept” rather than a single continuous build. Its plan is organised as three distinct pieces: a single-level Forest Pavilion designed to nearly disappear into the landscape, a two-storey Main House built around an internal atrium for daylight and privacy, and the Bridge itself, which your notes call “more than a circulation element... the architectural symbol of the project.” Between “Eight Years to a Home,” the Fish Island house still listed as in progress since 2020, and now a nine-year evolution on the Bridge House – is this simply what building privately in Ukraine over the last decade has looked like for everyone in your position, or is a project that's allowed to evolve across many years actually closer to how you'd choose to work even without a war or a pandemic pushing the timeline?
OW: The Bridge House was first called The House Above an Old Road in 2017.
I do agree that, looking at it now, it appears almost as a bridge between my past career and the work I do today.

Much of what I had learned through my years of working in the Netherlands and the UK found its place in this house. But its story is not only about a timeline. There was another, more personal connection: my client had lived and studied in the Netherlands for many years.
In a way, the materials became the language through which the three of us – the architect, the house and the client – were connected to that place.
We chose MIB GeoStylistix facing bricks, concrete junctions inspired by the House on the Fish Island, and Alpi veneer, which I had first discovered in Amsterdam.

Perhaps this is why the house has always felt to me like more than a project. It carries pieces of places, experience and memory from different periods of my life, brought together in one piece of architecture.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotea15zlq4v.jpg
content.caption: Bridge House: the Forest Pavilion, shaped around the trees that were kept rather than cleared.

content.content: 04 · Unbuilt, and still alive

VM: In Tuscany, you sketched an extension – 2024 – for what your own project notes describe as a “1 Euro House”: one of the abandoned homes Italian municipalities sell for a symbolic euro to buyers who commit to restoring them, in towns trying to survive depopulation. Your plan called for selectively demolishing the existing structure, removing an intermediate floor to create a double-height space, and building a new balcony to connect the old house to a new 60-square-metre extension. What drew you personally to a project built on a premise so different from the rest of your portfolio – not a client with an unlimited wish-list, but a near-abandoned building in a town that is, in its own way, asking to be saved?

OW: It was a precious time to learn and to create a house for my friends from Israel. It was a voluntary project, but it gave me something I needed very much that summer in Kyiv in 2023: a reason to create, and a way to survive the summer emotionally.

Kate, the daughter of my friend, was already dreaming of her future adult life in Italy. So I began to imagine the extension almost as a doll’s house for that future life – a small world of her own, rather than simply an addition to the existing house. Her mother sent me the brief and the possible site, and I began to write a story for the future.

I studied the village from a distance, learning its details online and reading the structure of the surrounding landscape through Google Maps. I was also inspired by the quiet architecture of contemporary Tuscan wineries – their relationship with the land, their simplicity, and the feeling that the building had always belonged there.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucoteq6vnbj1k.jpg
content.caption: TOSCANA HOUSE: the proposed extension to a one euro house, glazed towards the valley.

content.content: VM: “House near the Dam” is a 2019 sketch, never (as far as your portfolio shows) built: two connected volumes in Kyiv's Dam District, clad in red brick and wood to match the surrounding red pines, with a sloped roof planted with wild herbs specifically so the house would blend into the meadow rather than announce itself from the road. A living roof is a very particular kind of promise – it asks a client to accept years of upkeep for the sake of near-invisibility. What usually happens to a design like this one, that asks that much commitment for that much restraint – does it stay unbuilt because the ambition was too specific for the client who eventually came along, or because the right site and the right client for it simply haven't met yet?

OW: The house remained a sketch, as the client eventually relocated to the UK as a Ukrainian refugee. The land is still waiting for them, and the sketch – something we were both rather proud of – still exists.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojr5smt4w9p.jpg
content.caption: House near the Dam: timber and brick among the red pines of Kyiv's Dam District.

content.content: 05 · A restaurant, a studio, a penthouse

VM: CICADA, your restaurant and wine bar project from 2018, came with an unusual condition attached to the brief itself: the client – who had researched the restaurant industry extensively through travel across Europe and Australia – specifically wanted an architect with no previous experience designing restaurants, precisely so the process could stay collaborative and the ideas could stay unconventional. The restaurant's chef, meanwhile, had circled the world three times gathering inspiration for a genuinely multicultural menu. What does it actually feel like to be hired because you're inexperienced in a category, rather than in spite of it – and did that freedom from precedent change how boldly you were willing to work, on a project that went on to be featured in ATTITUDE Magazine?

OW: I had spent many years visiting restaurants across Europe and the UK, observing not only how they looked, but how they made one feel, how people moved through them, and how a room could shape an evening.

My work was always rooted in the client’s brief, but I have never been very interested in clichés about what a restaurant is supposed to be. I wanted to understand how this particular one might live, and then allow the idea to take its own shape.

The entire project was carried out online. We spoke with builders and contractors through a screen; samples of materials travelled to me in Kyiv. At the time, it felt almost audacious to imagine that everything could be created this way – a restaurant existing, for a while, between a distant site and a desk in Kyiv.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojsdijslkdx.jpg
content.caption: CICADA restaurant and wine bar, designed entirely through a screen from a desk in Kyiv.

content.content: VM: You also designed the office for your own practice, Olga Akulova DESIGN – completed in 2010, photographed once that year and again six years later in 2016, and highly commended at the International Property Awards in London in 2012. That's the one project in your portfolio with no outside client to negotiate against, argue with, or ultimately answer to. Looking back at a space you designed entirely for yourself, and that still held up well enough to be re-photographed six years on – what did you learn about your own taste when there was no one else's taste to balance it against, and is there anything in that office you would design differently today?
OW: I designed my studio in three days. Perhaps because it was my own space, there was no need to explain the idea to anyone before making it happen.

Fourteen years later, I am restyling the interior as I continue to grow as an architect. New materials have appeared, new technologies have changed what is possible, and I have found a colour for the walls that feels more right now – Rolling Fog by Little Greene.

And yet the room still draws me back to Kyiv. There is the view of the garden, my own little England; the Boffi K4, around which the kitchen was shaped; and the wooden floor, which has aged beautifully over these fourteen years.

All this time, the studio has also been a kind of working catalogue of my practice. It is where I have met clients, and where they could see, rather than simply hear me describe, the junctions, materials and language of the interiors I make.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojsxsvru3jf.jpg
content.caption: A sectional study from the studio's working drawings.

content.content: VM: Your NPL Penthouse – the 30th floor of the Novopecherskie Lipki condominium in Kyiv, bought by your client purely as an investment property – came with a brief that was really an absence of a brief: exposed concrete ceilings, full-height glass, and then almost total silence, because the client had “limited time to be involved” and asked you to complete the entire interior and fit-out independently. The project went on to be featured in Dezeen, Moroso and Leibal. When a client effectively hands you the keys and steps back entirely, is that the freest you ever get to work, or does an absent client's silence create its own, quieter kind of pressure that a demanding one never would?

OW: Exactly. The pressure created by the absence of a client was enormous. To prove to myself that I was worthy of making the project without a client’s editorial hand, I brought everything I knew at that time to it, and pushed my knowledge and possibilities as far as I could.

My travels to the UK became an important part of the process.
