I bought some of the accessories for the penthouse in London, at the Designers Guild showroom, and the poster for the kitchen in London as well. They were not souvenirs of a journey, but things that had already found their place in the project in my mind.
My contractors worked with remarkable precision and care, following the project closely. And, eventually, the penthouse travelled further than any of us had imagined – into worldwide publications.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojt7bapt3de.jpg
content.caption: NPL Penthouse, thirtieth floor of Novopecherskie Lipki in Kyiv: exposed concrete, full height glass and oak joinery.

content.content: 06 · Method and motifs

VM: A project titled simply “House near the Dam” is filed in your portfolio under the single word “minimalism” – a word that can mean an empty room just as easily as it can mean a room where every remaining object had to earn, and fight for, the right to stay. When you strip a house down that far for a real client with a real life to live inside it, what is your actual working method for deciding what earns that right – and has a client ever fought you to keep something you were certain had to go?

OW: When my clients are unsure about a particular piece of furniture or an item in the project, I first try to understand what lies behind their hesitation. It may be the budget, a style they have not mentioned in the brief, or simply that my idea is more daring than they had imagined for themselves.

When we discuss a possible change, I look for something that answers their concern without disturbing the composition that already exists. The new piece still has to belong to the whole, and, most importantly, to my client at that particular moment.
That is part of the work: not persuading a client to accept my idea, but understanding when an idea needs to change – and when it simply needs to be explained.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotf5wvs8qek.jpg
content.caption: An attic bedroom in progress: the point where a minimal room decides what stays.

content.content: VM: Several of your project titles read less like catalogue entries and more like private diary lines – “With a dream of KENZO,” “Uplifted House,” “Interior for Kate & Corgis” – the kind of phrase that usually stays inside a client's head, not on a public portfolio page. Where do these titles actually come from: are they yours, coined out of how the project felt to live through as its designer, or do they belong to the clients – a private joke, a private hope, a pet's name – that somehow made it, intact and unedited, all the way into your public-facing work?
OW: You made me smile.

I live through each project, and its name usually comes to me as a result of the work rather than at the beginning. It is almost a conclusion – the main idea that has slowly shaped the project through months, sometimes years, of working together.

Each project becomes a story in its own right. We see it afterwards in photographs, but my clients continue to live inside it. Perhaps that is why the name appears only when the story has already revealed itself.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojun09ei7x3.jpg
content.caption: One of the Kyiv interiors whose name arrived only once the project was finished.

content.content: VM: Looking at your Bridge House concept specifically – a pavilion designed to vanish into a pine forest, connected by a bridge you call the project's “architectural symbol” to a house organised around an internal garden bringing light into its own centre – how literally do you take the idea of a threshold in your work generally? Is the bridge, the terrace, the balcony that keeps recurring across your projects (the terrace in “Eight Years to a Home,” the balcony in TOSCANA HOUSE, the riverside terrace on Fish Island) a functional feature you return to because clients keep asking for it, or is it the closest thing your work has to a genuine, recurring architectural signature?
OW: Bridge House.
The shape was created by the existing trees. We cherished them, rather than asking them to give way to the house.
The Eight Years to a Home.
The garden – nature itself – is the element that connects all my projects.
Toscana House.
The roof terrace and balcony were conceived as a way of bringing the house towards the mountain view.
Fish Island House.
The terrace is set into the hill to find the best possible view of the water on the site.
Perhaps this is what I could call my architectural signature: I always try to connect my clients with nature. It is the most inseparable relationship a house can have.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotfjf3mxutj.jpg
content.caption: The sitting room opening onto the terrace: the threshold Olha Wood calls her architectural signature.

content.content: 07 · Distance, and what it costs

VM: Your work now moves between Kyiv, Denmark, and clients across the UK, frequently without you standing physically inside the rooms you're shaping until very late in the process, if at all – site visits replaced by video calls, timber and stone chosen from photographs and swatches sent by courier rather than held in your own hand. Materials like your namesake wood are famously about grain, weight, and how light actually falls across a surface in person. What does an interior architect concretely lose when a project has to be built at that kind of distance – and is there anything, unexpectedly, that the distance makes easier, clearer, or even better?
OW: Strong communication with clients – video calls, being in regular contact, friendship and empathy – can create a surprisingly close connection with a building site, even from a long distance.

Materials are now available across countries, too. And after 25 years of experience, I know how to find the right ones, work with people locally, and keep the architectural idea consistent, wherever the site may be.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojvm6r3rgi5.jpg
content.caption: Site and finished room side by side, the process Olha Wood now follows at a distance.

content.content: VM: “Eight years to a Home” ends, in your own account, in August 2026 – the work “very close to the end” – in a Kyiv that is still, as you're answering this, a city living through war. When you finally hand your clients the keys to a home eight years, one pandemic, and one full-scale war in the making, what do you think that specific moment will actually feel like, for them and for you – and is it a feeling any earlier, easier project in your portfolio could possibly have prepared you for?
OW: The building site is still ongoing. In Kyiv, we do not have an abundance of contractors at the moment, as many of them are protecting our country.
We hope to complete part of the work this autumn. My clients can hardly wait to begin their life in the space they have dreamed of for so many years.

The garden, which was completed on the terrace a year ago, has already given them something to live with while the house is still being made. They have spent this time among the greenery, watching it grow, and hoping that soon their life in the house will begin.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotfyucooqvn.jpg
content.caption: The terrace garden at Eight Years to a Home, completed a year before the house it belongs to.

content.content: VM: You've now spent years designing homes for people staying in a country at war, for an apartment building's shared future on an island, for a nearly abandoned house in a depopulating Italian town, and for landscapes – a stream, a pine grove, a riverbank – that were there long before any client and will presumably outlast the buildings too. If a future client asked you to design something with no constraints at all – no budget ceiling, no site, no deadline – what is the one idea sitting somewhere in your unbuilt sketches, the Tuscany extension or the Dam District house or something you haven't shown anyone yet, that you would actually choose to build first?
OW: It would be wonderful to allow myself to dream about a future project.
Perhaps it would be a house in the UK – an extension to an old house at the end of a quiet road, in the forest, with a hill and a meadow opening towards the trees.
I imagine a studio for work attached to the main house, and a terrace at the top of the hill, looking across the meadow towards the forest.

Wood, glass and local stone. A house that belongs to its place rather than simply occupying it. Sustainable and energy-independent, but without making sustainability the aesthetic. It would simply be part of the way the house lives.

articles.title: The Doors Are Opening: EPRIS Museum and Architectura, This October
articles.author: Maria Ivanova & Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Every civilisation has announced itself through a door. This October EPRIS Journal opens two: EPRIS Museum, a museum without walls that never closes, and Architectura, an atlas and a school that teaches the three-thousand-year grammar in which Italy has been built.

content.content: Nihil est tam populare quam bonitas. – There is nothing so much the people's as what is good. Cicero, Pro Ligario

Every civilisation has announced itself through a door. The bronze doors of the Pantheon have turned on their hinges for nineteen centuries; Ghiberti spent half his life on the doors that Michelangelo called worthy of Paradise. A door is a promise: that what lies beyond is kept, is cared for, and is meant to be entered. This October, EPRIS Journal opens two doors of its own. They are made not of bronze but of light and line, and they will not close at dusk.

The first is EPRIS Museum, a museum of painting, sculpture and photography with no walls, no ticket and no closing hour, at museum.eprisjournal.com. The second is Architectura, an atlas and a school for iPhone and iPad, which teaches the oldest grammar in Europe: the language in which Italy has been building for three thousand years. One is a place to walk through; the other a discipline to be learned. Both rest on a single conviction, which we hold as firmly as anything we publish: that beauty belongs to whoever is willing to look at it closely, and that looking closely can be taught.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mujzwy61nxk1qi.jpg
content.caption: The threshold of EPRIS Museum: the Pantheon, cut through its axis. The light upon the coffers is the true sun over Rome, moving hour by hour as you read.

content.content: I · Museum sine muris: the museum without walls

André Malraux dreamed of a musée imaginaire, a museum without walls assembled from every reproduction the century could make. EPRIS Museum is our answer to that dream. Today it holds forty-five halls, some six hundred and forty works and three hundred and seventy-five artists, from the marble of archaic Greece to photographs taken this very year. Nothing in it is borrowed on false terms: every work lies in the public domain or was given freely by its author under an open licence, and beneath every one we set down, as an act of honour, the artist, the date, the licence and the house where the original lives. The Art Institute of Chicago, the Cleveland Museum of Art and the National Gallery of Art in Washington opened their treasuries to the world; we have simply walked in and hung what they offered with the reverence it deserves.

A museum without walls must still have architecture, or it is only a list. And so the visitor is received, as the Romans were received, by the Pantheon. It is drawn in section from portico to apse, its heights lettered in metres as an architect of the Académie would have inscribed them. The disc of light that falls through its oculus is no ornament: it is the true sun over Rome, computed at the very moment the page is opened. At noon it rests upon the pavement; towards evening it climbs the coffers of the dome; and when night falls over the Campus Martius, the oculus fills with stars. Further on stands the Colosseum, half façade and half section, and every one of its arches is a gate into a hall.

alts: The original of our threshold: the sun through the oculus of the Pantheon. Photo: NormanB, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
The Colosseum by night, whose arches lead into the halls. Photo: Anil Öztas, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: A museum should be open at any hour, and it should always tell you where a work really lives.

Within, each hall is a hang of its own, introduced by a few lines that tell you what binds the works together and leave the feeling to you. Antiquity gathers eight centuries of Greek, Etruscan and Roman sculpture around the Cleveland Apollo. Built Light offers fourteen buildings photographed in the past twelve months by people who sign their work with their own names. The Room Itself turns to face the architecture of the museum as such. Stone and Memory and A Year of Looking Closely hang this year's international laureates of Wiki Loves Monuments and Wiki Loves Earth. Then the halls follow the procession of the centuries, and at last there is a wall on which every work is drawn at its true size, so that a Chardin no larger than a book may stand in dignity beside a Tintoretto two and a half metres wide.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mujzwyj0t7l6g4.jpg
content.caption: The hall of Antiquity, with the Cleveland Apollo as its key work. Every label gives the date, the material, the collection and the licence.

alts: The halls in order, each with its text and its first works
The index of artists: every name in the collection, by surname
The open call: chosen work hangs in a hall, credited in full

content.content: And the museum is an invitation, standing and perpetual. Its open call welcomes photographers and artists from every country: to submit costs nothing, the work that is chosen is hung in a hall under its maker's name, and the author keeps the authorship entire. A modest curatorial fee of fifty cents per image is asked only after acceptance, and every term is published plainly for all to read. The halls of the future are not yet hung. Some of them are waiting for you.
II · Architectura: Italia, linea per linea

It was the drawings that held our readers longest. They lingered over the coffers of the Pantheon, counted the orders of the Colosseum and wrote to ask the names of the small arches crowning its attic. Curiosity of that kind is the beginning of every education, and it deserves more than a caption. Architectura is our answer: the measured line drawing, that ancient instrument of the architect, placed in your hands to be held, questioned and understood.

The atlas holds forty-seven plates, and not one region of Italy is left without its monument: from the Arch of Augustus at Aosta, beneath the Alps, to the golden cathedral of Monreale and the nuraghe of Barumini, raised in Sardinia before Rome was founded. Here are the buildings the whole world knows: the Pantheon, the Colosseum, Trajan's Column, the Tower of Pisa, Brunelleschi's dome, the Palace of the Doges. And here, with equal honour, are the quieter ones: the Cattolica of Stilo in Calabria, the nine-pointed star of Palmanova, the gate of Saepinum in the hills of Molise. Milan, the city in which EPRIS is edited, receives a chapter of its own, from the Roman columns of San Lorenzo to the Bosco Verticale, with a walk that carries you through two thousand years of the city on foot.

content.caption: Three of the buildings behind the plates, as they stand today
alts: Milan Cathedral. Photo: Francesca Milanini, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Brunelleschi's dome over the roofs of Florence. Photo: GiovanniPen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Piazza del Campo in Siena, seen from the Torre del Mangia. Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
The opening page of Architectura
The Pantheon, with the sun of Rome and an hour slider
Milan Cathedral in section, up to the golden Madonnina

content.content: Open a plate, and it inks itself before your eyes, stroke after stroke, as a drawing grows beneath the hand of its maker. Then the reading begins. Five hundred and ninety-nine parts are marked across the atlas, and each is given its true name, the word an Italian guide would speak, a clear explanation and one fact worth carrying for the rest of your life. Touch the oculus, and you learn that it is nearly nine metres wide and has never once been glazed: the rain of Rome has fallen through it for nineteen hundred years. Touch the Torre del Mangia, and you meet the bell-ringer whose nickname the tower still bears. A narrator speaks every term first in Italian, for a word that has been heard is a word that is kept.
Architecture is a language before it is a style. Learn its words, and every city in the world becomes a book you can read.

We have written as the finest teachers speak before a building: never hiding behind jargon, never stooping to condescension. A frieze is a band of carving that runs along the head of a wall like a line of verse; an entablature is everything a column bears upon its shoulders. The facts are held to the same standard. Every date, height and name has been checked against published scholarship, and behind every plate stands a small library: its official Italian name, its place, its builders, its UNESCO inscription where it has one, and a list of books for those who would go further.
III · Schola: a school worthy of the name

To look is to begin; to understand requires a path. Schola, the heart of the app, is a true course of study, ordered as a university orders its reading. Seven courses stand open. Fundamenta teaches the grammar itself: how to read a drawing, the classical orders, the arch and the dome. Roma Aeterna walks the Eternal City. Italia crosses the peninsula. Ingenium honours the engineers. Magistri tells of the patrons, architects and writers who made the buildings possible. Peregrinatio is a pilgrimage through all twenty regions. And Mediolanum is Milan, in depth. Forty books, eighty-six lessons.

alts: Schola: seven courses, forty books
An examination: find the part upon the drawing
Tempora: thirty-six centuries on a single line

content.content: Every book closes with an examination, its questions drawn afresh each time: whose detail is this, when was it begun, how high does it rise, where does it stand. The student chooses the severity of the trial, from Tiro, the recruit, to Magister, the master, and a completed course is sealed with a diploma bearing the student's name. For those who teach, every book prints as a handout with its plates, its questions and a key; and in Aula, the classroom mode, a single plate fills the projector, lettered to be read from the last row of the hall, revealed one part at a time, its names withheld until the class has answered.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mujzx2h3li6wnb.jpg
content.caption: Aula, the classroom mode, on iPad: one plate, one part at a time, the names withheld until the class has answered.

content.content: Around the school lies an atlas in the fullest sense of the word: a map of Italy with every plate set in its place, plans of Rome and Milan, a timeline of thirty-six centuries from the nuraghi to the Bosco Verticale, and a page on which every building stands shoulder to shoulder at one scale, so that Trajan's Column may be measured against the Tower of Pisa with a single glance. And two studies reach deeper still. The first reopens the great dispute of 1391, when the masons of Milan argued over the geometry that would decide how high their cathedral should rise. The second recalls the anxious years of the 1740s, when mathematicians were summoned to judge whether the cracked dome of St Peter's would stand, and lets you test their verdict with weights, as Giovanni Poleni did.

alts: Architectura on iPad: the opening page
The map of Italy with every plate upon it
The cathedral of San Vigilio in Trento, one of the northern plates
Tabula Italiae: every plate on the map
The Palazzo Pubblico in Siena on the Charta paper
The Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan

content.content: IV · Silentium: the dignity of quiet

Neither work raises its voice. The museum speaks in a single typeface and draws its architecture in hairlines. The app is printed on three papers: Nox, lines of light upon the night; Charta, sepia and red chalk upon parchment; Caerulea, white lines upon the blue of an old blueprint. There are no advertisements. The app asks for no account and gathers no data; what you learn remains yours alone. It speaks English, Italian and Russian, and VoiceOver reads every plate aloud, while questions that depend on the eye are asked in another way for those who listen.

Neither is offered as a substitute for the journey. A drawing of the Pantheon is not the Pantheon, and no screen will ever give you the scale of the Colosseum or the cold of Sant'Ambrogio on a January morning. What they can do is prepare the eye, so that on the day you finally stand beneath the dome, you will know where to look, and you will know the names of the things you see. That is all we have ever wanted a journal to do.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/muk06f246h0i2h.jpg
content.caption: The Pantheon and the Piazza della Rotonda, Rome: M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT. Photo: Nicholas Hartmann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: When and where: EPRIS Museum opens officially in October 2026 at museum.eprisjournal.com. Entry is free, at every hour, and the halls already stand open to those who wish to walk them first. Architectura: Italy Drawn arrives on the App Store for iPhone and iPad in October: free, without account, without advertising, without tracking. We will announce the App Store link here and in our newsletter on the day the doors open.
Enter EPRIS Museum
The open call for photographers and artists

To the teachers, the students, the travellers and the simply curious: the doors are open, and they were made for you. Write to us. Tell us which building you would have us draw next, and which hall you would have us hang. Intrate. Come in.

articles.title: In Praise of Shadow: Colour and Light in Clair-obscur at the Bourse de Commerce
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: For six months the most luminous building in Paris agreed to go dark. A work-by-work reading of Clair-obscur at the Bourse de Commerce, and what Polke, Victor Man, Frank Bowling, Carol Rama and Laura Lamiel teach about colour in an age of too much light.

content.content: The contemporary is the one who keeps his gaze fixed on his own time, to perceive not its light but its darkness. – Giorgio Agamben, What Is the Contemporary?

For six months this year, the most luminous building in Paris agreed to go dark. From 4 March to 24 August 2026 the Bourse de Commerce, where Tadao Ando set a concrete cylinder inside the old grain exchange beneath its painted dome, gave itself over to Clair-obscur: around a hundred works from the Pinault Collection by some twenty-seven modern and contemporary artists, arranged, in the words of its curator Emma Lavigne, as a landscape at once luminous and crepuscular. The exhibition has now closed. It deserves a second look, because it asked a question our screens have taught us to forget: what does colour mean when it is not simply bright?

We live inside an excess of light. Phones glow at the brightness of noon; advertising has made saturation the default voice of the visible world; the colours of our century arrive already lit from behind. Clair-obscur proposed the opposite discipline, the one Italian painters called chiaroscuro: colour that is measured, withheld, allowed to emerge from shadow rather than shouted into it. What follows is a reading of the exhibition work by work, as a lesson in how the art of our own time handles colour, light and their absence.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwghgln6v911.jpg
content.caption: The painted dome and upper storey of the Bourse de Commerce, Paris, after its transformation by Tadao Ando (2021). Photo: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: I · The inheritance: a ray of light, a wall of black

The title looks back four centuries. When Caravaggio painted The Calling of Saint Matthew for San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome, he did not light the whole scene; he cut it with a single diagonal beam. The tax collectors sit in a tavern gloom, and the colour of their sleeves, their hats and their faces exists only where that beam falls. Colour, in chiaroscuro, is not a property of objects. It is an event, something that happens to an object when light reaches it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwght0499mnq.jpg
content.caption: Caravaggio, The Calling of Saint Matthew, 1599–1600, oil on canvas. Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome. Photo: Gleb Simonov, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: The second ancestor is Goya. Between 1820 and 1823, in his house outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo, the old painter covered the walls with what we now call the Pinturas negras, the Black Paintings. The press notes of the exhibition describe their palette precisely: blacks tempered with ochre and earth tones. It is a palette of almost nothing, and it produced some of the most frightening images in European art. Here colour is not taken away to make light dramatic, as in Caravaggio; it is taken away because the world it describes has lost its daylight.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgigsrtuaip.jpg
content.caption: Francisco de Goya, Saturn Devouring His Son, 1820–1823, one of the Black Paintings from the Quinta del Sordo, transferred to canvas. Museo del Prado, Madrid. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Philippe Parreno took Goya literally. His film La Quinta del Sordo (2021), shown in the Studio of the Bourse, reconstructs the room where the Black Paintings were made and lets a single beam of light travel across it in the dark. At moments the light only grazes the surface, so that the paint becomes dust and relief rather than image; at others it breaks through to reveal the haggard faces on the walls. Nothing is shown whole. In thirty-nine minutes of darkness Parreno teaches the first rule of the exhibition: a colour we are allowed to see only partly is a colour we look at twice.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgj1pr2u15w.jpg
content.caption: Philippe Parreno, La Quinta del Sordo, 2021, 4K film (colour, multi-channel soundtrack), 39 min. Pinault Collection. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: II · Sigmar Polke: colour held in suspension

If one work justified the exhibition, it was Sigmar Polke's Axial Age (2005–2007), nine panels painted for the 52nd Venice Biennale and shown in Gallery 2. Its title comes from Karl Jaspers, who called the centuries of Confucius, the Buddha, Homer and Plato the axial age of human thought. Its technique is its argument. Polke did not lay colour on the canvas; he suspended dry pigment in artificial resin on fabric, so that the support becomes a translucent screen and light passes through the picture as well as falling on it.

The result is colour that seems to be forming rather than finished: pools of amber and violet, smoky blues, areas where the resin clouds like breath on glass and areas where it clears into something close to a window. The curators describe the cycle as a vast liquid mirror from which ghosts of the past emerge. Standing before it, one understands why Polke, a lifelong alchemist of materials, spoke of painting as a chemical as much as an optical art. The lesson for anyone who works with colour is exact: transparency is a colour too, and the most living hues are the ones we see through.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgjejmf433m.jpg
content.caption: Sigmar Polke, Axial Age (detail), 2005–2007, nine panels, artificial resin and dry pigment on fabric. Pinault Collection. © The Estate of Sigmar Polke, Cologne / ADAGP, Paris, 2026. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: In the Salon, two earlier Polkes carried the same idea into dialogue: Stairwell (1968) and Loop – The Prayer Book of Maximilian (1986). The second is a homage to the pen flourishes Albrecht Dürer drew in the margins of the prayer book printed for the Emperor Maximilian I in 1513. Polke enlarged those loops onto a canvas two and a half metres square and set them in semi-transparent varnish, where darker areas read, in the words of the critic Bice Curiger, like traces of gunpowder. Dürer's marginalia were already a lesson in shading done with a single line. Polke turned them into weather.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgjp27m0o81.jpg
content.caption: After Albrecht Dürer, marginal drawing from the Prayer Book of the Emperor Maximilian I (1513), lithograph by Johann Nepomuk Strixner, 1808. CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgk7dt942gk.jpg
content.caption: Sigmar Polke, Loop – The Prayer Book of Maximilian, 1986, resin, graphite, pigment and emulsion on canvas, 250.2 × 250.2 cm. Pinault Collection. © The Estate of Sigmar Polke, Cologne / ADAGP, Paris, 2026. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: III · Victor Man: the palette of distance

Gallery 3 belonged to one painter, the Romanian Victor Man (born 1974), in a room curated by Jean-Marie Gallais, who calls him the contemporary painter of chiaroscuro. Man's pictures are small, often painted on cardboard, and nearly monochrome: olive darks, bruised greens, a flesh that seems lit by a single candle in a far room. Titiriteros (2023), oil on cardboard, 60 by 84 centimetres, takes its Spanish title from the puppet masters who pull the strings; Maternity with Legend (2024) sets a penitent saint crawling on all fours in its foreground.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgknw4k3dm5.jpg
content.caption: Victor Man, Titiriteros, 2023, oil on cardboard, 60 × 84 cm. Pinault Collection. © Victor Man © ADAGP, Paris, 2026. Photo: def image. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: His method is instructive precisely because it is so restrained. Man takes an image, often from the history of painting, and passes it through what Gallais calls two filters: art history, and his own dusky palette, which places the subject at a distance. He has reworked El Greco's Fábula, the enigmatic scene of a boy blowing on an ember between a monkey and a fool; and he makes darkened copies of Italian Trecento scenes of the Passion, by Sassetta, Lorenzetti and Giovanni di Pietro, deliberately desaturating them into a group of black paintings. The gold grounds and lapis blues of the fourteenth century go out, and what remains is the violence they once decorated.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgl00tlrxi2.jpg
content.caption: El Greco, An Allegory (Fábula), c. 1580–1585, oil on canvas. National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. One of the images Victor Man has repainted in his own darkened palette.

content.content: It would be easy to call such painting gloomy. It is better described as a refusal of seduction. Man uses colour the way a careful writer uses adjectives: rarely, and only where a sentence would collapse without one. His pictures pull the eye first to the texture of the surface and only then to the subject, so that we meet the image, as Gallais writes, without illusion.
IV · Colour as climate: Bowling, Tillmans and a room of fog

If Man withholds colour, Frank Bowling floods it. Gallery 6 was called Fog, and there the curators set what they describe as a vaporous map painted by Bowling, born in Guyana in 1934. The Pinault Collection's own Bowling is Texas Louise (1971), acrylic on canvas nearly seven metres wide, one of the Map Paintings he made in New York between 1966 and 1971: a field of incandescent pink-red through which the outlines of the American continents, sprayed through stencils, rise and dissolve like coasts seen at dusk. The collection's own description is exact: one geography concealing another.

Here colour is not the light on a thing; it is the air itself. Bowling's pinks and oranges have no source and cast no shadow. They behave like a climate, and the continents float in them the way memory floats in feeling. The exhibition read the painting as an Afro-diasporic counter-map, where fog erases the borders of territories and recalls ocean crossings marked by the violence of uprooting. Chiaroscuro survives here in a new form: not light against dark, but clarity against haze.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgldjxr36xj.jpg
content.caption: Wolfgang Tillmans, Day/Night II b, 2010. Pinault Collection. Courtesy Galerie Buchholz. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: Beside it hung Wolfgang Tillmans's Day/Night II b (2010), from the vertical landscapes he began photographing in 1995 to record the variations of colour and light in the sky, and nearby works by Trisha Donnelly and Bruce Conner, whose film of the 1946 nuclear test at Bikini turns a catastrophe into slow, pale billows of spray. And as summer came, the Rotunda itself filled with fog: the Japanese artist Fujiko Nakaya, who has been sculpting water vapour since the 1970s, let a cloud gather and dissolve beneath Ando's concrete ring and the painted dome. In the brightest room in Paris the colours went out altogether, and came back one by one as the cloud thinned. Before the fog, the same circular stage had held Pierre Huyghe's Camata (2024), a film of a metaphysical ritual shot in the Atacama desert and edited in real time by self-learning algorithms: night turning to day, shadow to light, earth to sky.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgln84def4h.jpg
content.caption: Pierre Huyghe, Camata, 2024, robotics driven by machine learning, self-directed film edited in real time by self-learning algorithms, sound, sensors. Pinault Collection. © ADAGP, Paris, 2026. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgm4t9pkwxb.jpg
content.caption: Fujiko Nakaya, Foggy Forest, Fog Environment #47660, Children's Forest, 1992, Showa Memorial Park, Tachikawa, Tokyo: an earlier fog sculpture, shown in the press kit to introduce her piece for the Rotunda. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: V · Colour as matter, colour as fire

Gallery 5, Incandescence, turned from atmosphere to substance. Carol Rama, who worked for decades in her apartment in Turin, was represented by three of her Bricolages. The one reproduced in the press kit, Untitled (1967), is made of tempera, bronze dust, pigmented plaster, glue, glass pearls and dolls' eyes on Masonite: a crust of coagulated paint in which marks of blue and red surround the staring eyes. Colour here is not described; it is stuck on, crusted, found. It has weight, and it looks back.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgmh1vjabtr.jpg
content.caption: Carol Rama, Untitled, from the Bricolage series, 1967, tempera, bronze dust, pigmented plaster, glue, glass pearls and dolls' eyes on Masonite, 28 × 45 cm. Pinault Collection. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: Beside her, the Swiss Louis Soutter, confined to a home for the elderly poor as the Second World War began, drew his hallucinatory rites with his fingers in ink and gouache; the collection's Dusk of the Gangster (1937–1942) belongs to that late, dark period. And filling the main space, Bill Viola's Fire Woman (2005), made for his Tristan Project at the Opéra Bastille, showed a dark silhouette advancing before a wall of flame and dissolving at last into waves of glowing red: chiaroscuro reversed, the figure dark and the light consuming it.

content.caption: Two kinds of incandescence: fingers in ink, a body in fire
alts: Louis Soutter, Dusk of the Gangster, 1937–1942, ink and gouache on paper. Pinault Collection. Photo: Jochen Littkeman, Berlin. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)
Bill Viola, Fire Woman, 2005, video and sound installation, 11 min 12 sec. Pinault Collection. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: Gold had its own chapel. James Lee Byars, for whom gold was the colour of the sublime and the immortal, was present with The Golden Tower (1974), a cylinder of gold leaf, a sphere of 3,333 red roses, and Byars Is Elephant (1997), camel-hair rope and golden fabric conceived in Cairo shortly before his death. Next to Polke's resins, Byars's gold was a reminder that the oldest colour of the sacred is also the one that most depends on darkness: gold is only gold where there is shadow for it to shine against.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgnah789zgw.jpg
content.caption: James Lee Byars, Byars Is Elephant, 1997, rope and golden fabric, variable dimensions. Pinault Collection. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: VI · Light used as a brush

The subtlest room was not a room at all. In the twenty-four vitrines of the Passage, the ring corridor that survives from the old grain exchange, and in the Machine Room below, Laura Lamiel (born 1943) built a sequence of installations curated by Alexandra Bordes under a line from Beckett: They make a sound like wings, like leaves, like sand. Children's shoes, gloves, compressed fabric, enamelled bricks, bird bones, the gilded edges of stacked missals; and fluorescent tubes that reveal some objects and leave others in shadow. Lamiel says she uses light in a vital way, as though she were working with brushes.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mukwgnmls1tixb.jpg
content.caption: Laura Lamiel, _ _ _ puis un saut (detail), 2025–2026, bricks in enamelled steel, bird bones, fluorescent light, objects from the artist's collection. © ADAGP, Paris, 2026. Photo: Nicolas Brasseur. Image: Pinault Collection, Clair-obscur press kit (2026)

content.content: That phrase could serve as the motto of the whole exhibition. In Lamiel's cases, as in Parreno's film and Polke's resin, colour is not a coat applied to a surface. It is a relation between light, material and time: black paint beside immaculate white cotton, a sliver of gilt catching a tube of cold light. The work asks the viewer to slow down until the eye can tell a white from a white.
VII · What the exhibition got wrong, and why it still mattered

Clair-obscur was not a flawless show. Writing for Slash, the critic Guillaume Benoit praised its philosophical ambition around the question of the gaze, and singled out the pure sobriety of Polke's Axial Age, but found the construction haphazard: themes stretched thin, artists spotlit without a real monographic commitment, some works reduced to accessories. We share part of that verdict. The organisation by keyword, Germination, Incandescence, Fog, Shadows, sometimes set works side by side because they rhymed rather than because they spoke to one another, and the post-war sculpture of Giacometti, Richier, Dubuffet and Maria Martins in Gallery 7 deserved a room with its own argument.

And yet the exhibition did something few institutions dare: it made a whole building quieter than its visitors' phones. In doing so it showed four ways in which the art of our time thinks about colour, and they are worth carrying out of the museum.

Colour withheld. Victor Man and Parreno show that the absence of colour is itself a palette, and that a desaturated image keeps its distance and so keeps its mystery. Colour in suspension. Polke's resins show that transparency and depth are properties of colour, not of drawing. Colour as climate. Bowling, Tillmans and Nakaya make colour into air and weather, a field we stand inside rather than an object we look at. Colour as matter and as light. Carol Rama crusts it, Byars gilds it, Lamiel paints with the light itself.
Colour is not what we add to the world. It is what the light allows us to find in it.

Caravaggio's beam and Goya's black walls were not lessons in darkness for its own sake. They were lessons in attention: in how a single lit sleeve can carry the whole meaning of a picture. Four hundred years later, in a building made to shine, twenty-seven artists made the same case. In an age that lights everything at once, the most radical colour may be the one that waits for us in the shadow.

Clair-obscur was shown at the Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection, 2 rue de Viarmes, Paris, from 4 March to 24 August 2026. General curator: Emma Lavigne, with Nicolas-Xavier Ferrand; Victor Man room curated by Jean-Marie Gallais; Laura Lamiel by Alexandra Bordes (her installation remained on view in the Passage until 21 September 2026). Images of the works in the exhibition come from the Pinault Collection's press kit for Clair-obscur and are reproduced for review with the credits it gives; the works remain the property of their artists and estates. The historical images are in the public domain or under open licences, credited in their captions. Frank Bowling's map painting is not illustrated here: the press kit carries no image of it.

articles.title: The Forms That Refuse a Name: Richard Pearson on Painting Other Worlds
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Richard Pearson
articles.excerpt: Somerset painter Richard Pearson on returning to art after Covid, learning to question what a painting is for, building oil over acrylic, and why the forms in Other Worlds must remain unrecognisable.

content.content: Richard Pearson does not describe the return to painting as a career plan. It began during Covid, then accelerated after he and his partner David moved to Somerset: a bolt out of the blue, followed by the discipline and companionship of a local art group. The work that emerged there is abstract but not detached from experience. Childhood years in the Middle East return as desert light and sandstorms; lessons from Wolverhampton Polytechnic return as questions about intention; years spent near textile designers return as a memory of colour being adjusted by hand until it was ready for the world.

His recent series, Other Worlds, is built around forms that resist becoming objects. They may suggest rocks, bodies or organisms, but Pearson keeps them unresolved so that a viewer has room to recognise an emotion rather than a thing. Paintings are layered, revised and sometimes nearly destroyed before they settle. Acrylic can become an illuminated ground beneath oil; a first image may survive only as pressure under what replaces it.
We spoke with Richard about the education that stayed with him, the slow and fast times of oil and acrylic, and why a painting sometimes has to be made before it can be painted over.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-other-worlds-hero.webp
content.caption: Untitled abstract painting by Richard Pearson. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: 01 · Learning to ask why

Viacheslav Munister [VM]: You grew up in the West Midlands, spent eight years in the Middle East and later studied on the foundation course at Wolverhampton Polytechnic. Which part of that life most clearly shaped how you paint now?

Richard Pearson [RP]: I couldn’t name one part of my life that shaped my practice. I think all your life experiences shape how you now work, and even more recent things will contribute. But if I had to name one, it would have to be Wolverhampton Polytechnic. It was a great college, led by some very inspirational teachers and filled with wonderful students.
VM: After the foundation course you moved to London and spent years working for creative organisations. What did that work teach you about how art and design actually get made?

RP: My first job was with a fabric manufacturer, and I worked in the same office as the designers. I used to watch them work. The process was all by hand then: no computers, just drawing, paints and a wonderful eye for detail. The designs, painted in gouache, would go into manufacturing, and eventually we would receive the fabrics from the printers. The colours went through adjustments until they were commercially ready.
02 · The shift back into painting
VM: You committed seriously to art only in the last few years. What tipped the balance?

RP: I started painting again during Covid, but the real shift came when my partner David and I moved to Somerset. I just started. It was a bit of a bolt out of the blue. Then I joined the local art group, which has been amazing and has really opened my mind to so much.
VM: Was there a specific lesson in that group that changed how you approached the canvas?

RP: The moment was when our tutor, Vera, asked us to really question why we were making the work, how we were going to do it and what message we wanted to communicate. It made me think seriously about what we do and why we paint and create.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-studio.webp
content.caption: Richard Pearson with his work during a two-week group exhibition. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: 03 · A series that had to grow naturally
VM: How did Other Worlds begin?

RP: I didn’t set out to paint a series, but the forms I started creating in Other Worlds seemed to multiply. The first painting was called Drifting Forms, and it went from there. The ideas needed to flow naturally without being at all contrived. It was a lovely process to go through, and hopefully more works will be added in an organic way. It can’t be planned; it has to happen naturally.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-drifting-forms.webp
content.caption: Drifting Forms, from the Other Worlds series. Photo courtesy of Richard Pearson.

content.content: VM: You work in oils and acrylics. What does each medium let you do?

RP: Sometimes I mix them, starting with an acrylic underpainting and following with oil. Acrylic can add a wonderful light that shines through the oil, and oil can do the same through lovely thin glazes. The great thing about oil is that it dries so slowly, so you can move the paint around. Acrylic is more immediate; it depends on what you want to do. I recently made a large painting in acrylic and then added oil on top, which enabled lots of layers.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-acrylic-oil-layers.webp
content.caption: Oil and acrylic layers in a painting by Richard Pearson. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-work-in-progress.webp
content.caption: A large painting in progress, photographed in Richard Pearson’s garden. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: 04 · Making in order to destroy
VM: Do you know how a piece will end before you start?

RP: I never know where it will end. Quite often I paint over the original and more or less start again. It’s almost as if I have to create something in order to destroy it. Hopefully something better comes out of it. I have to go through this process to reach something I’m happy with.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-repainting.webp
content.caption: A densely revised abstract painting by Richard Pearson. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: VM: Can you trace anything in the work back to your childhood in the Middle East?

RP: A lot of what an artist paints comes from memory and the subconscious. I couldn’t pinpoint a single source, but desert landscapes appear in Other Worlds. One painting I titled Desert Storm comes close. We quite often had huge sandstorms that lasted for days.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-desert-storm.webp
content.caption: Desert Storm, from the Other Worlds series. Photo courtesy of Richard Pearson.

content.content: 05 · What an unnamed form can hold
VM: What would the forms in Other Worlds lose if you made them recognisable—as a rock, body or building?

RP: The amorphous forms in the series are metaphors for our emotions rather than tangible or recognisable objects. That allows viewers to make up their own minds and leave with their own answers, or with more questions. If a form were made recognisable, I think the viewer would move on rather than think about what they were seeing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-other-worlds.webp
content.caption: A work from Richard Pearson’s Other Worlds series. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: VM: You recently showed alongside Ksenia Cieslak and Rosaria Valenti at Ilminster Arts Centre. What did you notice about your own work when it shared the room with theirs?

RP: It was great to have my paintings next to my friends’ work. We are all very different, but somehow it worked together—mainly because we all use strong, saturated colour. I noticed that my colours were darker and that my paintings were smaller compared with some of the others, but that was fine. It was a cool contrast, and I loved it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/richard-pearson-studio.webp
content.caption: Richard Pearson in the group exhibition at Ilminster, Somerset. Courtesy of the artist.

content.content: It’s almost as if I have to create something in order to destroy it. Hopefully something better comes out of it.
Interview by Viacheslav Munister. Answers by Richard Pearson, lightly edited for clarity and punctuation. All artworks and photographs courtesy of Richard Pearson.

articles.title: The World Is Not What It Says: Magritte’s Afterlife at Gagosian London
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: At Gagosian London, René Magritte is placed beside more than forty artists to test not who copied his motifs, but who inherited his deeper proposition: that an ordinary image can become unreliable without ceasing to look ordinary.

content.content: A pipe is useful until it becomes an image. Then it stops carrying smoke and begins carrying doubt. René Magritte understood that the smallest distance between a thing, its picture and its name could be made wide enough to contain an entire philosophy. At Gagosian’s Grosvenor Hill gallery, This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte asks what happened after that distance entered visual culture and never closed again.

Organised with the Fondation Magritte and curated by Jasper Sharp and Bernard Lagrange, the exhibition brings paintings, works on paper and sculpture from across Magritte’s career into contact with more than forty artists. The important word is not influence but afterlife. This is less a family tree of quotations than a test of which of Magritte’s problems remain active: the unreliable word, the theatrical object, the scale that turns familiarity into menace, and the image that withholds exactly what it appears to show.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/magritte-afterlife-installation-01.jpg
content.caption: This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte, installation view, Gagosian Grosvenor Hill, London, 2026. Photo: Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd. Artwork credits: Gagosian/Fondation Magritte.

content.content: I · Not a retrospective, but a pressure test

The exhibition begins with a historical span that is unusually broad without becoming dutiful. Its earliest Magritte, Les Fleurs du voyage (1926), appeared in his first one-person exhibition in Brussels. Nearby works carry the painter through the Paris years, the cloud-filled sky of La Malédiction (1931), the word-image puzzles of the 1930s, the deliberately coarse vache period of 1948 and the late, polished paradoxes for which he became globally recognisable.

Placed alone, these works might describe the evolution of a career. Placed among objects and paintings made decades later, they behave differently. They become propositions waiting for replies. The gallery’s installation makes that argument spatially: Magritte is not given a sealed historical room. His pictures keep reappearing between Robert Gober, Vija Celmins, Maurizio Cattelan, Mona Hatoum, Sarah Lucas, Jeff Koons, Issy Wood, Victor Man and newly commissioned works.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/magritte-afterlife-installation-02.jpg
content.caption: Installation view with works by René Magritte, Pol Taburet, Issy Wood and Victor Man, Gagosian Grosvenor Hill, London, 2026. Photo: Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd.

content.content: II · The painting that behaves like evidence

L’Apparition (1928) demonstrates the structure beneath Magritte’s familiar imagery. A dark field holds forms that seem to have arrived from incompatible systems: fragments of landscape, bodily suggestion, diagram and object. The surface does not ask to be admired as brushwork. It asks to be inspected as if it were evidence from an event whose rules have not been disclosed.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/magritte-apparition-1928.jpg
content.caption: René Magritte, L’Apparition (The Apparition), 1928, oil on canvas, 54 × 73 cm. © 2026 ADAGP, Paris, and DACS, London. Image courtesy Gagosian.

content.content: That evidentiary flatness matters. In a conversation published by Gagosian Quarterly, Alex Da Corte distinguishes Magritte from painters whose thinking is visible in the movement of paint. Magritte often appears to have the image already decided and then executes it with the cool precision of an illustration or a distorted camera. The lack of painterly confession is not an absence of thought. It is what transfers the burden of thought to the viewer.
III · A sky becomes an object

La Malédiction (1931), the earliest single-panel canvas in which Magritte devoted the entire field to a cloud-filled sky, removes the ground without turning the painting into pure atmosphere. The sky becomes a thing: bordered, transportable, owned. Once framed, even infinity acquires edges.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/magritte-curse-1931.jpg
content.caption: René Magritte, La Malédiction (The Curse), 1931, oil on canvas, 54 × 73 cm, Museum Voorlinden, Wassenaar. © 2026 ADAGP, Paris, and DACS, London. Photo: Antoine van Kaam.

content.content: This is one reason Magritte’s clouds survive so easily in advertising and design. They are both weather and graphic device, nature and ready-made backdrop. But the commercial afterlife can conceal the original disturbance. His sky is not freedom. It is a surface pretending to be depth.
IV · The artist as his own impossible object

La Lampe philosophique (1936) is often understood as a conceptual self-portrait. A face, a pipe and a candle are locked into a circuit of looking and consumption. The nose enters the pipe; the candle bends with an almost bodily exhaustion. Nothing in the scene is painted as a dream effect. Every component is materially plain, and the impossibility lies only in their relation.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/magritte-philosophers-lamp-1936.jpg
content.caption: René Magritte, La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), 1936, oil on canvas, 50 × 66 cm. © 2026 C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York. Photo courtesy Private Collection, Brussels.

content.content: Magritte repeatedly called ordinary objects “problems”: the problem of the window, the door, the mountain. The formulation remains useful because it denies symbolism an easy victory. A pipe does not need to stand for one stable idea. It becomes a problem because painting separates it from use while leaving its identity intact.
V · Day and night refuse to take turns

The late L’Empire des lumières (1961), loaned by the Heidi Horten Collection, is the final painting in Magritte’s celebrated sequence of landscapes where a bright daytime sky hangs above a nocturnal street. It is also the only one in the series to include a bowler-hatted figure silhouetted against the sky.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/magritte-dominion-of-light-1961.jpg
content.caption: René Magritte, L’Empire des lumières (The Dominion of Light), 1961, oil on canvas, 50 × 73 cm, Heidi Horten Collection, Vienna. © 2026 ADAGP, Paris, and DACS, London. Photo: Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd.

content.content: The device is famous because it is instantly legible. It is lasting because legibility does not resolve it. The sky and street are both convincing, and therefore their coexistence cannot be dismissed as fantasy. Magritte does not invent a new world; he forces two true descriptions of this one to occupy the same moment.
VI · What the descendants inherited

The strongest contemporary responses do not reproduce the apple, cloud or bowler hat. They inherit Magritte’s method of making an object betray its category. Vija Celmins’s Pink Pearl Eraser (1966–67) enlarges a disposable correction tool into a painted balsa-wood sculpture. It remains recognisably an eraser while becoming incapable of erasing. Use has been displaced by scale.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/vija-celmins-pink-pearl-eraser.jpg
content.caption: Vija Celmins, Pink Pearl Eraser, 1966–67, acrylic on balsa wood, 17.1 × 49.5 × 8.3 cm. © Vija Celmins. Image courtesy Gagosian.

content.content: Dana Schutz’s new painting The Singer (2026) operates further from Magritte’s iconography but close to his theatrical logic. The figure and the picture plane seem to negotiate which one is permitted to contain the other. It is not a quotation; it is a continuation of the same distrust in stable pictorial space.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/dana-schutz-the-singer-2026.jpg
content.caption: Dana Schutz, The Singer, 2026, oil on canvas, 203.2 × 175.3 cm. © Dana Schutz. Photo: Stephen Arnold.

content.content: VII · Why Magritte now

Magritte’s relevance is often explained through ubiquity: his images anticipated advertising, music videos, fashion and the visual shorthand of the internet. That is true but insufficient. Ubiquity can make an artist harmless. What the exhibition restores is the friction beneath recognition.

Our contemporary image systems promise transparency while producing uncertainty. AI-generated pictures can be entirely plausible and entirely without a photographed event behind them. Interfaces label objects, faces and places with increasing confidence. Magritte’s old separation between word, image and thing no longer reads as a philosophical joke; it reads as basic media literacy.

Da Corte identifies something still more unfashionable in Magritte: opacity. These pictures do not reveal the artist’s inner process, supply a correct interpretation or reward the viewer with full access. They remain clear and withholding at once. In a culture organised around explanation, disclosure and instantly searchable context, that refusal feels newly contemporary.
Magritte’s pictures do not ask whether the world is real. They ask why an image should be trusted simply because it looks familiar.
VIII · Verdict

This Is Still Not a Pipe succeeds when it treats influence as a working problem rather than a resemblance game. With more than forty contemporary artists, the exhibition inevitably produces uneven lines of descent. Some works sit close to Magritte’s vocabulary; others require the curatorial premise to make the relationship visible. But that unevenness is productive. It shows that Magritte’s afterlife is not a style. It is a set of permissions: to let the ordinary become unstable, to make scale carry meaning, to allow an image to contradict its caption, and to leave the central mechanism unexplained.

The exhibition is therefore most useful not as a celebration of a canonical Surrealist, but as a manual for looking at images now. The pipe is still not a pipe. The more urgent discovery is that the photograph may not be evidence, the label may not be knowledge, and the familiar may be the least trustworthy category of all.

This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte is at Gagosian, 20 Grosvenor Hill, London W1K 3QD, from 24 September to 12 December 2026. Tuesday–Saturday, 10am–6pm. Curated by Jasper Sharp and Bernard Lagrange in collaboration with the Fondation Magritte. This article was prepared from the exhibition materials and official installation photography; it does not claim an in-person visit. All artworks and photographs are reproduced for editorial review with the credits supplied by Gagosian.
Exhibition page — Gagosian
Alex Da Corte on René Magritte — Gagosian Quarterly

articles.title: Where Darkness Begins to Listen: Roy DeCarava in Los Angeles
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: At David Zwirner Los Angeles, more than 130 photographs from Roy DeCarava’s the sound i saw turn jazz, labor and street life into a score made from shadow, interval and attention.

content.content: Some photographs describe sound by showing its source: a trumpet lifted, a hand striking a drum, a mouth held close to a microphone. Roy DeCarava did something more difficult. He photographed the conditions in which sound becomes meaningful—the pause before a phrase, the body at work, the density of a room, the street that continues after the music has stopped.

At David Zwirner Los Angeles, the sound i saw gathers more than 130 images from a project DeCarava developed between the late 1940s and the 1960s. Curated by Ebony L. Haynes, it is the largest presentation of this body of work since its first exhibition at the Studio лMuseum in Harlem in 1983. An adjacent listening room, SIDE B: the sounds, extends the exhibition through records and programs shaped by the artist’s own musical life.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-jackie-at-the-barricade.jpg
content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Jackie at the barricade, c. 1956, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.

content.content: I · A book before an exhibition

the sound i saw began not as a commission or a documentary assignment but as a handmade artist’s book: a private sequence of roughly 300 photographs and text. This origin matters. The project does not behave like a catalogue of jazz history. Musicians appear beside children, workers, intersections and rooms because DeCarava was composing a lived environment rather than illustrating a genre.

When 125 photographs were shown at the Studio Museum in Harlem in 1983, curator C. Daniel Dawson described the work as a reflection on life made with jazz and photography as instruments. The distinction protects the pictures from a familiar reduction. DeCarava photographed Black musicians, but he refused to turn them into spectacle. He photographed Black life, but he refused the demand that every image perform as social evidence.
II · The street keeps time
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-woman-children-intersection.jpg
content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Woman and children at intersection, 1952, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.

content.content: In Woman and children at intersection (1952), the city is divided by a bright wedge of winter sky and the dark walls of buildings. The figures are small, yet the crossing does not diminish them. Their movement activates the geometry. A photograph that might be called quiet contains several tempos at once: the pace of traffic, the careful step across snow, the duration of looking from a distance.

DeCarava worked with a handheld 35mm camera, moving through New York without the ceremony of a large apparatus. Mobility gave him proximity, but proximity was never permission to intrude. His pictures are intimate because they preserve the subject’s interiority. They do not explain people into submission.
III · Shadow is information

DeCarava’s darkness is often treated as a signature effect. It is better understood as an ethics of attention. In his prints, shadow does not conceal a lack of information; it changes the speed at which information arrives. The eye must adjust. A face, hand or doorway emerges gradually, and the viewer becomes conscious of the labor of seeing.

content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Blue Morocco, 1955, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.
content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-blue-morocco.jpg

Blue Morocco (1955) turns a nightclub interior into a series of thresholds. Curtains frame a room whose occupants are visible but not offered up. The photograph holds back just enough to make atmosphere structural. Darkness becomes the architecture through which one enters.
IV · Music as relation

content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Percy Heath, 1957, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.
content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-percy-heath.jpg

The portrait of bassist Percy Heath concentrates on an instrument, a hand and the partial presence of a face. DeCarava does not need the full performance. The photograph locates music in touch: the pressure of fingers against strings, the physical intelligence through which a note is made.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-art-blakey.jpg
content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Art Blakey, 1958, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.

content.content: Art Blakey appears at a greater distance, isolated by the pool of light around his drums. The surrounding black is not empty. It measures the intensity of concentration. DeCarava said that he photographed musicians as people rather than as musicians, responding to the commitment they brought to life in a particular moment. The best of these images make work itself visible without turning labor into performance for the camera.
V · The break is part of the score

content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Ellington session break, 1954, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.
content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-ellington-session-break.jpg

Ellington session break (1954) looks toward the interval that conventional music photography might discard. A coat rack occupies the centre; figures wait at the edges; ceiling lights repeat like notes above them. The session’s pause is not outside the music. It is where fatigue, preparation and ordinary time return.

This is DeCarava’s radical correction to the mythology of jazz photography. Billie Holiday, Miles Davis, John Coltrane and Count Basie appear across the larger project, but celebrity does not organize the sequence. The musician on stage and the deliveryman on the street share a world of skill, pressure, rest and attention.
VI · A politics without slogans
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-force-new-york.jpg
content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Force, New York, 1963, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.

content.content: Force, New York (1963) records a Brooklyn protest against the destruction of residents’ homes for an expansion of Downstate Medical Center. Bodies press together in a frame where power is felt physically—in arms, shoulders, cloth and compression. DeCarava later described the deeper force in the image as the desire of people to reach sunlight.

The photograph’s politics are neither hidden nor converted into a slogan. Its argument comes from relation: the state acts upon bodies, and bodies answer through collective will. DeCarava understood that serenity could carry power without softening conflict.
VII · Dance and duration
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/roy-decarava-dancers-harlem.jpg
content.caption: Roy DeCarava, Dancers (Harlem), 1956, silver gelatin print. Courtesy The Estate of Roy DeCarava and David Zwirner.

content.content: In Dancers (Harlem) (1956), movement is dispersed across a dark floor. The image is not a single decisive instant so much as a field of rhythms. Figures advance, turn and recede; light catches the ground like a faint pulse. The photograph feels less like a frozen event than a duration briefly made visible.

That quality explains why the exhibition’s listening room is more than an accessory. DeCarava’s sequencing asks to be experienced musically: repetition produces difference, silence gives shape to sound, and the gap between images functions like an interval. The viewer does not merely identify subjects. The viewer learns a tempo.
DeCarava did not photograph jazz as an event. He photographed the world that made its intensity possible.
VIII · Verdict

the sound i saw is important because it refuses the false choice between formal beauty and social meaning. DeCarava’s tonal control is inseparable from the dignity he grants his subjects. His shadows ask for patience; his sequences resist extraction; his photographs make attention feel like a form of responsibility.

Seen in Los Angeles more than four decades after the project’s first public presentation, these pictures remain insistently contemporary. They answer an image culture built for brightness, speed and immediate recognition with a different proposition: look longer, accept partial knowledge, and let a photograph retain the right to be quiet.

Roy DeCarava: the sound i saw, curated by Ebony L. Haynes, is at David Zwirner, 606 N Western Avenue, Los Angeles, from 19 September to 31 October 2026.
