articles.title: The Ocean Is Not Blue: Torkwase Dyson and the Politics of Abstraction
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: In Seeing in Blue, Torkwase Dyson asks whether painting can hold the ocean as physics, memory, extraction and freedom at once—and whether abstraction can make climate crisis felt before it becomes an image.

content.content: The ocean is not blue. Water has no colour of its own; it borrows, scatters, absorbs and returns light. Blue is therefore not a property but an event—a relation between depth, distance, matter and an eye. This unstable fact is the beginning of Torkwase Dyson’s new paintings, and it prevents them from settling into the category that their beauty initially suggests.

At Pace Gallery in New York, Seeing in Blue presents paintings informed by more than a decade of swimming and deep-sea diving. Their dark aquatic fields are crossed by arcs, strings, seams, brass bars and small apertures. They appear at once as maps, instruments, night skies and fragments of architecture. Yet they illustrate none of these things. Dyson’s question is more demanding: can painting carry the physical knowledge of water—and the political histories contained within it—without reducing either to an image?
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-daydreaming-2026.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, Daydreaming, 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, bronze and cotton string on canvas, 48 × 48 × 5 in. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: I · Against the climate image

Contemporary culture has developed a stable visual language for ecological crisis. Aerial photographs show burning forests, retreating ice, poisoned rivers and coastlines seen from satellites. These images are necessary as evidence, but their repetition produces a paradox: the more completely catastrophe is pictured, the more easily it becomes scenery. The viewer is placed safely outside the event, looking down.

Dyson removes that distance. Her paintings do not show an ocean; they ask what it means to have a body inside one. Pressure replaces panorama. Buoyancy replaces horizon. Breath becomes a measure of time. Navigation is no longer a line drawn over a map but the continuous negotiation between density, darkness and movement.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-to-plunge-to-see.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, To Plunge, To See, To Never, To Time, To Shadow, To Remember, 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass and cotton string on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: II · Physics and memory

Dyson describes working with water as moving “between physics and memory.” The phrase resists the division between objective environment and subjective experience. Water obeys pressure, gravity and temperature; it also stores histories of transport, extraction, labor, migration and death. To enter it is to meet both systems at once.

Her studio process repeats this double movement. She begins with canvases laid on the floor, allowing washes of diluted colour to spread, pool and escape complete control. She then answers that errancy with measured geometric construction. Flow is followed by structure; accident by decision. The painting becomes a negotiation between what matter does and what a body asks it to do.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-to-plunge-side.jpg
content.caption: Side view of To Plunge, To See, To Never, To Time, To Shadow, To Remember, showing the painting’s constructed depth and brass element. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: III · Abstraction is the subject

Dyson has made an essential distinction: she does not describe herself simply as an abstract artist; she has chosen abstraction as a subject. The difference matters. Abstraction is not a style applied after the political content has been decided. It is itself a political operation: the process by which bodies, territories and resources are converted into categories, property lines, statistics and zones of control.

A map is an abstraction. So is a shipping route, a flood-risk boundary, a prison plan, a deed, an insurance district and the financial instrument that makes extraction profitable before anything has been removed from the ground. Abstraction can erase lived specificity. It can also allow a person to imagine space otherwise. Dyson works inside this conflict rather than pretending abstraction is innocent.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-hand-to-hand-one.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, Hand to Hand, Heart to Heart (Unknown of Us 1), 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass, bronze and cotton string on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: IV · Black geography is not a theme

For Dyson, ecology cannot be separated from Black spatial history. The Atlantic is a living system and a historical structure: a medium of forced movement, trade, colonial extraction and diaspora. Land is never only landscape when plantations, property and environmental exposure have determined which bodies may occupy it safely.

This is why “Black geography” in her work is not iconography to be located in a picture. It is a way of thinking about movement under unequal conditions. Her shapes draw from histories of self-emancipation and improvised shelter: how to hide, turn, pass, breathe, build and remain indeterminate inside systems designed to make a body legible and controllable.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-hand-to-hand-three.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, Hand to Hand, Heart to Heart (Unknown of Us 3), 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass, bronze and cotton string on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: V · Geometry after freedom

Dyson calls parts of her formal vocabulary “hypershapes.” Curves, wedges, apertures and compressed rooms are distilled from liberation strategies rather than from geometry as an autonomous language. Their sources include the spatial intelligence through which enslaved and fugitive people survived: the hull, the garret, the hidden route, the narrow opening and the architecture made usable against its intended purpose.

The forms do not decode into a single story. That refusal is crucial. A symbol becomes governable once its meaning is fixed. Dyson’s geometries remain available for movement; they can be read as enclosure and exit, pressure and protection, structure and breach. Freedom appears not as unlimited open space but as the ability to compose within constraint.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-the-distance-inside-us.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, The Distance Inside Us, 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass and cotton string on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: VI · A painting with an edge

Photographed frontally, these works can look restrained and almost immaterial. Seen obliquely, they disclose their objecthood. Cotton string stands away from the surface; brass and bronze interrupt the painted field; canvases possess substantial depth; circular and irregular supports reject the neutral rectangle.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-daydreaming-side.jpg
content.caption: Oblique view of Daydreaming, 2026. The bars, string and deep support turn the painting into a spatial proposition. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: The side view changes the argument. A line is not only drawn; it is tensioned across space. A bar is not only a colour; it has weight, conductivity and resistance. The work oscillates between diagram and construction. It does not depict architecture so much as make the viewer encounter painting architecturally—through distance, position and bodily scale.
VII · Blue without innocence

Dyson’s earlier paintings often approached blackness through layered mixtures rather than a single black pigment. In Seeing in Blue, aquatic colour comes forward, but the blue is equally impure. Titanium white can make it seem incandescent; green flickers below it; rust-red passages suggest oxidation, sediment or an atmosphere losing equilibrium.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-a-blue-tongue-a-blue-song.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, A Blue Tongue, A Blue Song, 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass, bronze and cotton string on canvas, 42 in diameter. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: The blue therefore refuses the cultural promise commonly attached to it: serenity, infinity, escape. Dyson rejects what she calls the merely “vacation beautiful.” Her oceanic beauty is prehistoric, vulnerable and terrifying. It includes artificial reefs and living ecologies, but also seafloor drilling, military posts, acoustic surveillance and the ruins of the built world.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-blue-tongue-side.jpg
content.caption: Oblique view of A Blue Tongue, A Blue Song, showing the work’s elliptical depth and metal edge. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: VIII · Beauty as a method of staying

There is a temptation to treat beauty as politically suspect whenever the subject is disaster. The fear is understandable: beauty can aestheticize damage and make violence consumable. Dyson proposes another function. Beauty can hold attention where spectacle exhausts it. It can keep a viewer inside complexity long enough for relations to emerge.

Her surfaces do not reward a quick scan. Near-black passages require the eye to adjust; fine strings and graphite marks disappear and return; metallic interruptions alter with the viewer’s position. Looking becomes slow, physical and incomplete. That incompleteness is not evasive. It is a rehearsal for encountering an ecology that cannot be mastered from a single point of view.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-clear-sacred-focus.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, Clear Sacred Focus, 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass, bronze and cotton string on canvas, 42 in diameter. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: IX · The scale of intimacy

Much of Dyson’s practice has moved across monumental painting, sculpture, architecture and collective study. These new works compress that research into a more intimate register. Their scale does not make the subject smaller. It changes the relation from public address to proximity.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/torkwase-dyson-blue-worlding-for-love.jpg
content.caption: Torkwase Dyson, Blue Worlding for Love, 2026, acrylic, ink, graphite, brass and cotton string on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery.

content.content: Blue Worlding for Love pushes beyond the wall as a support. Its layered planes and brass member resemble a compact shelter, instrument or incomplete model. The title matters: “worlding” names the active construction of relations rather than the passive occupation of a given world. Love enters not as sentiment but as a spatial practice—the work of making conditions in which another body can live.
X · What the paintings cannot do

No abstract painting can explain climate science, repair an ecosystem or redistribute environmental risk. Dyson’s theoretical vocabulary is dense enough that the works can appear inaccessible without prior knowledge. The gallery context adds another contradiction: objects concerned with liberation and unequal space circulate through one of the most exclusive spatial economies in culture.

But demanding that a painting solve the crisis it addresses would repeat the instrumental logic the work opposes. Its function is different. Dyson makes visible the habits through which knowledge is organized: the preference for views from above, for clean boundaries, for catastrophe rendered as an image happening elsewhere. Her paintings shift knowledge back toward the body—not as pure feeling, but as a sensing instrument implicated in history.
Dyson does not paint the ocean as a place to look at. She paints what happens to knowledge when the body is already inside it.
XI · Verdict

Seeing in Blue succeeds because it refuses to make ecological painting legible through familiar signs of nature. There are no waves to admire, no horizon to lose oneself in and no ruined coastline to confirm what the viewer already knows. Instead, water becomes a method for rethinking painting: fluid and constructed, material and mnemonic, beautiful and compromised.

The deepest proposition is that abstraction does not move away from reality. It reveals how reality has already been abstracted—into territory, infrastructure, value and risk—and asks whether those systems can be recomposed. In Dyson’s hands, a line can be a route, a barrier, a breath or a relation. Blue can be light and depth, but never innocence.

Torkwase Dyson: Seeing in Blue is at Pace Gallery, 540 West 25th Street, New York, from 11 September to 24 October 2026. The exhibition presents new paintings informed by Dyson’s experiences as a swimmer and deep-sea diver. articles.title: The Ordinary Life Is Not a Small Subject: Louis Fratino and the Painting of Intimacy
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: In Prose, Louis Fratino paints lovers, relatives, baths, gardens and subway cars—and asks why an ordinary queer life, given the scale of history painting, can still feel radical.

content.content: A life becomes visible in fragments: coffee cups on a crowded table, a lover turning in bed, a mother’s garden seen at the hour when colour begins to loosen, a naked body folded into bathwater, strangers packed into a subway car. None of these events announces itself as history. Louis Fratino paints them as if the distinction between a major and minor subject were no longer useful.

His new exhibition Prose, at David Zwirner in London, contains paintings, drawings and sculpture made from observation and memory. The title is exact. Prose is what carries most of a life: not the exceptional line preserved for quotation, but the continuous language between moments. Fratino’s paintings ask what happens when this ordinary continuity—especially the continuity of queer life—is granted the concentration once reserved for mythology, power and public catastrophe.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-jasmine-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Jasmine, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: I · After visibility

Queer figurative painting has often been discussed through visibility: which bodies were absent from museums, which desires were concealed, and what political work is performed when they enter the frame. Fratino belongs to a generation for whom the problem has changed without disappearing. The male body can now be shown desiring another male body, but visibility alone no longer guarantees complexity.

The harder task is to paint queer life without requiring it to remain exemplary, transgressive or tragic. Fratino’s figures eat, wait, bathe, read, travel and become bored. Sex appears, but it belongs to a larger ecology of domestic life. The radical claim is not simply that these bodies deserve representation. It is that their uneventful time deserves form.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-ale-moms-bedroom-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Ale in his mom’s bedroom (after Corot), 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: II · Memory is not an archive

Fratino paints from memory, even when observation begins the process. This does not mean retrieving an intact mental photograph. Memory edits scale, exaggerates colour, compresses rooms and brings emotionally adjacent moments into the same field. A body can become too large for the bed because its felt presence was larger than the room.

In Ale in his mom’s bedroom (after Corot), the seated figure is held inside greens and muted reds that make the room feel remembered rather than measured. The parenthetical “after Corot” identifies an artistic ancestor while also admitting that influence reaches the present through private experience. Art history is not outside the bedroom. It is one of the things remembered there.
III · The crowded picture
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-coffee-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Coffee, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: Coffee is a social painting structured by objects. Cups, glasses, chairs and bodies compete for the same shallow space. The table does not organise the gathering so much as record its aftermath. Fratino’s compressed perspective allows every detail to insist on itself: the drink, the hand, the face partly hidden behind another person.

This density carries an ethical position. No figure becomes the sovereign subject around whom the scene is arranged. Intimacy is distributed. A gathering is made from simultaneous acts of attention and distraction, and the painting refuses to decide which one matters most.
IV · Pleasure without defence

Pleasure in contemporary art is frequently asked to provide its own alibi. It must be critical pleasure, wounded pleasure, pleasure made acceptable by an explanatory structure. Fratino resists this economy. He has said that he wants to remain vulnerable in the studio and to work without embarrassment—as if the private dialogue of painting should not begin by anticipating prosecution.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-the-sauna-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, The sauna, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: The sauna turns a communal interior into a field of orange and red bodies. Anatomy is elastic; limbs intersect; heat seems to deform the room. The painting is erotic, but its eroticism does not depend on a single exposed act. It comes from proximity, repetition and the temporary suspension of distance between bodies.

To paint pleasure without defence is not politically naïve. Queer culture has been made visible through histories of prohibition, medicalisation and loss. An image of ease can therefore carry historical pressure even when it refuses to illustrate suffering. The right to appear unafraid is not the absence of politics; it is one of politics’ unfinished outcomes.
V · The body as landscape
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-the-green-bath-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, The green bath, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: In The green bath, a body folds so completely into the vessel that figure and container begin to share a contour. The view from above abolishes a stable horizon. Knees, chest, water and enamel become a single knot of green volumes.

Fratino’s distortions are sometimes placed in a lineage running through Picasso, Matisse and Marsden Hartley. The references are real, but resemblance can become a lazy conclusion. What matters is how inherited distortion changes when the body being painted is not an anonymous model but a lover, friend or self. Formal freedom becomes inseparable from relational knowledge.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-nude-black-hair-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Nude with black hair, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: VI · Looking without possession

The reclining nude is among Western painting’s most burdened formats. It converts a body into an available surface and assigns the viewer a privileged position outside the scene. Fratino inherits this structure and makes it unstable. His nudes are often aware of being seen, yet they do not organise themselves for the viewer’s control.

In Nude with black hair, the figure’s horizontal body occupies almost the full canvas, but the face does not offer access. Flesh is painted with tenderness without becoming smooth. The image distinguishes intimacy from possession: familiarity allows the painter to remain close, not to claim total knowledge.
VII · Painting as a form of care

Fratino has described painting as an act of respect or care because it demands time, skill and a kind of abasement. The formulation is useful in an era when images are made and discarded with almost no friction. A painting holds someone in attention for longer than convenience requires.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-chrissie-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Chrissie, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: Chrissie is small enough that the face must be approached rather than consumed at a distance. The surface remains worked and unresolved; likeness is constructed through accumulated decisions rather than photographic completeness. Care appears not as idealisation but as sustained looking.
VIII · The city enters the room
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-the-subway-car-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, The subway car, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: Domestic intimacy is not sealed off from public life. The subway car compresses strangers, reflections, advertisements and metal structure into a vertical chamber. The transit system becomes another interior—shared without being private, physically close without promising recognition.

The picture complicates the comforting idea that Fratino paints only a protected world of lovers and family. Urban queer life is shaped by public codes of looking: the glance that tests safety, the body that recognises another body, the practiced indifference of strangers. The subway car is a social composition in which everyone sees and avoids being seen.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-summer-in-the-city-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Summer in the city, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: IX · Art history at home

Fratino’s paintings openly converse with European and American modernism: Matisse’s decorative interiors, Corot’s figures, Picasso’s compressed bodies, Hartley’s masculine charge, Bonnard’s domestic colour and Alice Neel’s psychological line. The risk of such fluency is that citation can become a certificate of seriousness attached to private life.

His strongest works reverse that relation. They do not use art history to legitimise queer experience; they use queer experience to test what art history can still do. A modernist distortion that once signalled formal revolution is returned to the kitchen, bath and bed, where it must become emotionally specific again.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-prose-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Prose, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: X · Why “prose” matters

Poetry is conventionally granted compression, intensity and transformation. Prose carries sequence: one sentence after another, one day following the previous day. By calling the exhibition Prose, Fratino chooses duration over climax. A life is not proven by its most dramatic image. It accumulates through repeated rooms, bodies and objects.

This is also a theory of painting. Each canvas is discrete, but the subjects age and return. A niece appears first as a baby and later as a child; partners and relatives occupy new rooms; the artist imagines painting himself when he is old. Autobiography becomes serial rather than confessional. The work’s meaning lies not only in disclosure but in continuity.
XI · The still life is never still
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-apples-pears-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Apples and pears, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: A bowl of fruit seems to suspend politics entirely. Yet still life has always been a record of access: what could be bought, stored, displayed and allowed to decay. Fratino’s apples and pears are compressed into a dark bowl on striped cloth, painted with the same bodily pressure as his nudes.

The equivalence is important. Fruit, flowers and flesh belong to one visual world because intimacy is not confined to interpersonal drama. It is a way of assigning attention. The ordinary object is not elevated out of ordinary life; ordinary life is revealed as already dense with form.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/louis-fratino-snowdrops-hellebores-2026.jpg
content.caption: Louis Fratino, Snowdrops and hellebores, 2026, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: XII · The problem of the beautiful life

Fratino’s work is easy to love, and that ease creates suspicion. The paintings are colourful, sensual, art-historically literate and highly desirable within the market. The intimacy they depict can be converted into a style: the queer domestic interior as a recognisable and collectible genre.

The problem is not that the work is beautiful or commercially successful. It is whether vulnerability survives repetition. When the same compressed anatomy and saturated palette move from lover to flower to city scene, they risk becoming a guarantee of authorship rather than a fresh encounter. The paintings remain alive where the subject resists the painter’s known solution.

Fratino’s answer appears to be expansion rather than reinvention. The world of the paintings grows as his world grows: family, travel, public space, aging and new forms of attachment. This is a modest strategy, but modesty is the premise of the work. A style changes because a life does.
Fratino’s most consequential claim is not that queer intimacy belongs in art history, but that ordinary time is one of history’s primary materials.
XIII · Verdict

Prose matters because it refuses the hierarchy that makes public violence historically serious and private pleasure merely personal. Fratino does not deny conflict; he declines to let conflict monopolise the meaning of queer life. His paintings preserve affection, boredom, appetite, embarrassment and rest as forms of knowledge.

The ordinary life is not a small subject. It is where political victories and failures become inhabitable: in who can share a room, touch without fear, build a family, age visibly and expect another morning. Painting cannot secure those conditions. It can insist that they are worth the time required to see them.

Louis Fratino: Prose is at David Zwirner, 24 Grafton Street, London, from 18 September to 31 October 2026. The exhibition is the artist’s first solo presentation in London and his first with the gallery since representation was announced. articles.title: The Painting Is Still Wet: Emma McIntyre and Art That Refuses to Finish
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Emma McIntyre paints with rust, oxidised copper, bone black, gravity and time—making works that continue to change after the artist has stopped touching them.

content.content: The fiction of a finished painting is useful. It gives the museum a date, the market a stable object and the art historian a boundary: before completion, the artist was deciding; after completion, the work began to mean. Emma McIntyre’s paintings disturb that sequence. Rust keeps blooming. Copper continues to oxidise. A surface changes after the hand has withdrawn.

In This body holds / swamp stuff, at David Zwirner’s 52 Walker in New York, McIntyre treats painting less as the execution of an image than as the temporary organisation of reactions. Oil, iron, copper, bone black, solvent, pressure, gravity and bodily contact meet on canvas. The artist initiates conditions, but matter retains the right to answer.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-violet-temple-veil-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Violet for the temple veil, 2026, oil, Flashe, iron oxide and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: I · Who finishes the painting?

Western painting has long attached authority to the final touch. Completion confirms authorship: the painter has decided that no further mark is necessary. McIntyre replaces this sovereign model with collaboration. She pours and tilts, presses bubble wrap into wet pigment, oxidises metal-based paint and takes impressions from her own palette and body.

None of this means surrendering intention. Chance is prepared, watched and edited. The relevant distinction is not control versus accident, but complete control versus responsive control. McIntyre makes a move, observes what the material does, and composes the consequence.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-solve-et-coagula-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Solve et coagula, 2026, oil, oil stick, copper paint and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: II · Alchemy without mysticism

Solve et coagula names the alchemical instruction to dissolve and recombine. The phrase can sound mystical, but McIntyre’s process is stubbornly physical. Iron meets an oxidising solution and becomes rust. Copper produces blue-green compounds. Pigment thinned with solvent follows gravity across a horizontal support.

Alchemy here is not a fantasy of turning base matter into gold. It is a method for letting substances disclose behaviours that conventional studio technique tries to stabilise. Paint ceases to be colour carried by a neutral medium; it becomes an active chemistry with duration, incompatibility and risk.
III · Rust is a clock
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-pearls-ambergris-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Pearls of ambergris, 2026, oil, iron paint and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: Rust is usually understood as failure: evidence that a protected surface has been breached and time has entered. McIntyre makes that breach productive. Oxidation creates orange and brown blooms whose edges record the movement of liquid and air. The mark is not painted to resemble corrosion. It is corrosion.

This difference collapses representation into event. A landscape painter may depict weather; McIntyre allows atmosphere to participate chemically in the work. Each oxidised passage is a clock whose units are moisture, oxygen and exposure. The painting possesses a time that does not coincide exactly with the artist’s labour.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-iliaster-flowers-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, This iliaster flowers like the wind, 2026, oil and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: IV · A body made of swamp stuff

The exhibition title comes from Diane di Prima’s poem “Show Me Your Other Body”: “this body holds / swamp stuff / thick viscous / life-generating Mud.” The body imagined here is not a sealed figure separated from environment. It is porous, mineral, wet and generative.

McIntyre’s abstractions repeatedly move between bodily and geological scales. A stain can resemble bruised skin, a cloud system, pond water or a microscopic culture. None of those readings becomes definitive. The painting behaves like a body precisely because it cannot be reduced to anatomy: it absorbs, reacts, scars and changes state.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-bright-medusas-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Bright medusas, 2026, oil, oil stick and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: V · The body without a figure

Abstract expressionism made gesture into evidence of the artist’s body, but often converted that body into heroic signature. McIntyre uses bodily contact differently. Impressions, drags and pours appear alongside repeated industrial patterns and chemical reactions. Agency is distributed among hand, tool and substance.

In Bright medusas, a bubble-wrap grid crosses a vivid pink field. The humble packing material produces a cellular pattern that can read as skin, eggs, pixels or a protective membrane. Mechanical repetition and sensuous colour are not opposites. The painting’s body is built from their collision.
VI · Giotto enters through copper
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-beautiful-old-lies-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Beautiful old lies, 2026, oxidised copper paint, oil and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: Beautiful old lies turns oxidised copper into a saturated blue field. The colour invokes the prestige of lapis lazuli in Giotto’s Scrovegni Chapel while arriving through an entirely different material history. Medieval blue signified the expense of mineral pigment and the authority of the sacred image. McIntyre’s blue is produced by change, exposure and corrosion.

A semiabstract angel’s wing derived from Giotto enters the surface as a recognisable fragment. Figuration does not organise the painting; it alights briefly within a material weather system. The historical reference is therefore neither quotation nor homage. It tests whether the sacred can survive when its image and substance no longer guarantee permanence.
VII · Painting against the screen

A digital image promises consistency. The same file can appear on thousands of screens, varying in calibration but not in its underlying data. McIntyre’s paintings resist this form of identity. Their colour depends on reflected light; metallic and oxidised passages shift with angle; slow chemical change separates the object of tomorrow from the photograph taken today.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-swear-by-shadows-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Swear it by the shadows, 2026, oil and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: This does not make them pure or technologically innocent. They circulate online, through fairs and as market images. But the reproduction contains an honest failure: it cannot fully stabilise its subject. At a moment when synthetic images can imitate almost any pictorial style, material duration becomes more than craft. It becomes a form of difference.
VIII · Monochrome as weather
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-muted-rain-tones-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Those muted those rain tones, 2026, oil and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: Several paintings lean toward monochrome without accepting its historical claim to purity. A McIntyre monochrome is crowded with temperature, stains, buried marks and competing densities. It does not remove the world from painting. It lets the world arrive as weather.

The atmospheric field changes as the viewer’s attention moves. A pale zone thickens into a body; a dark wash becomes space; a scratched line briefly reads as writing and dissolves again. Perception repeats the material process: forms coagulate and disperse.
IX · Bone black and the ethics of material
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-crackle-and-drag-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Crackle and drag, 2026, oil, bone black and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: In Crackle and drag, white paint crosses a ground made with bone black—a pigment traditionally produced from charred animal bone. The name forces an awareness that colour is never merely optical. Pigments have bodies, sources, trade routes and residues.

Contemporary painting often speaks about materiality as tactile pleasure, but materials are also evidence of extraction and transformation. Copper must be mined; iron corrodes; bone becomes carbon. McIntyre does not turn every ingredient into an explicit moral argument. She keeps its prior life audible inside the painting.
X · The diptych as experiment

Violet for the temple veil began as two panels poured separately with blue-black paint before being joined. The resulting symmetry resembles a Rorschach test, an open book or a body split along a vertical axis. Yet the halves do not mirror one another perfectly. Material variance interrupts the desire for equivalence.

The diptych makes method visible. Joining is not the final concealment of difference but its display. Painting becomes comparative: two surfaces receive related conditions and produce distinct outcomes. The viewer looks not for a single image but for the interval between reactions.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-the-blue-hour-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, The blue hour, 2026, work on paper. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: XI · Paper remembers the palette

McIntyre’s works on paper are not preparatory illustrations for larger canvases. They often begin with leftover mixtures from earlier paintings or direct impressions of the palette itself. A by-product becomes a beginning. Waste becomes an archive of possible colour.

This cyclical studio economy complicates the fantasy of the isolated masterpiece. Each work shares matter and decisions with others. Paint travels between supports; motifs migrate; an ending leaves the residue from which another composition starts. The practice is rhizomatic because influence moves sideways rather than down a clean line from sketch to finished work.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-hawthorn-eyes-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, Hawthorn eyes, 2026, work on paper. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: XII · The romance of chance

Process-driven abstraction carries a familiar danger: chemical effects can become spectacle, and “letting materials speak” can disguise weak decisions. Rust, blooms, pours and imprints are visually persuasive before they are compositionally necessary. Accident is not automatically freedom.

McIntyre’s best paintings avoid this trap by making contingency answer to structure. A crisp figurative fragment cuts through a dispersed field; a hard edge halts a wash; an ugly colour prevents atmosphere from becoming tasteful. The work succeeds when material surprise is not the conclusion but the next problem.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/emma-mcintyre-roses-of-pieria-2026.jpg
content.caption: Emma McIntyre, The roses of Pieria, 2026, oil and mixed media on canvas. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner.

content.content: XIII · What remains unfinished

No artwork literally escapes completion. At some point the painting leaves the studio, receives a title, enters an exhibition and becomes an object of ownership. Conservation may eventually work to slow the very transformations the artist invited. Institutional life rebuilds stability around unstable matter.

But McIntyre’s work retains a productive remainder. Completion becomes a negotiated threshold rather than a natural fact. The artist stops composing; the chemistry does not entirely stop. The collector acquires an object but not perfect control over its future appearance. Time is not damage arriving from outside. It is one of the materials already included.
McIntyre does not paint an image of change. She gives change a limited authorship inside the painting.
XIV · Verdict

This body holds / swamp stuff offers a compelling answer to a central problem in contemporary abstraction: how can a painting remain materially intelligent after the language of gesture, stain and chance has become familiar? McIntyre’s answer is to make those marks consequences of real reactions, bodily procedures and historical materials.

The paintings are not alive, but neither are they inert in the way their digital reproductions suggest. They oxidise, reflect, absorb and age. Their refusal to finish is modest rather than theatrical. It reminds us that every stable image is a temporary agreement between matter, time and the conditions under which someone is looking.

Emma McIntyre: This body holds / swamp stuff is at David Zwirner, 52 Walker Street, New York, from 18 September to 24 October 2026. All works in the exhibition were made in 2026. articles.title: The Building Wears Its Forces: Inside the Radical Structure of Powerhouse Parramatta
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Powerhouse Parramatta puts a three-layer steel lattice outside the museum so that its vast rooms can remain almost impossibly free—a building in which structure, spectacle and civic promise become the same argument.

content.content: Most buildings conceal the labour that keeps them standing. Columns disappear into walls; trusses retreat above ceilings; mechanical systems are tidied into zones the public never sees. Powerhouse Parramatta reverses that etiquette. Its white steel lattice wraps the museum like an enlarged scientific diagram, turning load, span and resistance into the first thing the city encounters.

Designed by Moreau Kusunoki with Genton, and engineered across more than twenty disciplines by Arup, the new institution in Western Sydney is due to open on 7 November 2026. Before a single object is interpreted inside, the building has already made an audacious claim: engineering is not the mute servant of architecture. It can be architecture’s public language.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-north-view.jpg
content.caption: Powerhouse Parramatta, north view. Image courtesy Genton and Powerhouse Parramatta.

content.content: I · A museum built from incompatible demands

The brief asked for seven enormous presentation spaces, some capable of holding machines and objects that ordinary galleries cannot admit. It also asked for openness to the city, a generous public ground, views toward the Parramatta River, future adaptability and the environmental discipline expected of a major public project. Each ambition pressures the others.

A large span wants depth and mass. A transparent edge wants slenderness. Museum conservation wants sealed, controlled interiors; civic life wants porosity. A flood-adjacent site demands resilience, while the institution promises intimacy and ease. Powerhouse Parramatta is compelling because it does not smooth these contradictions into a neutral box. It lets their negotiation determine the form.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-frame-construction.jpg
content.caption: The primary frame during construction. The steelwork carries gallery volumes while preserving unusually large clear interiors. Courtesy Genton.

content.content: II · The exoskeleton is not an ornament

The diagonal façade can be mistaken for a graphic pattern applied after the fact. Structurally, it is the opposite. Developed from the competition concept with engineer Jun Sato and advanced by Arup, the “lattice³” system is a three-layered exoskeleton: large V, X and N arrangements manage forces at the scale of the building, while finer chords and diagonals work as laced columns.

This hierarchy matters. A conventional frame repeats columns through the plan and asks exhibitions to adapt around them. Here, structure migrates toward the perimeter so that the interior can become radically available. The image of freedom inside is purchased by an exceptionally specific discipline outside.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-exoskeleton-prototype.jpg
content.caption: Full-scale exoskeleton prototype. The apparent irregularity is governed by force paths rather than by a decorative grid. Courtesy Genton.

content.content: III · Freedom has a shape

Architects often describe flexible space as though flexibility meant absence: fewer walls, fewer columns, fewer decisions. Powerhouse Parramatta reveals the hidden cost of that word. To make a room capable of receiving changing exhibitions, performances and exceptionally large objects, the building must make hard decisions elsewhere—about transfer, bracing, tolerances, access and the route of every service.

The largest presentation volume is column-free and comparable, according to Arup, to fifteen Olympic swimming pools in volume. Its northern elevation can open toward the river through an immense mechanical hoisting door. The room therefore operates less like a conventional gallery than a piece of civic machinery: enclosure can become aperture, and a controlled interior can momentarily address the city.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-presentation-space-one.jpg
content.caption: Presentation Space 1, conceived as a vast column-free volume for objects, installations and events that exceed the scale of a conventional gallery. Courtesy Moreau Kusunoki, Genton and Powerhouse Parramatta.

content.content: IV · The door is architecture at the scale of infrastructure

A domestic door separates two rooms. The hoisting façade at Parramatta separates two environmental regimes and two ideas of publicness. When closed, it helps maintain the conditions a museum requires. When open, it converts the gallery into a stage facing the river and turns the building envelope into an event.

This is kinetic architecture without the usual fantasy that movement alone makes a building alive. The important fact is not that a huge wall can move, but that the institution must decide when to expose itself. Openness becomes operational, scheduled and negotiated—not a permanent transparency rendered harmless in glass.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-river-opening.jpg
content.caption: The opening of Presentation Space 1 toward the river. The façade acts as an environmental boundary, loading interface and urban proscenium. Courtesy Genton and Powerhouse Parramatta.

content.content: V · A stack, not a procession

The seven presentation spaces are conceived as distinct boxes stacked into a compact body. This abandons the classical museum’s orderly sequence of galleries. Visitors move among volumes with different scales, proportions and atmospheres; circulation looks across a shared interior and toward the public realm.

Stacking is both an urban and structural act. It reduces the footprint, releasing more of the site as public space, but intensifies the transfer of loads through the building. It also produces intervals between rooms—those ambiguous zones that Moreau Kusunoki connects to the Japanese idea of ma, the active space between defined things.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-discovery-space.jpg
content.caption: A discovery and learning space within the stacked museum. Courtesy Moreau Kusunoki, Genton and Powerhouse Parramatta.

content.content: VI · The difficult politics of lightness

The competition jury praised the proposal’s lightness. Yet a building of 34,000 square metres, made from major quantities of steel and concrete, is not materially light. Architectural lightness here is perceptual and organisational: the ground is opened, the frame appears porous, and huge rooms are lifted away from a forest of supports.

That distinction should remain visible. Contemporary architecture frequently converts engineering intensity into an image of effortless elegance. At Parramatta the effect is beautiful, but the lattice also gives the effort a face. Its density registers that openness is constructed, calculated and materially expensive.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-lattice-detail.jpg
content.caption: Detail of the multi-scale steel lattice. Large braces and finer laced elements make different orders of force legible on the same elevation. Courtesy Genton.

content.content: VII · A science museum that demonstrates itself

For a museum devoted to applied arts and sciences, exposed structure carries an unusual pedagogical charge. The building does not merely contain accounts of engineering; it offers itself as an argument about how engineering can work. Load paths become spatial experience. A visitor may not calculate the frame, but can sense that the diagonals are doing more than composing a façade.

This is not the old modernist promise of total legibility. The structure remains profoundly complex, dependent on digital modelling, fabrication tolerances and specialist coordination invisible to most visitors. What becomes public is not a complete explanation, but evidence that the building has an intelligible logic.
VIII · Twenty disciplines in one envelope

Arup records more than 240 staff working across structural, civil, flood, fire, façade, acoustic, mechanical, electrical, security, blast, pedestrian-flow and other fields. That list is not incidental project trivia. It describes the true authorship of a contemporary building of this complexity.

The romantic image of architecture begins with a singular sketch. Powerhouse Parramatta begins there too, but survives only through coordination: ducts must pass without weakening the frame; façade tolerances must meet structural movement; fire strategy must accommodate monumental voids; crowds and enormous objects need separate yet intersecting routes. Complexity is less a spectacular geometry than the sustained resolution of dependencies.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-north-view.jpg
content.caption: North view toward the Parramatta River. The exoskeleton must coordinate structure, façade, environmental control and the public identity of the museum. Courtesy Moreau Kusunoki, Genton and Powerhouse Parramatta.

content.content: IX · The river is not scenery

Architectural descriptions often turn water into a view. At Parramatta, the river is also a dynamic system and a source of flood risk. The project’s public promise—to reconnect the city centre with the river—therefore cannot be separated from civil engineering, landscape levels, evacuation planning and the design of resilient infrastructure.

This produces an important tension. The museum presents itself as porous and river-facing, while the institution’s collections and technical systems depend on protection from environmental instability. The architecture must make contact and defence coexist. Its civic openness is credible only because harder layers of risk management support it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-drone.jpg
content.caption: The compact museum footprint beside the Parramatta River releases ground for a new civic landscape while intensifying the demands placed on the building. Courtesy Powerhouse studio.

content.content: X · Sustainability beyond the badge

The completed project has received a 6 Star Green Star Design rating and is planned as an all-electric building supplied by renewable energy, with a climate-positive operational ambition. These are significant commitments for a museum, a building type burdened by long hours, high visitor loads and strict environmental conditioning.

Yet operational targets are only one part of the environmental account. A steel exoskeleton and vast controlled volumes contain substantial embodied carbon. The more difficult question is whether the adaptability promised by the frame can extend the building’s useful life enough to repay that initial investment. Flexibility becomes an ecological claim only when institutions actually use it to avoid premature demolition and refit.
XI · The institution and the city

Powerhouse Parramatta is described as a cultural platform for Western Sydney, a region historically underserved by the metropolitan distribution of major institutions. The architecture answers through scale and visibility: this is not a satellite or a modest local annex, but a building intended to alter the cultural map of Sydney.

Such claims deserve both recognition and scrutiny. Monumental investment can create access, employment and civic identity, but a public building does not become socially generous through transparency alone. Its schedules, ticketing, programming, employment, transport connections and relationships with local communities will determine whether the open ground is truly public.
XII · The risk of the icon

The lattice gives Powerhouse Parramatta an instantly recognisable image, and recognisability is a powerful currency for a new museum. The danger is that structural honesty hardens into branding: a complex system becomes a logo, photographed from the same angles until the institution and its city disappear behind white diagonals.

The building’s best defence against that fate lies in use. If the enormous rooms accept unruly programmes, if the river opening alters how events meet the city, and if the public spaces remain hospitable without requiring consumption, the exoskeleton will be more than an icon. It will be the apparatus that enables institutional change.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/powerhouse-parramatta-aerial.jpg
content.caption: Powerhouse Parramatta as urban figure: a compact stack of cultural rooms, wrapped in structure and set within a river landscape. Courtesy Moreau Kusunoki, Genton and Powerhouse Parramatta.

content.content: XIII · A building that explains its price

Public architecture is always asked to justify itself twice: first through what it provides, and then through what it visibly symbolises. Powerhouse Parramatta makes its expenditure legible as capacity. The span, the opening wall, the suspended volumes and the public ground are not finishes applied to a standard container. They are difficult things the building can do.

That does not settle every debate about cost, site or institutional priorities. Architecture cannot answer political questions with engineering virtuosity. But it can prevent complexity from becoming mere opacity. Here, part of the answer stands outside, in full view, bearing the loads.
The building’s freedom is not the absence of structure. It is the result of moving structure to the edge, multiplying its intelligence and allowing the public to see the bargain.
XIV · Verdict

Powerhouse Parramatta belongs to a lineage of buildings—from Centre Pompidou onward—that turn technical systems into civic theatre. Its contribution is subtler than simple exposure. The lattice does not display every pipe and duct. It concentrates a vast field of coordination into a single structural language capable of appearing intimate in detail and monumental across the skyline.

The result is contemporary architecture at its most ambitious and most vulnerable: technically exact, institutionally symbolic, environmentally accountable, politically loaded and dependent on future use for the fulfilment of its promises. When the museum opens, the decisive question will not be whether the exoskeleton photographs well. It will be whether all that visible force has created room for forms of public life the architects could not predict.

Powerhouse Parramatta is scheduled to open on 7 November 2026. Designed by Moreau Kusunoki with Genton; multidisciplinary engineering by Arup, with the competition-stage exoskeleton developed with Jun Sato Structural Engineers. articles.title: Who Owns the Hours? Audemars Piguet and the Art of Manufacturing Time
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: A watch measures seconds, but a luxury brand manufactures something larger: authorship, scarcity and cultural time. Inside Audemars Piguet’s radical return to collective craft.

content.content: A mechanical watch is an absurd object in the most productive sense of the word. The telephone in a pocket measures time more accurately, updates itself automatically and costs a fraction of a complicated movement. Yet collectors wait years and spend fortunes for a machine that gains or loses seconds. Its value begins precisely where utility ends.

Audemars Piguet understands this paradox better than almost any modern watchmaker. The company does not simply sell instruments that tell time. It constructs a cultural system in which steel can behave like a precious metal, hand-finishing becomes evidence of authorship, scarcity becomes desire, a museum becomes a movement, and contemporary art teaches the brand how to speak beyond the wrist.
I · The product that cannot justify itself by function

Luxury watches are often described as art because they are difficult to make. Difficulty alone is not enough. A jet engine is difficult; a medical scanner is difficult. Art enters when technical labour is made available for contemplation – when a solution exceeds its practical task and begins to organise attention, memory and interpretation.

The decisive material in watchmaking is therefore not gold, ceramic or steel. It is time twice over: the time indicated by the hands and the time sedimented in the object. Polishing a bevel nobody will see, adjusting a repeater by ear, or cutting a stone to fit one irregular link converts hours of labour into an almost invisible surplus. The collector purchases condensed duration.
The first century: complexity before the icon

Audemars Piguet began in 1875, when Jules Louis Audemars and Edward Auguste Piguet established their workshop in Le Brassus. The location was not picturesque branding invented later. The Vallée de Joux had developed a dispersed economy of highly specialised makers whose long winters encouraged domestic precision work. The company emerged from that network rather than from a modern factory system.

From 1882 onward, grande complication work became a continuous thread through periods when such objects had almost no rational commercial future. A grande complication combines several demanding functions – traditionally a calendar, chronograph and chiming mechanism – inside one coordinated movement. Its significance is not the number of functions but their negotiation for space, energy and reliability.

The 1899 Universelle pocket watch, now positioned at the centre of the Musée Atelier, condensed nineteen complications and 1,168 components into one object. It established an enduring AP strategy: technical density becomes cultural authority when the mechanism can be narrated as the limit of what a generation knows how to make.
II · Royal Oak: when steel became an argument
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-royal-oak-1972.jpg
content.caption: The 1972 Royal Oak: Gérald Genta’s 39 mm steel sports watch overturned the hierarchy between precious material and precious labour. Courtesy Audemars Piguet Heritage.

content.content: The Royal Oak, launched in 1972 from Gérald Genta’s design, remains Audemars Piguet’s central act of cultural engineering. Its 39-millimetre body was large for the period; the octagonal bezel, eight visible screws, integrated bracelet and patterned dial refused the discreet codes of traditional luxury. Most provocatively, it was executed in hand-finished stainless steel and positioned with the seriousness of gold.

This was not the elevation of cheap matter through marketing alone. Steel is unforgiving: alternating satin-brushed planes and polished bevels must remain exact across the case and every articulated bracelet link. The design makes finishing structural. Light travels across the watch and reveals any broken edge. Craft is no longer hidden inside the mechanism; it becomes the surface language.

Royal Oak’s great invention was conceptual. It separated preciousness from raw material and attached it to design, labour and controlled difficulty. The visible screw did not pretend the object had descended intact from heaven. It made assembly part of the image. Industrial signs became luxury because they were executed with jeweller-like discipline.
Finishing is not decoration

A movement can function before it is beautifully finished. Anglage, black polishing, circular graining and Geneva stripes do not necessarily make it keep better time. Their purpose is epistemic as much as aesthetic: they expose the maker’s control over surfaces at a scale where a fraction of a millimetre changes the reflection.

Anglage turns a sharp machined edge into an even, gleaming bevel. Interior angles are particularly revealing because a rotating industrial tool cannot form them cleanly; they must be approached by hand. Black polishing produces a plane so flat that it alternates between mirror brightness and apparent blackness according to the angle of light. The eye reads precision through behaviour, not ornament.

This is why transparent casebacks matter. They transform labour once reserved for a watchmaker’s bench into a spectacle for the owner. The movement is no longer only an engine. It is an exhibition whose smallest surfaces carry the proof of time spent.
III · The danger of becoming your own icon

An icon solves recognition and creates another problem: repetition. The Royal Oak silhouette is so legible that colour, complication, ceramic and celebrity collaboration can be placed inside it almost indefinitely. Commercially, this is extraordinary. Culturally, it risks reducing innovation to variations on a secure outline.

Audemars Piguet’s identity is therefore caught between dependence and escape. The brand must protect the object that made contemporary haute horlogerie possible while demonstrating that its imagination is larger than one octagon. The new Atelier des Établisseurs is the clearest attempt in years to reopen that space.
The calendar that remembers February

A perpetual calendar is a miniature model of an irregular human convention. It must distinguish 30-day months, 31-day months and February, then insert a leap day every four years without ordinary manual correction. In 1955 Audemars Piguet introduced the first wristwatch perpetual calendar to display the leap-year cycle, turning hidden calculation into readable information.

The complication is philosophically strange. The mechanism does not measure an astronomical truth directly; it mechanically remembers a calendar assembled through centuries of political and religious adjustment. A perpetual calendar is therefore a machine that performs culture as though culture were nature.

This distinction clarifies why watchmaking belongs in an art journal. Its highest achievements are not simply accurate. They materialise abstract systems – calendars, celestial cycles, elapsed intervals, musical sequences – and force them to coexist inside a wearable volume.
IV · 2026: the return of the établisseur
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-etablisseurs-triptych.jpg
content.caption: The three inaugural Établisseurs creations – Galets, Peacock and Nomade – bring independent specialists back into a named network of collective authorship. Courtesy Audemars Piguet.

content.content: Before the vertically integrated manufacture became the dominant ideal, Swiss watchmaking depended on établissage: a network of specialised workshops coordinated by an établisseur. One maker produced an escapement, another a case, another a dial; the finished object was not the output of a single factory but the orchestration of distributed intelligence.

In 2026 Audemars Piguet revived that model inside the Musée Atelier at Le Brassus. The Atelier des Établisseurs connects the manufacture’s watchmakers with independent engravers, enamel specialists, skeletonisers, gem-setters, lapidaries, designers and precision engineers. The radical gesture is not nostalgia. It is credit: the principal artisans behind each object are named.

That change matters because luxury usually performs collective labour as singular brand authorship. Hundreds of hands disappear beneath a logo. By restoring names to the network, AP moves closer to the credit structures of film, architecture and contemporary art – fields in which authorship remains unequal, but collaboration can at least become visible.
Calibre 3098: engineering an asymmetry

The Galets case is not a conventional round housing given a decorative outline. Its asymmetry obliges the calibre to answer the case. Calibre 3098 was developed from the historical 3090 architecture and reshaped so that movement, case and stone composition share the same off-centre logic.

A balance oscillates at one end of this miniature landscape while bridges distribute support across the available volume. Hand-grained surfaces and chamfered edges make the movement legible without forcing it into bilateral symmetry. The achievement is integration: engineering does not correct the designer after the fact; it participates in the form.
V · Galets: nature disciplined without becoming uniform
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-etablisseurs-galets.jpg
content.caption: Audemars Piguet, Établisseurs Galets, presented in 2026. Natural stones turn the watch into a singular composition rather than a repeatable industrial surface. Courtesy Audemars Piguet.

content.content: Établisseurs Galets uses turquoise and tiger’s eye for its dial and bracelet links. Each stone carries veining, density and colour that cannot be perfectly repeated. Its pebble-like geometry refers to the shores of the Lac de Joux, but the important fact is technical: irregular mineral matter must be cut into an exact wearable system.

The watch stages a negotiation between uniqueness and standard. Calibre 3098 is a contemporary movement developed for the piece; the asymmetric case and sapphire crystals require precise repeatability. Yet each arrangement of stone refuses total equivalence. Nature supplies difference, while craft gives difference a durable frame.

This is the opposite of merely decorating a familiar watch with an exotic dial. The oval case, the curved movement and the stone-set bracelet share one syntax. Material does not illustrate a story added by marketing. It changes the geometry of the object.
VI · Peacock: a secret watch and the theatre of disclosure
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-etablisseurs-peacock.jpg
content.caption: Établisseurs Peacock revives the nineteenth-century secret watch: an engraved and enamelled creature whose display appears through movement. Courtesy Audemars Piguet.

content.content: Établisseurs Peacock belongs to the history of the secret watch, in which the time display is concealed within a jewel. Designer Kenan Geraud’s peacock opens into colour; engraved wings, translucent enamel and articulated gold links transform checking the hour into a small performance.

The object refuses modern watchmaking’s obsession with instant legibility. Time must be revealed. That delay is not an inconvenience accidentally preserved from the nineteenth century; it is the work’s central choreography. The wearer activates the piece and momentarily becomes its performer.
Here the boundary between jewellery, automaton and watch collapses. Function remains, but it has been deliberately subordinated to encounter. One does not glance at Peacock. One enters its sequence.
VII · Nomade: time leaves the wrist
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-etablisseurs-nomade.jpg
content.caption: Établisseurs Nomade can move between pocket watch and table object. Its identity changes with its support and situation. Courtesy Audemars Piguet.

content.content: Établisseurs Nomade can operate as a pocket watch or a small table clock. This mobility recalls the long history before the wrist became time’s default address. It also shifts the object from accessory to sculpture: placed upright, it occupies a room and establishes a relationship with architecture.

Its skeletonised calibre exposes depth rather than merely removing material for visual drama. Bridges, voids and hand-finished edges compose a mechanical interior that changes with viewpoint. The watch does not carry a picture; the movement is the picture, and its subject is organised energy.
One watchmaker, one chain of responsibility

Each Établisseurs piece is assembled and adjusted by one master watchmaker. That continuity differs from a production line in which specialised operations pass anonymously from station to station. A single maker follows the behaviour of the movement through assembly, regulation and casing, accumulating knowledge of one object’s particular resistances.

Individual responsibility does not mean solitary creation. Galets depends on gemmologist and lapidary Mario Senape, specialist case makers, jewellers and movement constructors; Peacock brings together designer Kenan Geraud, engravers, enameller Vanessa Lecci and goldsmiths; Nomade requires stone cutting, skeletonisation and minute case tolerances. The single watchmaker is the final integrator of a visibly plural authorship.

The model resembles an orchestra more than the mythology of the lone artist. Specialisation increases difference, while coordination prevents difference from becoming noise. The brand’s meaningful role is not to claim every gesture as its own but to sustain the conditions under which the gestures can meet.
VIII · A museum shaped like a mainspring
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-musee-atelier-spiral.jpg
content.caption: The Musée Atelier’s spiral route tightens and releases like a watch spring. Its 470-ton roof is carried by 108 curved structural-glass panels. Courtesy Musée Atelier Audemars Piguet.

content.content: Audemars Piguet’s most complete self-portrait is not a watch but a building. BIG’s glass spiral connects the founders’ 1868 house to the contemporary Musée Atelier. Visitors move clockwise toward the centre and unwind in the opposite direction, following a path modelled on a coiled spring.

The metaphor is unusually literal, yet the engineering prevents it from becoming stage scenery. A 470-ton steel roof is held by 108 unique curved glass panes, some composed of seven layers and reaching twelve centimetres in thickness. Structure performs the same trick as haute horlogerie: great force appears as precision, and precision appears as lightness.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-musee-atelier-exterior.jpg
content.caption: Musée Atelier Audemars Piguet at Le Brassus links the historical workshop to BIG’s glass spiral. Courtesy Musée Atelier Audemars Piguet.

content.content: Inside, approximately 300 watches sit beside live workshops for restoration, métiers d’art and grandes complications. The museum does not merely preserve completed masterpieces; it displays labour in progress. Brand history becomes present tense.
Architecture as a regulating mechanism

The Musée Atelier’s glass does structural and environmental work simultaneously. Curved panels carry the roof, admit the valley as a continuous horizon and are screened by a brass mesh that moderates light and temperature. The grass-covered steel roof adds thermal mass and manages rainwater. The apparently immaterial spiral is, in fact, a calibrated environmental machine.

Its exhibition route also manages narrative energy. Scenographer ATELIER BRÜCKNER conceived the displays as a musical score with interludes, crescendos and a climax around the Universelle. Time is not represented by a straight chronology alone. It is paced through compression, release and recurrence.
IX · When a brand becomes a curator

Audemars Piguet Contemporary has commissioned international artists since 2012. Crucially, the resulting works belong to the artists and enter their own practices rather than a corporate collection. Two in-house curators support projects from inception to exhibition, often with partner institutions.

The programme’s artists – including Cao Fei, Ryoji Ikeda, Alexandra Pirici, Tomás Saraceno, Sallisa Rosa, Yu Ji and others – are not selected to decorate boutiques with images of watches. Their works address data, ecology, performance, memory, sound and unstable material systems. The relationship to the brand is structural rather than iconographic: sustained production, technical ambition and the measurement of change.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-contemporary-ryoji-ikeda.jpg
content.caption: Ryoji Ikeda’s data-based practice turns measurement into an overwhelming field of perception. Audemars Piguet Contemporary commissioned works from his data-verse project. Courtesy the artist and Audemars Piguet Contemporary.

content.content: X · Ryoji Ikeda: precision beyond comprehension

Ryoji Ikeda works with numerical data at scales the senses cannot assimilate. Points, frequencies and streams are subjected to extreme formal precision, yet the result is not clarity. It is sublimity: knowledge becomes so dense that it is experienced as light, vibration and vertigo.

The affinity with watchmaking is exact and dangerous. Both fields begin with measurement; both convert systems into perceptual form. But Ikeda’s work also reveals measurement’s limit. More data does not necessarily produce more understanding. A perfect instrument can confront us with our inability to read the world it quantifies.
XI · Alexandra Pirici: the body as an unstable archive
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-contemporary-alexandra-pirici.jpg
content.caption: Alexandra Pirici’s performative work replaces the permanent object with bodies, relations and recurring acts. Courtesy the artist and Audemars Piguet Contemporary.

content.content: Alexandra Pirici’s practice seems to contradict the luxury watch. A watch promises a lasting object; performance persists through bodies, memory and reenactment. Pirici makes that opposition productive. Her living formations ask whether an archive can exist without freezing what it preserves.

For a company whose economic authority depends on durable objects and traceable provenance, supporting work that cannot be possessed in the same way is culturally significant. It allows the patronage programme to test a form of value that does not sit comfortably in a safe.
XII · Yu Ji: matter remembers pressure
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/audemars-piguet-contemporary-yu-ji.jpg
content.caption: Yu Ji’s sculptural environments attend to weight, erosion, bodies and the slow agency of materials. Courtesy the artist and Audemars Piguet Contemporary.

content.content: Yu Ji’s sculpture brings the argument back to matter. Stone, concrete, metal and organic forms appear not as passive supplies but as substances with histories of pressure, extraction and weathering. Time is registered through fracture and accretion rather than hands on a dial.

This expands the brand’s preferred notion of craftsmanship. A perfectly finished watch tends to erase the violence of transformation: ore becomes alloy, stone becomes a component, abrasive labour becomes immaculate surface. Contemporary art can restore resistance to matter and ask what elegance has edited out.
What the commissions actually change

The strongest AP Contemporary projects do not translate watch components into enlarged sculpture. Ryoji Ikeda turns datasets into audiovisual environments whose precision exceeds comprehension. Alexandra Pirici uses living bodies to question whether memory requires an object. Yu Ji works with erosion and material fatigue. These practices complicate the brand’s own promises of permanence, mastery and possession.

Because the commissioned works remain the artists’ property, the programme avoids one common form of corporate extraction: funding a work and absorbing it permanently into a branded collection. The arrangement still produces cultural capital for AP, but it also permits the artwork to develop an institutional life beyond its sponsor.
That distinction is more consequential than visual alignment. Patronage becomes credible when it finances difference rather than demanding resemblance.
XIII · Patronage is never innocent

No luxury-funded art programme exists outside marketing. Cultural association transfers prestige; Art Basel access produces clients; the language of experimentation refreshes a heritage brand. Pretending otherwise would make criticism useless.

But commercial motive does not cancel cultural consequence. The relevant questions are more exact: Does the artist retain ownership? Is the work allowed to resist the sponsor’s image? Are curatorial decisions sustained beyond a campaign cycle? Does funding create work that would not otherwise exist? AP’s model earns attention because its commissions remain with artists and travel through institutions rather than functioning only as branded décor.
XIV · Scarcity, price and the aesthetics of waiting

The luxury watch market converts restricted supply into social energy. Waiting lists, allocation systems and auction premiums make access part of the object. Time is not only displayed by the watch; it is imposed on the buyer. Desire is administered through delay.

The ultra-limited Établisseurs pieces intensify that economy, but they also expose its material basis. Each watch takes weeks and depends on specialists whose capacity cannot be scaled without changing the work. Scarcity can be manufactured as strategy, yet it can also be the honest consequence of refusing industrial acceleration. The two forms are often entangled.
The secondary market and the second clock

A watch has a second clock running beside its movement: the market. Auction results, discontinued references, condition reports and provenance convert ownership history into price. Patina can be valued as evidence of time, while replacement parts may reduce value even when they improve function. Collectors do not simply want an old object; they want continuity that can be authenticated.

This produces a paradox. The manufacture promises service over generations, but intervention can erase the very traces the market rewards. Restoration must decide which time to preserve: the ideal form intended by the maker or the accumulated life carried by the object. The Musée Atelier’s restoration workshop sits precisely inside that ethical problem.
The best watch conservation does not return every surface to youth. It distinguishes damage from history, maintaining mechanical life without manufacturing a false past.
XV · What a brand can learn from art

Brands usually approach art hoping that art will make them appear imaginative. The more interesting possibility runs in the opposite direction: art can teach a company to tolerate outcomes it does not fully control. A commissioned work that remains recognisably the artist’s – not an illustration of corporate values – is evidence of that tolerance.

The Atelier des Établisseurs applies the same lesson internally. Naming independent makers distributes credit and allows their differences to enter the object. The brand remains the organiser and beneficiary, but authorship becomes a network rather than a sealed signature.
A mechanical watch does not defeat time. It gives time a body – and then asks us to decide whose labour, memory and desire that body contains.
XVI · Verdict

Audemars Piguet is most persuasive when it stops insisting that watchmaking simply is art and instead reveals the conditions under which the comparison becomes meaningful: conceptual risk, exacting form, embodied labour, material intelligence, historical self-criticism and authorship that exceeds a logo.

Royal Oak made steel precious by making workmanship visible. The Musée Atelier turned the spring into architecture. Audemars Piguet Contemporary moved patronage toward artist-owned commissions. Now the Atelier des Établisseurs brings individual makers back into the story of the manufactured object. Together these projects propose a demanding definition of luxury: not expense alone, but time made legible as collective human attention.

This independent editorial article was prepared from official Audemars Piguet, AP Chronicles and Musée Atelier sources. It is not sponsored and does not claim an in-person visit. Product and programme images are reproduced for editorial review with credits supplied by Audemars Piguet.
