articles.title: Cathy de Monchaux: The Poise of Wounds
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: At the Palais de Tokyo, Cathy de Monchaux turned metal, velvet, dust and fragile armatures into a sculptural language of desire, danger and extraordinary beauty.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-05.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Antoine Aphesbero. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: Some exhibitions make sculpture look monumental. Cathy de Monchaux’s first major retrospective at the Palais de Tokyo made it look alive. Across roughly fifty works dating from 1984 to the present, metal, velvet, dust, tracing paper, straps, rivets and delicate armatures formed an unsettled ecology of bodies. Nothing simply stood still. Even the most rigid structure seemed to be breathing, bracing itself or remembering an injury.

Studio, wounds and battles, desire is the reiteration of hope closed on 13 September 2026, but its images remain unusually difficult to put away. The exhibition was beautiful in the way a thorn, a relic or a half-remembered dream can be beautiful: not because it reassures, but because it gives form to the contradiction between vulnerability and force.

Independent editorial review by Viacheslav Munister. Exhibition dates, descriptions and image credits are based on official Palais de Tokyo materials. Images are reproduced from the institution’s press visuals; rights remain with Cathy de Monchaux, ADAGP and the credited photographers.
The sculpture that refuses a clean edge

De Monchaux’s objects are never satisfied with a single category. They can be sculpture, reliquary, anatomical fragment, stage set, machine, shell or weapon. They often occupy the wall like a drawing that has thickened into matter, or the floor like a body that has not decided whether to crawl, stand or disappear.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-002.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, “Studio, wounds and battles, desire is the reiteration of hope”, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Aurélien Mole. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: This refusal of a clean edge is central to the exhibition’s sensuality. A surface may appear soft until the eye notices its armour. A metal structure may look severe until it begins to resemble a rib cage, a flower or a nest. The works are made from transitions. They live in the moment when one material becomes another kind of image.
An intimacy made from metal

The most striking quality of de Monchaux’s work is not its darkness but its intimacy. The sculptures seem to know the scale of the body. They bend, clasp, fold and open like gestures that have been enlarged without losing their private origin. Even the more spectacular installations retain the feeling of something handled, repaired or protected.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-009.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Aurélien Mole. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: Her vocabulary is full of structures that support and restrain at the same time. Straps can hold a form together, but they can also bind it. Ribs can protect, but they can also become a cage. The work does not decide which reading is correct. It makes the viewer feel the pressure between them.

That pressure is why the sculptures never become decorative, even when they are extraordinarily refined. Beauty is not a surface applied to difficult material. It is the exactness with which difficulty has been given a body.
The forest inside the gallery
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-32.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Quentin Chevrier. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: In the gallery, pale branches and clustered forms project from the wall like a forest translated into nerves. The effect is both natural and artificial. It recalls roots, antlers, coral, lace and the architecture of an inner organ, yet every part remains visibly made. The eye moves from the overall silhouette to the individual joint, then back again, as if the work were asking to be read at two speeds.

De Monchaux’s sculptures often create this double scale. From a distance, they become landscapes or battle scenes. Up close, they reveal minute acts of construction: a rivet, a fold, a seam, a rough edge. Grandeur is built from attention. The monumental is not the opposite of the intimate; it is the intimate carried carefully to another register.
Desire is never innocent

The exhibition’s title places desire beside wounds and battles, and the pairing is exact. De Monchaux’s work is sensual, but never passive. Its surfaces invite the eye and then make the eye cautious. The viewer is drawn toward velvet, cavities, polished metal and soft-looking forms, only to discover a hidden threat: a spine, a point, a hard seam, an opening that refuses to explain itself.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-19.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Quentin Chevrier. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: This is not the eroticism of smooth surfaces. It is an eroticism of hesitation. The body recognises something in the work, but cannot immediately decide whether that recognition means attraction, fear, memory or all three at once. De Monchaux makes sculpture out of the delay between these responses.
The archive of the damaged

The retrospective included technical drawings and archives of destroyed works, and this widened the exhibition’s emotional range. The finished sculptures were not presented as isolated miracles. They were surrounded by evidence of trial, failure, disappearance and reconstruction. A destroyed work still has a body in the archive. Its absence becomes another material.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-05.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Antoine Aphesbero. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: This matters because de Monchaux’s work is fundamentally about what holds. An armature holds a form; a memory holds an event; a title holds an image open; a museum holds a fragile object long enough for strangers to encounter it. But every support can fail. The exhibition never hides that fact. It gives failure a quiet dignity.
A sculpture of the almost-human

The works often hover near the human figure without becoming figurative in any conventional sense. A vertical structure suggests a torso. A cluster becomes a group of bodies. A protrusion feels like a limb, a horn or an architectural brace. This almost-human quality is where the sculptures become most psychologically intense.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-32.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Quentin Chevrier. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: The viewer begins to project a story onto the object, then the object withdraws. It refuses to become a character in a simple narrative. It remains matter, and that refusal is liberating. The sculpture does not have to represent a person in order to carry the pressure of a person’s life.
Against the straight line

The Palais de Tokyo presentation was also a quiet critique of the straight line: the straight line of the pedestal, the clean line of progress, the hard line of authority. De Monchaux bends, tangles and interrupts those lines. Her forms make room for asymmetry, softness and the intelligence of the detour.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-002.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Aurélien Mole. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: The effect is not chaos. It is a different order. The sculptures are carefully composed, but their order is organic rather than administrative. It grows by repetition, pressure and response. One shape touches another; one material changes the temperature of the next. The gallery becomes a field of relations rather than a sequence of isolated objects.
The elegance of resistance
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/cathy-009.jpg
content.caption: Cathy de Monchaux, installation view, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photo: Aurélien Mole. © Adagp, Paris, 2026.

content.content: There is a particularly British severity to de Monchaux’s sensibility: a willingness to let elegance coexist with discomfort, and to let humour appear at the edge of the grotesque. But the exhibition’s emotional geography is wider than national style. These works speak to the body under pressure, to the architectures that protect and confine it, and to the strange optimism of continuing to make something delicate after damage.
The beauty of Cathy de Monchaux is never innocent. It is beauty that has learned how to brace itself.

That is why the exhibition stayed with me after its closing date. Not as a catalogue of forms, but as a physical intelligence: the knowledge that fragility can be engineered, that a wound can become an aperture, and that a sculpture can be both warning and shelter.

Studio, wounds and battles did not ask to be admired from a safe distance. It made the distance unstable. The closer one looked, the more the works changed register – from ornament to anatomy, from relic to threat, from private memory to collective image. Their beauty was not an escape from the world. It was a way of remaining awake inside it.
Palais de Tokyo – official exhibition page

Image credits: Cathy de Monchaux installation views, Palais de Tokyo, 2026. Photos by Antoine Aphesbero, Aurélien Mole and Quentin Chevrier. © Adagp, Paris, 2026. articles.title: How to Stand in an Unstable World: Mona Hatoum at Fondazione Prada
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Three rooms, more than thirty thousand glass spheres and a metal tower that repeatedly loses its balance: Mona Hatoum turns sculpture into an instrument for measuring instability.

content.content: Mona Hatoum’s new installation at Fondazione Prada begins with a simple correction to the way exhibitions are usually seen. The visitor does not stand outside the work and interpret it from a stable position. The floor may be clear, the walls may be still, but the body is already implicated: looking upward through a suspended web, circling a world map that could scatter underfoot, listening to a nine-storey metal frame strain against its own collapse. “Over, under and in between” is less a sequence of objects than a set of physical propositions about how it feels to occupy a world whose structures remain visible while their promises have become unreliable.

Installed in the three rooms of the Cisterna, the project brings together two new works made for Milan, Web and Map (red), with all of a quiver from 2022. The economy is severe: glass, cable, aluminium, hinges, a motor; transparency, geometry, repetition. Yet this restraint does not produce calm. Hatoum takes the inherited language of Minimalism — the grid, the module, the industrial surface — and returns to it everything the modernist ideal attempted to exclude: the vulnerable body, the unstable border, the possibility of rupture, the noise of fear.

Independent editorial review by Viacheslav Munister. “Mona Hatoum. Over, under and in between” is on view at Fondazione Prada, Milan, from 29 January to 9 November 2026. Factual details and work specifications are based on the institution’s official exhibition materials.
A building that remembers containment

The Cisterna was built in 1909 to contain three storage tanks for the former distillery. Its conversion into exhibition space did not erase that history. Each tall concrete chamber still feels like a vessel: enclosed, vertical, slightly disproportionate to the person entering it. Hatoum’s decision to give one installation to each room turns the architecture into more than a backdrop. The visitor moves through three distinct conditions of containment — caught beneath a network, held at the edge of a diagram, and confronted by a structure that cannot keep its composure.

This matters because Hatoum has never treated space as neutral. Since moving from performance and video toward installation and sculpture in the early 1990s, she has made familiar forms behave strangely: domestic objects become threatening, maps refuse political certainty, grids become cages or nervous systems. Born in Beirut in 1952 to a Palestinian family and based in London since the Lebanese Civil War made her return impossible in 1975, she works from a biography marked by displacement without reducing every object to autobiography. The political force of her art lies precisely in this refusal of illustration. History enters as pressure, scale, temperature and distance.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-portrait-cisterna.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum with all of a quiver at Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2026. Photo: Marta Marinotti. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: Mona Hatoum stands in front of the folded metal grid of all of a quiver.
content.credit: Photo: Marta Marinotti. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: Web: beauty becomes a condition of capture
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-web-room.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, Web, 2026. Hand-blown clear glass spheres and stainless-steel cable. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: A suspended web of clear glass spheres stretches across a tall concrete gallery.
content.credit: Installation view of “Mona Hatoum. Over, under and in between”, Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2026. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: Web spans the first chamber overhead. Clear hand-blown spheres, irregular in size, are threaded along stainless-steel cable into a network that appears both precise and improvised. From the doorway it can resemble a constellation or a molecular model. Walking beneath it changes the register. The sparkling points become droplets under tension; the geometry lowers itself into the visitor’s field of movement. What looked celestial begins to feel adhesive.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-web-human-scale.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, Web, 2026. The suspended installation is calibrated against the scale and movement of visitors. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: Two visitors walk beneath a wide suspended net of clear glass spheres.
content.credit: Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: The work succeeds because its seduction is not incidental to its menace. A web is simultaneously a home and a trap, an image of connection and a technology of capture. Hatoum does not choose between these meanings. Nor does she allow transparency to stand for innocence. Every glass sphere receives light, but every sphere also marks a node in a structure that holds. The room is visually open and psychologically occupied.

There is a risk, in work about precarity, that fragility becomes an elegant effect — danger made beautiful enough for institutional display. Hatoum acknowledges that risk and folds it into the piece. The blown glass is genuinely vulnerable, yet the web is engineered and taut. Its beauty does not soften the contradiction; it makes the viewer remain inside it. One looks longer because the object is beautiful, and that prolonged attention is exactly when beauty reveals its disciplinary edge.
Map (red): no border is the same as no violence
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-map-red.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, Map (red), 2026. Clear red glass balls, 25 mm diameter. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: A world map assembled from thousands of loose red glass balls lies directly on a concrete floor.
content.credit: Installation view of “Mona Hatoum. Over, under and in between”, Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2026. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: In the second room, more than thirty thousand loose red glass balls form a world map directly on the floor. There are no national borders. The projection is Gall–Peters, which preserves the relative area of landmasses more accurately than the familiar Mercator projection and therefore refuses one of cartography’s most persistent hierarchies: the visual inflation of Europe and North America at the expense of regions closer to the equator.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-map-red-visitors.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, Map (red), 2026. Visitors move around more than thirty thousand unfixed glass spheres. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: Two visitors carefully circle a red glass world map viewed from above.
content.credit: Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: At first, Map (red) seems to offer a repaired image of the world — borderless and proportionally corrected. But Hatoum does not confuse correction with resolution. The continents are made of identical units that are not fixed to one another or to the floor. A careless step, a vibration or a small displacement could deform a coastline. Geography appears legible only because the room is temporarily calm.

The red is crucial. It can suggest warning, blood, heat, ideology or emergency, but the balls remain translucent; light moves through them. The colour does not assign a single message. Instead, it denies the map the cool authority of information. This is not a neutral diagram seen from nowhere. It is a world at the viewer’s feet, vulnerable to proximity and power.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-map-red-detail.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, Map (red), 2026, detail. Loose 25 mm clear red glass balls form a geography that can be physically disturbed. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: Close view of thousands of translucent red glass balls forming Europe, North Africa and Asia.
content.credit: Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: Hatoum has returned to maps across decades because they compress political decisions into apparently natural shapes. Here she removes borders but leaves the problem of territory intact. The work’s most difficult insight is that a world without drawn boundaries is not automatically a world without domination. Scale can be corrected while movement remains unequal; a border can disappear from an image while becoming harder in lived experience. The installation does not illustrate this argument. It gives the argument a material condition: one beautiful arrangement, maintained only by collective restraint.
The map is most political at the point where it stops pretending to be permanent.
all of a quiver: the grid develops a nervous system
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-all-of-a-quiver.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, all of a quiver, 2022. Aluminium square tubes, steel hinges, electric motor and cable. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: A nine-level black metal grid rises like an unstable tower inside a concrete gallery.
content.credit: Installation view of “Mona Hatoum. Over, under and in between”, Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2026. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: The final chamber contains the exhibition’s loudest and most explicitly animated work. all of a quiver is a nine-level frame made from aluminium square tubes connected by steel hinges. At full height it resembles scaffolding, a skeletal tower or the diagram of a building stripped of everything but its claim to order. Then a motor and cable initiate its transformation. Levels fold, the frame lowers and the geometry gives way with a metallic creak before the structure is drawn upright again.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-quiver-collapse.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, all of a quiver, 2022, during its motorised cycle of collapse and re-erection. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: The tall hinged grid bends and folds through its middle during its kinetic cycle.
content.credit: Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: Nothing literally falls. That distinction is essential. The sculpture performs collapse while remaining held inside a system designed to repeat it. Disaster is not a single event but a cycle: tension, failure, suspension, reconstruction. Watching the work, one begins to notice how much confidence is usually invested in the right angle. The grid has long signified rationality, repeatability and control. Hatoum leaves its logic visible but makes every joint articulate. The abstract frame becomes bodily — it braces, buckles, groans and rises.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/hatoum-quiver-detail.jpg
content.caption: Mona Hatoum, all of a quiver, 2022, detail. Aluminium square tubes, steel hinges, electric motor and cable. Installation view, Fondazione Prada, Milan. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.
content.alt: A close view through the hinged aluminium grid of Mona Hatoum’s kinetic tower.
content.credit: Installation view of “Mona Hatoum. Over, under and in between”, Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2026. Photo: Roberto Marossi. Courtesy Fondazione Prada.

content.content: Of the three installations, this is the most theatrical, yet it is also the most exact. Its drama comes from engineering rather than illusion. The mechanism never permits complete catastrophe, and that limit makes the work more disturbing rather than less. It recalls infrastructures maintained just above failure, institutions that survive by rehearsing crisis, and bodies asked to recover without being allowed to change the conditions that exhausted them.
https://player.vimeo.com/video/1176891027
content.caption: Over, under and in between | Mona Hatoum | Fondazione Prada Milano

content.content: Minimalism after certainty

Hatoum’s relation to Minimalism is often described through resemblance: modular structures, industrial materials, repeated units, the removal of expressive gesture. But resemblance is not allegiance. Historical Minimalism frequently offered the object as a self-contained fact and the gallery as a field for phenomenological encounter. Hatoum keeps the encounter and removes the security. Her modules can scatter, her grid can fail, her transparent surface can ensnare. The supposedly universal viewing body becomes a particular body aware of risk.

This is why the exhibition feels current without chasing topicality. Its materials do not name a war, a migration route, a border regime or a collapsing institution, yet they sharpen the sensorium through which those realities are experienced. Uncertainty is not represented as fog. It is given structure. There are clear lines, measurable spheres, visible joints and identifiable mechanisms. Everything can be described, and still nothing feels secure.

The show is also a corrective to the idea that political art must deliver a readable position at first glance. Hatoum’s politics are spatial before they are declarative. The visitor discovers them through posture: the neck tilted upward, the feet held back from the glass map, the body waiting for the tower’s next movement. Interpretation follows sensation rather than replacing it.
The body as a measuring instrument

Across the three rooms, the body repeatedly becomes an instrument for measuring what cannot be trusted. Under Web, height is felt as exposure. Beside Map (red), distance becomes an ethical decision not to disturb. Before all of a quiver, time is counted through expectation: when will the structure move, how far will it give way, will it return? The works do not immerse the viewer through spectacle. They make perception responsible.

That responsibility distinguishes Hatoum’s use of fragility from a broader contemporary taste for ruins, broken grids and precarious materials. Here instability is never merely a look. It governs the viewer’s behaviour and the object’s survival. The installations remain austere enough to resist narrative illustration, yet sensuous enough to prevent detachment. Glass catches light; metal produces sound; scale works on the lungs before language has settled.
How to stand

“Over, under and in between” does not offer resilience as a comforting conclusion. The tower rises again because a cable pulls it. The map remains intact because people keep their distance. The web is beautiful because its tension holds. Every equilibrium is conditional, supported by labour, restraint or force that the work makes visible.

What Hatoum finally asks is not whether the world is stable. It plainly is not. The more difficult question is how to stand inside instability without mistaking survival for safety or order for justice. In the Cisterna, sculpture becomes a rehearsal for that position: alert but not paralysed, implicated but still capable of attention. The exhibition’s deepest achievement is to make precarity neither abstract nor spectacular. It becomes the space between the object and the body — the interval in which looking turns into responsibility.
Fondazione Prada — official exhibition page

articles.title: A Little More Room for Life
articles.author: EPRIS Editorial Team
articles.excerpt: On World Architecture Day, a small love letter to the people and places that make us feel at home. With warmth, from the EPRIS editorial team.

content.content: World Architecture Day · 5 October 2026
Dear architects, students, makers and lovers of places,

Before a building becomes part of a city, it is something small enough to hold in your hands. A pencil line. A folded sheet. A piece of card patiently cut and glued. A model turned towards the window to see where the light will fall. Architecture begins in these modest gestures – and in the extraordinary belief that an ordinary day can be made better.

Today we are celebrating that belief, and the people who keep it alive. The sketches redrawn, the models rebuilt, the questions asked one more time. The care that rarely appears in the finished photograph: a handrail that feels right, a door that opens easily, a room that leaves enough space for someone else. Thank you for the imagination – and for the patience behind it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-architecture-day-model-detail.jpg
content.caption: The idea, up close: a detail of the physical “Affordable Palace” model (2019), Opposite Office / Benedikt Hartl. Crop of the cover photograph · CC BY 4.0.
content.alt: The idea, up close: a detail of the physical “Affordable Palace” model (2019), Opposite Office / Benedikt Hartl. Crop of the cover photograph · CC BY 4.0.

content.content:
For the rooms that welcome us.
For the cities that let us belong.
For the people who imagine both.
The human measure

At EPRIS, architecture is close to the heart. It shapes the way we notice light, tell stories and look for meaning in a detail. We love its great gestures. But we also love the quiet ones: a shaded courtyard, a generous threshold, a bench where you can stay without having to buy anything.

This year’s World Architecture Day theme, “Housing is a Human Right. Build It.”, brings us back to the essential. Beauty should not stop at the image of a building. It should reach the person who lives inside it. A safe, dignified home is the beginning of that promise, not its finishing touch.
A wish from our worktable to yours

May you find collaborators who listen, clients who trust and the courage to protect a good idea. May there be fewer exhausted nights and more mornings when a difficult drawing suddenly makes sense. May your spaces hold conversations, childhoods, small celebrations and the simple relief of coming home. And may you never lose the pleasure of noticing how sunlight changes a wall.

Happy World Architecture Day.
Thank you for making a little more room for life.

With warmth,
the EPRIS editorial team.

articles.title: The Second Exposure: What Photography Does to Architecture, Sculpture and Painting
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: From the measured neutrality of architectural typologies to Medardo Rosso’s dissolving sculpture and Ann Hamilton’s tactile scans, the camera does not merely reproduce art – it rebuilds it in light.

content.content: A photograph of an artwork is often introduced as evidence: proof that an object existed, that an exhibition happened, that a building looked a certain way before the weather, the public or the next installation altered it. Yet every serious photographer knows that evidence begins with a refusal. The camera excludes almost everything. It converts depth into a plane, duration into an instant, atmosphere into exposure and the wandering body into one fixed point of view. What we call documentation is therefore already an argument.

This argument has become more urgent as exhibitions are increasingly encountered first – and sometimes only – through images. Architecture travels as a frontal elevation emptied of people. Sculpture becomes a silhouette, a gleam, a dramatic shadow. Painting is detached from the wall, corrected into a perfect rectangle and made to emit the same light as the screen on which it appears. The camera does not stand after the work and report on it. It produces a second work: portable, repeatable, searchable and often more culturally powerful than the first.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-02.jpg
content.caption: Installation view, Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025. Courtesy Kunstmuseum Basel.
content.alt: Installation view, Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025. Courtesy Kunstmuseum Basel.

content.content: The photograph is not the artwork’s shadow. It is a second object made of light, with its own scale, exclusions and authority.
The photograph is never after the work

Three recent exhibitions make that second object unusually visible. Typologien: Photography in 20th-Century Germany, presented at Fondazione Prada in Milan from April to July 2025, assembled more than six hundred works by twenty-five artists. Its subject was not simply a national history of photography but the typological impulse: the desire to compare, order and stabilise the visible world. At Kunstmuseum Basel, Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture placed roughly fifty sculptures beside some 250 photographs and drawings, insisting that Rosso’s images were not secondary records but part of his sculptural thinking. In Cleveland, Ann Hamilton’s still and moving • the tactile image enlarged handheld scans of small historic figures until touch became architecture.

Together these exhibitions shift the question from whether a photograph is faithful to what stood before the lens to what kind of reality it builds. Typology claims knowledge through repetition. Rosso makes solidity unstable through light. Hamilton turns scanning – a procedure associated with administrative capture – into an intimate choreography of hand, object and delay. Each case exposes a different politics of looking.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-01.jpg
content.caption: Sculpture and photograph share the gallery as parallel forms of inquiry in Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture. Installation view, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.
content.alt: Sculpture and photograph share the gallery as parallel forms of inquiry in Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture. Installation view, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.

content.content: Architecture and the fiction of neutral light

Architectural photography has long depended on a fiction of neutrality. The exemplary image is clear, vertical, spacious and apparently inevitable. It suppresses the inconvenience of use: open doors, moving bodies, temporary signs, cleaning equipment, the shifting colour of daylight. Perspective correction makes walls stand straighter than vision experiences them. A long exposure erases pedestrians or converts them into translucent traces. Weather is waited out. Furniture is moved by centimetres. The result can be precise in every measurable respect and false in every social one.

The German tradition gathered in Typologien complicates this fiction because its discipline is explicit. Bernd and Hilla Becher photographed industrial structures under flat skies, from consistent positions, with minimal theatrical incident. Their grids make comparison possible: water towers, blast furnaces and winding towers become families of form. The method appears objective, but the exhibition’s typological structure reveals the paradox. A type does not exist naturally in the world. It is produced by selection – by deciding which objects belong together, which differences matter and which context can be removed.

The Bechers’ influence on Candida Höfer, Thomas Struth, Andreas Gursky and Thomas Ruff did not create one style so much as a sustained argument about distance. Höfer’s empty libraries, theatres and museums are never merely empty. Their vacancy makes institutional order visible: furniture aligned for absent users, routes of circulation, ornament calibrated to authority. Struth’s museum pictures reverse the convention. Instead of isolating the painting, they include visitors looking, waiting, drifting and blocking one another’s view. The museum becomes an image-making machine in which the public is both audience and material.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-03.jpg
content.caption: The exhibition design refuses a single ideal viewpoint; sculpture is encountered through changing distances and obstructions. Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.
content.alt: The exhibition design refuses a single ideal viewpoint; sculpture is encountered through changing distances and obstructions. Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.

content.content: Luisa Lambri takes another route. Her photographs of modernist interiors avoid the building’s iconic totality and move toward windows, corners, joints and the thin membrane where daylight meets a surface. Architecture is no longer a heroic object but a psychological aperture. The photograph measures what a room permits the body to sense. Light is not there to explain the building; it becomes the building’s most unstable material.

To photograph architecture responsibly is therefore not to eliminate interpretation but to make interpretation legible. A picture can acknowledge use, season, security, access and decay. It can preserve the difference between a room designed for contemplation and a room temporarily cleared for the camera. It can show that the polished image is a condition produced by labour. Neutrality is not the absence of style. It is a style whose choices have been made difficult to see.
When sculpture becomes weather

Sculpture creates an even sharper conflict. It occupies the same space as the viewer, yet the photograph must reduce that shared space to one surface. Scale becomes relative to the frame; weight becomes tonal contrast; the back of the work disappears. A camera can make plaster monumental and bronze weightless. It can detach a figure from its plinth, compress several objects into one silhouette or allow a cast shadow to become more active than the material that produced it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-04.jpg
content.caption: Installation view, Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture. Light, vitrines and sightlines are treated as part of the work’s reception. Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.
content.alt: Installation view, Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture. Light, vitrines and sightlines are treated as part of the work’s reception. Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.

content.content: Medardo Rosso understood this not as a limitation but as a medium. His wax, plaster and bronze figures appear to emerge from and return to their surrounding atmosphere. Faces are incomplete; shoulders merge with bases; surfaces catch illumination unevenly. In person, the object shifts as the viewer moves. In Rosso’s photographs, movement is replaced by another instability. He cropped, rephotographed, altered contrast and allowed light to veil the sculpture. The photograph does not clarify the object. It extends its refusal to become fully knowable.

The Basel exhibition was important because it resisted the familiar hierarchy in which sculpture is original and photography is supporting material. Rosso’s photographs stood as experiments in perception. The same figure could seem tender, spectral, damaged or almost abstract depending on angle and exposure. Repetition did not stabilise identity; it multiplied it. The work existed between states, and the camera was one of the instruments that kept it there.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-05.jpg
content.caption: A gallery sequence in the Basel retrospective. Rosso’s figures change character as illumination and viewing distance change.
content.alt: A gallery sequence in the Basel retrospective. Rosso’s figures change character as illumination and viewing distance change.

content.content: Constantin Brâncuși later treated photography with comparable seriousness. He objected when professional photographers made his sculptures look like discrete, well-lit commodities. His own images accepted flare, shadow and spatial ambiguity because the relation among object, base and studio mattered more than descriptive completeness. The photograph became an extension of installation. It instructed the future not only what the sculpture looked like, but how it wished to be seen.

This is why contemporary sculpture photography so often fails when it is merely spectacular. The dramatic black background, hard spotlight and low angle may produce a powerful object while destroying the sculpture’s actual relation to gravity and room. A good image need not imitate ordinary eyesight, but it should understand what it transforms. The question is not whether the photograph beautifies the work. The question is whether its beauty discovers a condition already latent in the work or replaces the work with an advertising effect.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-06.jpg
content.caption: Rosso’s sculptural surfaces hold and scatter light rather than presenting a stable contour. Installation view, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.
content.alt: Rosso’s sculptural surfaces hold and scatter light rather than presenting a stable contour. Installation view, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.

content.content: Touch without possession

Ann Hamilton’s Cleveland installation begins where conventional object photography is supposed to end: at the moment of contact. Using a handheld scanner, Hamilton moved across small ceramic and crèche figures from the museum’s collection, many rarely displayed. The scanner does not observe from a distance. It requires proximity, a paced movement and a narrow band of attention. What it records is not a single instant but the duration of a hand travelling over an object.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-07.jpg
content.caption: Ann Hamilton, image from still and moving • the tactile image, Cleveland Museum of Art, 2025–26. Courtesy the artist and Cleveland Museum of Art.
content.alt: Ann Hamilton, image from still and moving • the tactile image, Cleveland Museum of Art, 2025–26. Courtesy the artist and Cleveland Museum of Art.

content.content: Enlarged from hand-sized objects to floor-to-ceiling images, the scans produce a strange reversal. The historic figure is no longer a miniature to be mastered by the gaze. It exceeds the viewer. Seams, abrasions and distortions become landscape. The scanner’s failures – drag, doubling, temporal discontinuity – are not defects to be corrected. They register the negotiation between a moving hand and a resistant form.

Hamilton calls the result tactile because sight is made to remember touch. Yet the installation also preserves distance. The visitor cannot handle the collection object; conservation protocols and museum authority remain. The enlarged image mediates that denied contact. It offers intimacy without possession and magnification without pretending that scale is unchanged. In this sense the work is an ethics of reproduction: it makes the transformation visible rather than hiding it beneath seamless technical competence.
Painting under surveillance

Painting appears to be the easiest art to photograph because both painting and photograph are flat. That resemblance is deceptive. Paint reflects light; screens emit it. Varnish produces glare, impasto casts shadows, matte passages absorb illumination and metallic pigments change with position. A single exposure may render the colours plausibly while cancelling the physical decisions that made them. The perfect digital rectangle is often a very incomplete painting.

Museum documentation usually removes the frame, corrects perspective and balances colour against a calibration target. These procedures are indispensable for scholarship, conservation and access. But they also produce a peculiar image: the painting as if seen from nowhere, under light that belongs to no hour, without the wall or body that establishes its scale. Such an image is less a view than a data model. Its authority comes from suppressing the conditions of looking.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-08.jpg
content.caption: Installation view, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025. The photograph records not an isolated object but an arrangement of surfaces, intervals and reflected light.
content.alt: Installation view, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025. The photograph records not an isolated object but an arrangement of surfaces, intervals and reflected light.

content.content: Thomas Struth’s museum photographs restore those conditions by placing paintings inside crowded acts of attention. The viewers’ backs, clothes, gestures and hesitations become part of the image. Scale returns through bodies. So does conflict: one person’s contemplation is another’s obstruction. The painting is neither autonomous icon nor passive backdrop; it is a social event continuously reorganised by those who stand before it.

This social dimension matters in the age of the installation shot. Exhibitions are routinely photographed before opening, when every label is aligned and every surface untouched. These images are useful and often beautiful, but they portray an institution without friction. The public later enters a room already imagined as empty. Photography establishes the ideal state, and lived experience arrives as a disturbance.
Exposure has three meanings

The word exposure joins the problems at the centre of these exhibitions. In photography it names the quantity of light that reaches a sensitive surface. In display it means making something available to view. In ordinary speech it also means vulnerability: exposure to weather, judgment, danger or loss. Every reproduction of an artwork operates across all three meanings.

To expose a sculpture is to illuminate it, to place it before a public and to make it vulnerable to a framing it cannot control. To expose architecture is to transform occupied space into a claim about order. To expose a painting is to move colour from reflected light into a reproducible system. The technical decision is inseparable from the institutional one. What receives light receives attention; what remains outside the frame risks remaining outside history.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-09.jpg
content.caption: Medardo Rosso challenged the stable boundary between figure and atmosphere. Exhibition image, Kunstmuseum Basel.
content.alt: Medardo Rosso challenged the stable boundary between figure and atmosphere. Exhibition image, Kunstmuseum Basel.

content.content: Typologien demonstrates how seriality can become knowledge, but also how knowledge becomes power. A grid persuades because it appears to treat every image equally. Yet the equal format intensifies the curator’s decisions: these are the examples chosen to represent a category; these are the differences the viewer is invited to compare. Typology is never innocent. It can preserve threatened forms, reveal industrial histories and discover affinities. It can also turn singular places into specimens.

Rosso uses repetition against that stability. His sequences do not define a type; they dissolve certainty. Hamilton, meanwhile, turns the capturing device back into a bodily instrument. Together they suggest that responsible photographic practice does not renounce ordering, framing or transformation. It makes those operations available to thought.
The ethics of the perfect image

The contemporary image economy rewards immediate legibility. An exhibition photograph must function at the scale of a phone, survive cropping, leave space for text and announce its subject before the next swipe. Architecture is pushed toward symmetry; sculpture toward silhouette; painting toward saturated colour. The most distributable image becomes the exhibition’s unofficial cover, regardless of whether it represents the experience of the work.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-10.jpg
content.caption: A photographic work included in the Rosso retrospective. Reproduction becomes part of the sculptor’s method rather than a neutral report.
content.alt: A photographic work included in the Rosso retrospective. Reproduction becomes part of the sculptor’s method rather than a neutral report.

content.content: There is nothing inherently dishonest about seduction. Art has always required invitations, and photography can make inaccessible collections available across distance. The ethical problem begins when the image conceals the degree of its invention. Extreme tonal editing is presented as natural light. An empty room is presented as ordinary access. A temporary viewpoint is presented as the building’s essence. The camera’s rhetoric disappears behind the word documentation.

A more exact practice begins with captions. Who made the photograph? When was it taken – during installation, at opening, after conservation? Is the pictured state permanent? Has the image been cropped or composited? What does the credit line call the object: work, installation view, detail, rendering, archival photograph? Such language is not bureaucratic decoration. It tells the reader what kind of evidence is being offered.

Exactness also requires plurality. One frontal image can describe proportion but not movement. A detail can explain material but not scale. A crowded view can reveal social use while obscuring the work. The answer is not a mythical perfect photograph but a sequence in which the limits of one image are corrected by another. The serious visual essay is therefore closer to an exhibition than to an icon: it constructs relations across difference.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-11.jpg
content.caption: Overview of the Rosso galleries at Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025. A sequence of viewpoints resists reducing sculpture to a single emblematic shot.
content.alt: Overview of the Rosso galleries at Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025. A sequence of viewpoints resists reducing sculpture to a single emblematic shot.

content.content: A second object made of light

The most consequential photographs of art do not disappear in service to their subjects. They establish a productive distance. Höfer makes institutional space visible by withholding its users. Struth makes looking visible by including them. Lambri fragments architecture until light and enclosure become psychological. Rosso photographs sculpture until material becomes weather. Hamilton scans touch until a small object becomes an environment.

None of these practices offers neutrality. Each offers a position clear enough to be examined. This is the distinction between interpretation and distortion. Distortion pretends that its transformation is the world. Interpretation reveals a way of moving through the world and permits another viewer to disagree.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/second-exposure-12.jpg
content.caption: Exhibition image from Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.
content.alt: Exhibition image from Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture, Kunstmuseum Basel, 2025.

content.content: The camera is often described as preserving what time will destroy. It does preserve, but never without building something new. A building becomes a plane of decisions. A sculpture becomes an event of illumination. A painting becomes a proposition about colour under controlled conditions. An exhibition becomes an archive before it has finished happening.

The task is not to force the photograph back into obedience. It is to demand more intelligence from the second object: enough formal precision to deserve attention, enough historical context to resist spectacle, enough transparency to disclose its choices and enough imagination to show what ordinary looking misses. The artwork does not survive in the image unchanged. It survives as a renewed problem – exposed again.
A responsible photograph does not say: this is how the work was. It says: this is the encounter I have constructed, and these are the conditions under which you may judge it.

Essay by Viacheslav Munister for EPRIS Journal. The text draws on official exhibition materials for Typologien: Photography in 20th-Century Germany (Fondazione Prada, Milan, 3 April–14 July 2025), Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture (Kunstmuseum Basel, 29 March–10 August 2025), and Ann Hamilton’s still and moving • the tactile image (Cleveland Museum of Art, 14 December 2025–19 April 2026). It does not claim in-person attendance. Images are reproduced for editorial and critical discussion and remain credited to their institutions and authors.

Medardo Rosso: Inventing Modern Sculpture – Kunstmuseum Basel
