articles.title: The Luxury of What Is Not There: Winnie Tam of 28 a.m.
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Winnie Tam
articles.excerpt: The founder of 28 a.m. on touch and temperature, the intelligence of shadow, and why a calm room begins with restraint rather than appearance.

content.content: Architecture is often discussed as an image before it is understood as an atmosphere. Winnie Tam begins elsewhere: with the cool density of stone underfoot, the temperature of timber in the hand, the gradual change of daylight and the emotional force of an unfilled space. As founder of 28 a.m., an architectural and interior design studio based in London and Hong Kong, she treats calm not as a style but as a carefully constructed relationship between material, proportion, shadow and use.

The conversation centres on Fox Burrow, the studio’s single-storey rear extension and interior renovation of a substantial Victorian house in Redbridge, London. Conceived as a restorative family sanctuary, the project draws on shakkei, the Japanese principle of borrowed scenery, and on Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s writing about darkness and reflected light. The result does not imitate nature or quote Japanese form. It works more quietly, through thresholds, tactile surfaces, framed views and light that is allowed to remain incomplete.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-01.jpg
content.caption: Fox Burrow, Redbridge, London: the restored fireplace and deep red walls give the room warmth without visual excess. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: A living room at Fox Burrow with deep red walls, a white fireplace and a sculptural pendant light.

content.content: You often speak about designing through all five senses. Which sense is most underestimated in contemporary architecture and interiors?

Touch – specifically texture and temperature. Contemporary design has become increasingly image-obsessed, made to look striking on a screen rather than feel remarkable in person. We often underestimate the quiet weight of raw materials: the cool density of stone underfoot, or the gentle, unrefined drape of natural linen catching low light. True spatial luxury is not just seen; it is felt through the skin.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-03.jpg
content.caption: A close view of the timber joinery at Fox Burrow. Grain, shadow and the cool black handle make touch part of the composition. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: Close-up of dark timber cabinetry and black metal handles at Fox Burrow.

content.content: You describe your aesthetic as minimalist, effortlessly natural and profoundly calming. Is calm something you can design deliberately, or is it ultimately created by the person inhabiting the space?

Calm can absolutely be designed. As architects, we deliberately manipulate proportion, shadow and honest materiality to set an atmosphere. We remove visual noise to slow down the nervous system. The space sets the quiet rhythm; the person inhabiting it brings it to life. Calm is a shared dialogue between the architecture and the soul living within it.
The space sets the quiet rhythm; the person inhabiting it brings it to life.
content.caption: Winnie Tam

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-06.jpg
content.caption: The family room at Fox Burrow. Low light, pale upholstery and recessed alcoves produce calm through proportion rather than emptiness. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: A softly lit family room with pale modular seating, recessed shelves and a timber floor.

content.content: Nature is one of the strongest references in your work. How do you translate its qualities into architecture without simply reproducing its visual language?
To avoid literal translation, we move away from visual motifs and focus on atmospheric quality. Nature is never static; it is defined by light, atmosphere and time.

We capture these qualities by designing spaces that respond dynamically to their environment. We prioritise materials that wear their history openly and age with beauty. By honouring the quiet rhythm of the natural world – its light, shadows and subtle textures – we create interiors that feel deeply organic and alive, without relying on literal representations.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-04.jpg
content.caption: At Fox Burrow, a curved ceiling recess turns indirect light into an architectural surface. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: A sculpted ceiling recess illuminated by warm indirect light.

content.content: Your work draws on Eastern philosophies. What have Japanese ideas taught you about space that you felt was missing from architectural practice in the West?

The appreciation for transition and the unfilled void. Western practice frequently treats space as something to be maximised, brightly illuminated and dressed with decorative intent. Eastern spatial philosophy revealed what was missing: the beauty of what is not there.

I am particularly interested in the luxury that lies in restraint. By celebrating subtle transitions between rooms, honouring thresholds and letting shadows play across natural surfaces, space gains emotional depth. Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s In Praise of Shadows reminds us that beauty resides not in the object itself, but in the patterns of shadows, light and darkness that one object creates against another. Embracing this principle allows our work to feel quiet, unhurried and deeply grounded.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-08.jpg
content.caption: A pendant above the stair is read through shadow before it is read as an object. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: A translucent sculptural pendant glowing above a dark staircase.

content.content: Has contemporary Western architecture become too focused on adding – more objects, more functions, more visual information – rather than making space for absence?

For me, yes. Growing up in cities, I have long been overwhelmed by the availability of things. When I can no longer remember the story of an item and the reason for it to be there, it stops becoming meaningful to me. It is very much a personal choice, but I find I am most at peace when I have visual clarity, and that brings me calm.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-02.jpg
content.caption: The kitchen at Fox Burrow pairs a dark timber wall with a pale island and a precisely framed garden view. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: A contemporary kitchen with walnut cabinetry, a white island and a garden window.

content.content: Could you tell us about a small detail in one of your projects that might go unnoticed visually, but fundamentally changes how the space is experienced?

I find that the most successful design details are the ones that go unnoticed. In Wave Residence, for example, we added an extension and an external window became part of an internal wall. I placed a framed alcove shelf there. The fact that it used to be a window would go entirely unnoticed if it were not mentioned.

In a recent project, the extension created a drop in ceiling height. We used that point to change the ceiling material, so the drop appeared intentional. When details are done well, they simply feel as if they belong. They do not stand out; they are quietly confident.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-10.jpg
content.caption: The wider kitchen view shows how storage, structure and circulation are absorbed into one legible composition. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: Wide view of a kitchen with timber cabinetry, white worktops and restrained track lighting.

content.content: Do you think our homes can influence our habits and lifestyle, rather than simply accommodate them?

Totally. We are strongly influenced by the environment we are in. On a busy street, our hearts beat faster and we act faster. In a formal building, we are more cautious about how we walk, sit and speak. So when we design a home, we are not just designing the physical space; we are designing the lifestyle of the family inhabiting it.
Having lived and worked across London, Hong Kong, Tokyo and Paris, how have different cities shaped your understanding of what makes a place feel like home?

Each city taught me a different layer of sanctuary. Hong Kong showed me how to design tranquillity amid dense urban intensity. Tokyo revealed the emotional weight of quiet rituals and spatial discipline. London brought an appreciation for warm, tactile heritage. Together, they proved that home is not defined by geography. It is an internal feeling of quiet grounding, created when architecture honours how you live.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/28am-fox-burrow-07.jpg
content.caption: A quieter reading of the red room: mirror, hearth and pendant are held in a restrained, almost symmetrical frame. Photography: Nacho Rivera. Courtesy 28 a.m. Studio.
content.alt: Detail of a red living room with a white fireplace, mirror and pendant reflected above it.

content.content: How do you balance visual simplicity with the complexity required to make a home genuinely sustainable and comfortable?

Through thoughtful integration. True comfort and sustainability – clean air systems, acoustic warmth and energy efficiency – should be built into the very bones of the house, not tacked on as visual clutter. When technical systems are designed seamlessly into the architecture, the space remains open, natural and effortlessly calm to inhabit.

Fox Burrow is a residential extension and interior renovation in Redbridge, London, by 28 a.m. Studio. All project photographs in this article are by Nacho Rivera and are reproduced from the studio’s official project page with full editorial credit.
View Fox Burrow on 28 a.m. Studio

articles.title: What a Room Remembers: Interiors After the Image
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: From a reused museum apartment in Helsinki to a red-lit SoHo bar and a timber office beneath the Dutch heath, six projects reveal why the season’s strongest interiors are less concerned with style than with time, atmosphere and use.

content.content: An interior arrives online as a finished image: empty, corrected, evenly lit and detached from the hours for which it was designed. The more persuasive the photograph, the easier it becomes to mistake composition for experience. Yet the best rooms of autumn 2026 are interesting precisely where the image fails—where daylight changes a surface, where an old object interrupts a new system, where a floor receives wear, where darkness makes conversation possible, or where a material claim can be tested against the way a building is actually made.

This review brings together six projects across domestic, cultural, workplace and hospitality interiors. They are not a forecast of colours or furniture shapes. Nor do they share a look. A restrained apartment near Versailles, a North Sea penthouse, a temporary museum in Helsinki, a timber office in the Dutch landscape, the renewal of Hotel Kämp and a two-level bar in SoHo belong to different economies and social worlds. What connects them is a more consequential design question: how can an interior make time perceptible?
The season’s strongest rooms do not ask to be consumed at a glance. They construct conditions for attention.

Time enters these projects in several forms. It is historical fabric that must be neither erased nor sentimentalised. It is the future disassembly of a temporary exhibition. It is timber allowed to carry structure rather than imitate warmth. It is a hotel expected to survive intense use without becoming anonymous. It is the half-light of a bar, calibrated not for documentation but for the social permission night can offer. Together, the six projects suggest that contemporary interior design is moving away from the room as a still life and toward the room as an active agreement between matter, climate, memory and behaviour.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-admuseum-01.jpg
content.caption: Eteläranta 6, the temporary home of Finland’s Architecture & Design Museum in Helsinki. Existing furniture, museum holdings and reused elements are composed as a working public interior. Courtesy Studio Joanna Laajisto.
content.alt: Muted green rooms furnished with vintage seating and bookshelves at Eteläranta 6 in Helsinki.

content.content: 1. Versailles: preservation without obedience

In an eighteenth-century house south of Paris, Inès Deschodt and Johanne Le Griffon begin with an apparently familiar brief: make a historic apartment workable for contemporary life while retaining its architectural dignity. The danger is equally familiar. Conservation can become a tasteful freeze, while contrast can become a performance in which every new insertion loudly announces its date. This 135-square-metre pied-à-terre avoids both traps by treating the existing shell as a frame with enough authority to absorb disagreement.

Mouldings and proportions are preserved, but the rooms are not staged as an inventory of period correctness. A deep, low sofa settles into the salon without competing with the fireplace. Dark timber and black metal give weight to the otherwise pale envelope. The most forceful intervention arrives in the kitchen, where Calacatta Viola marble is placed beside stainless steel. Veining and reflectivity do not blend with the old house; they sharpen one another. Marble carries geological excess and domestic ceremony, while steel brings the unemotional precision of the professional kitchen.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-versailles-01.jpg
content.caption: The salon of the Versailles pied-à-terre. Historic mouldings remain legible while low contemporary furniture changes the room’s centre of gravity. Interior design by Inès Deschodt and Johanne Le Griffon. Photography: Oracle.
content.alt: A pale historic salon with a dark curved sofa, sculptural lighting and retained wall mouldings.

content.content: The project’s real intelligence is not contrast by itself, but the control of visual temperature. In the living areas, daylight is diffused through curtains and absorbed by dark upholstery. In the kitchen, metal catches and redistributes it. Elsewhere, sapele panelling and an electric-blue carpet create a denser, almost nocturnal register. The home is allowed to have several atmospheres instead of forcing every room into the same photogenic neutrality.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-versailles-02.jpg
content.caption: Calacatta Viola marble meets stainless steel in the kitchen. The opposition between geological pattern and industrial reflection is the project’s most decisive material gesture. Photography: Oracle.
content.alt: A kitchen island and backsplash in dramatically veined marble beside stainless-steel cabinetry.

content.content: Even the bathroom’s microtopping is less interesting as a fashionable seamless finish than as a pragmatic act: it is applied over existing surfaces, limiting demolition while giving the small room a continuous field. That choice is modest compared with the kitchen’s theatre, but it reveals the project’s method. The new work does not need to dominate every surface. It intervenes where performance, maintenance or spatial emphasis requires it, then recedes.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-versailles-03.jpg
content.caption: The bathroom is unified with a light microtopping applied over existing surfaces, reducing demolition and visual noise. Photography: Oracle.
content.alt: A compact pale bathroom with continuous mineral surfaces and restrained fittings.

content.content: Review verdict — Strongest move: allowing historic detail and contemporary material intensity to coexist without hierarchy. Risk: the marble-and-steel kitchen can read as an autonomous luxury image. What it changes: preservation becomes a flexible spatial discipline rather than a decorative style.
2. Residence DNB: the sea is not a colour palette

Residence DNB, a duplex penthouse in Knokke-Heist by Britt Van Namen, could easily have turned its North Sea view into a theme. Coastal projects are often reduced to beige textiles, bleached timber and a generalised language of calm. Here, the horizon is treated not as decoration but as a source of changing luminance. The interior remains quiet enough to register the weather, while its materials are substantial enough not to disappear against it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-dnb-01.jpg
content.caption: Residence DNB in Knokke-Heist frames the North Sea as changing light rather than decorative motif. Interior design by Britt Van Namen. Photography: Cafeine.
content.alt: A penthouse living room with a broad view across the North Sea and a dark circular table.

content.content: The rounded stainless-steel kitchen island is the clearest example. Its shape prevents the metal from becoming severe: light moves around the curve, blurring the boundary between object and reflection. Behind it, pale cabinetry and stone shelves are deliberately recessive. Two dark timber stools introduce a warmer contact point at the body. The arrangement looks simple because several kinds of hardness—metal, stone, glass—have been choreographed through radius, texture and distance.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-dnb-02.jpg
content.caption: The rounded stainless-steel island turns daylight into a moving surface; dark timber stools temper the kitchen’s mineral precision. Photography: Cafeine.
content.alt: A minimal kitchen with a curved stainless-steel island and two dark timber stools.

content.content: A rammed-earth floor gives the apartment an unusually grounded base, while storage made from scaffolding boards carries evidence of previous use. Green marble and Breccia Rosata appear as concentrated accents rather than an all-over statement. Van Namen has described atmosphere as something produced by textures, proportions, transitions and light. Residence DNB supports that claim because no individual material is asked to supply the whole identity. The experience accumulates across thresholds.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-dnb-03.jpg
content.caption: Pale upholstery, green marble and a low horizon line organise the living area around bodily scale and coastal light. Photography: Cafeine.
content.alt: A softly furnished living space with green marble accents and floor-to-ceiling coastal glazing.

content.content: The weakness of many luxury interiors is that tactility is offered as a substitute for social or environmental consequence. A rough wall, handmade tile or reclaimed board becomes a visual alibi. DNB is strongest when it resists that simplification. The reused boards do not make the whole apartment circular, and the rammed-earth surface does not neutralise the embodied cost of extensive glazing and bespoke stone. Yet the project demonstrates a more mature material literacy: provenance, sensory effect and technical performance are allowed to remain different questions.

Review verdict — Strongest move: translating the sea into a changing light condition rather than a decorative theme. Risk: material richness can still be mistaken for environmental responsibility. What it changes: luxury is located in calibrated transitions, not in the number of visible finishes.
3. Eteläranta 6: circularity becomes visible intelligence

The temporary Architecture & Design Museum at Eteläranta 6 in Helsinki is the most conceptually important project in this selection because it treats reuse as the origin of an aesthetic rather than a compromise applied after design. Studio Joanna Laajisto worked within a Jugend apartment designed by Mauritz Gripenberg in 1904. The museum needed event rooms, a library, workshops and spaces for public work, but its occupation was never meant to justify wasteful permanence.

Almost every decision therefore begins with an inventory: what can remain, what can be borrowed, what can be recovered, and what can later move elsewhere? Reclaimed Ecophon acoustic panels, Ege carpet tiles, a second-hand Kvadrat curtain, salvaged bespoke furniture and objects from the museum’s collection form the project’s material vocabulary. Minimal demolition preserves both embodied carbon and the legibility of the apartment.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-admuseum-02.jpg
content.caption: The museum library occupies a dark green room where collected furniture and books create density without a new fitted scenography. Courtesy Studio Joanna Laajisto.
content.alt: A dark green library with vintage velvet chairs, a timber table and bookshelves.

content.content: The result is not a collage of virtuous leftovers. Colour provides a strong ordering system. Dark green gives the library enclosure and concentration; pale blue-grey allows smaller rooms to receive daylight without losing softness; an acidic olive marks a modest table setting with almost theatrical clarity. Curtains absorb sound and define zones. Old chairs are not romanticised as antiques; they are selected for proportion, repairability and the way their worn materials negotiate public use.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-admuseum-03.jpg
content.caption: A reused table and stools sit within an olive room, where colour does more organisational work than new construction. Courtesy Studio Joanna Laajisto.
content.alt: A small olive-coloured room with a simple timber table, stools and a pendant lamp.

content.content: Circular design is often communicated through diagrams because its achievements are difficult to photograph. Eteläranta 6 solves that representational problem by making continuity itself sensuous. Nothing matches in the retail sense, but relationships are precise. Wood tones repeat across objects of different ages. Lamps locate islands of use. Textiles reduce the institutional hardness normally associated with temporary venues. The interior feels complete without pretending to be new.

There is a broader lesson here for cultural interiors. Temporary exhibitions frequently consume vast quantities of sheet material, paint, carpet and custom fabrication in pursuit of a supposedly neutral display. Laajisto demonstrates that limitation can produce a richer public character. Visitors encounter not an abstract museum brand but an assembly of Finnish design histories placed back into use. The museum becomes a live archive: not only a place where design is explained, but a room in which its afterlives can be tested.

Review verdict — Strongest move: turning material inventory into atmosphere. Risk: the cultivated elegance of the result may understate the logistical difficulty of reuse. What it changes: circularity is shown as authorship through selection, maintenance and recombination.
4. Office by Nature: when structure becomes the interior

At Tafelberg in Blaricum, Studio Massimo’s Office by Nature addresses a problem that workplace design often avoids. Corporate interiors are typically conceived after the building shell, then replaced on short cycles as tenants, branding or management fashions change. Here, structure, envelope and interior are designed as one timber system. The project’s environmental argument is therefore architectural before it becomes decorative.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-office-nature-01.jpg
content.caption: Office by Nature sits close to protected heathland at Tafelberg in Blaricum. A bark-clad envelope and planted roof reduce the distinction between building and landscape. Architecture and interiors by Studio Massimo. Photography: Riccardo De Vecchi.
content.alt: A low office building clad in textured bark with a planted roof among mature trees.

content.content: The 1,000-square-metre building uses Red Grandis glulam with spruce cross-laminated timber. Poplar bark gives the exterior a rough, weathering surface, while a green roof extends the surrounding vegetation across the building’s profile. Inside, the pitched timber geometry is not concealed above a suspended ceiling. It defines the rooms, catches daylight from long rooflights and gives shared workspaces a domestic scale without imitating a house.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-office-nature-02.jpg
content.caption: Glulam frames, spruce CLT and a long rooflight make construction, daylight and interior character inseparable. Photography: Riccardo De Vecchi.
content.alt: A long timber office interior beneath pitched ceilings and a continuous skylight.

content.content: Milled ventilation slots are integrated into timber surfaces rather than added as a competing technical layer. A spiral stair becomes a compact sculptural hinge between levels. Terrazzo incorporates quarry waste, introducing mineral density where the body needs a durable floor. These are not invisible technologies, but neither are they displayed as eco-gadgets. Performance is absorbed into the spatial language.

The project’s title risks the easy rhetoric of biophilia, a word now attached to almost any room with plants or timber. Office by Nature is more convincing when read structurally. Its achievement is not that workers can see greenery, although they can. It is that the interior’s principal visual order is also the building’s load-bearing and environmental order. The caution is maintenance: exposed timber, planted roofs and bespoke ventilation details demand long-term care. An ecological interior is credible only if its operational life confirms the promise of its photographs.

Review verdict — Strongest move: collapsing structure, servicing and atmosphere into one legible timber system. Risk: the language of ‘nature’ can conceal resource and maintenance questions. What it changes: workplace identity comes from construction rather than applied branding.
5. Hotel Kämp: durability is the real form of luxury

Hotel renovation tests a designer’s ethics of time more severely than a private home. Rooms are used intensely, photographed repeatedly and expected to communicate continuity to guests who may know the building only through reputation. At Helsinki’s Hotel Kämp, founded in 1887, Fyra’s renewal of guestrooms and corridors forms part of a larger expansion that includes Helander House and twenty-two additional rooms, fifteen of them suites.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-kamp-01.jpg
content.caption: The Sibelius Suite at Hotel Kämp balances retained cultural memory with furniture scaled for contemporary use. Interior design by Fyra. Photography: Riikka Kantinkoski.
content.alt: A light hotel suite with moulded walls, a curved sofa, a piano and a dark ceramic stove.

content.content: The project avoids the two standard responses to heritage hospitality. It does not reconstruct a nineteenth-century interior as spectacle, and it does not neutralise the building into international five-star anonymity. References to Finnish cultural life, including Helene Schjerfbeck and Jean Sibelius, appear through artworks, suites and atmosphere rather than themed decoration. Mouldings, ceramic stoves, warm timber, pale textiles and carefully chosen colour establish a layered chronology.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-kamp-02.jpg
content.caption: A dining space in the renewed Hotel Kämp uses a vivid rug and sculptural glass pendant to interrupt the controlled cream envelope. Photography: Riikka Kantinkoski.
content.alt: An elegant cream dining room with a vivid floral rug and clustered glass chandelier.

content.content: The strongest rooms contain a degree of visual friction. A bright rug sits beneath tailored furniture. A glass pendant gathers light into a dense cloud. Art is not centred merely to complete a wall. These gestures prevent heritage from becoming beige reassurance. They also recognise that a hotel interior must be understood in episodes: arrival, unpacking, working, eating, sleeping, waking. Each requires a different light level and a different relationship between exposure and enclosure.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-kamp-03.jpg
content.caption: The quieter guestroom palette relies on proportion, layered light and the tactile presence of the historic ceramic stove. Photography: Riikka Kantinkoski.
content.alt: A muted hotel sitting room with a curved sofa, brass sconces and a white ceramic stove.

content.content: Durability is the project’s unresolved but essential criterion. Luxury hotels frequently replace surfaces before they are physically exhausted because visual freshness is part of the product. Fyra speaks of combining modern technology with longevity; the claim will be proven by repair strategies, replaceable components and whether patina is accepted rather than treated as failure. The most sustainable heritage hotel is not the one that looks historic on opening day, but the one that can absorb thousands of nights without requiring another total image reset.

Review verdict — Strongest move: using Finnish cultural memory as spatial depth rather than literal theme. Risk: hospitality’s cycle of cosmetic renewal can undermine claims of longevity. What it changes: luxury is judged by repair, acoustic comfort and the ability to age, not by immediate novelty.
6. Bar Leone: the design of permission after dark

Bar Leone at 527 Broome Street, designed by BOND, is the selection’s most openly cinematic interior. Opened in September 2026, the 2,400-square-foot venue divides itself vertically into two related but distinct social worlds. The upper level uses sapele, corduroy velvet and red travertine to hold a slower, warmer ‘golden hour’. Downstairs, red velvet wallpaper, vinyl banquettes, lacquer and chrome produce the compressed energy of an Italo-disco.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-bar-leone-01.jpg
content.caption: The upper room at Bar Leone uses low amber light, polished metal and sapele to extend the psychological duration of golden hour. Interior design by BOND. Photography: Matthew Kappas.
content.alt: An amber-lit bar with sculptural floor lamps, reflective tables and a long banquette.

content.content: The project is valuable because it makes lighting perform more than visibility. Light defines distance between strangers, controls how quickly the room can be understood and gives materials a temporal role. Red travertine looks almost liquid under amber sources. Chrome turns each lamp into several reflections. Faces are legible without being exposed. The room offers a calibrated degree of privacy in public—one of nightlife design’s most important and least measurable achievements.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-bar-leone-02.jpg
content.caption: Red travertine, corduroy velvet and pools of reflected light organise the upper level around intimacy rather than spectacle. Photography: Matthew Kappas.
content.alt: A dark curved banquette surrounding red marble tables under low warm light.

content.content: Downstairs, the palette becomes denser and more synthetic. Upholstered chairs are almost bodily in profile. The colour red moves across carpet, walls, leather and light, but variation in sheen prevents monochrome from becoming flat. Custom lighting by Gantri and a scheme developed with Map Studio establish rhythm rather than blanket illumination. Furniture by Spinzi Studio is arranged to permit different forms of occupation: watching, gathering, withdrawing, approaching the bar.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/autumn26-bar-leone-03.jpg
content.caption: The lower level shifts toward an Italo-disco register: velvet walls, vinyl seating and vertical light create a denser social tempo. Photography: Matthew Kappas.
content.alt: A deep red nightclub interior with rounded leather chairs, marble tables and glowing wall lights.

content.content: The risk is obvious: a room this controlled can become a backdrop before it becomes a place. Its visual signature is immediately available to social media, and every polished reflection can be framed as content. Yet the plan’s division into two atmospheres gives the bar a resistance that a single iconic room would lack. Guests must choose a tempo. Movement between levels becomes part of the evening. The interior does not merely represent nightlife; it edits its sequence.

Review verdict — Strongest move: treating light as a social boundary and timekeeping device. Risk: the cinematic identity may be consumed faster than the rituals it is meant to host. What it changes: hospitality design is evaluated through permission, pace and acoustic intimacy, not only appearance.
What the six projects say together

Placed side by side, these interiors resist a single seasonal aesthetic. There is no responsible way to call green walls, stainless steel, timber structure, reused furniture or red light ‘the look’ of autumn 2026. Their value lies in different relationships between design and duration. Versailles shows that preservation can accommodate material disagreement. Residence DNB makes climate and horizon active components. Eteläranta 6 turns reuse into a curatorial method. Office by Nature gives construction the work usually assigned to corporate styling. Hotel Kämp asks whether luxury can survive repair. Bar Leone designs the night as a sequence of permissions.

Three criteria emerge. The first is temporal legibility: can a visitor sense what existed before, what has been added and how the room might change? The second is environmental specificity: does light, climate, acoustic behaviour or material sourcing genuinely shape the interior, or is context used only as a narrative? The third is operational truth: will the space remain convincing when people work, spill drinks, move chairs, open curtains, replace damaged parts and return for a second year?

These criteria make interior criticism more demanding than the ranking of images. A beautiful photograph remains useful evidence, but it is incomplete evidence. It cannot show glare at noon, the noise of a full dining room, the maintenance regime of a bark facade, the ease of repairing a hotel headboard or the labour required to catalogue reused exhibition furniture. Design culture needs images, but it also needs plans, specifications, post-occupancy accounts and honest statements about what was retained, removed and newly made.
A room matters when its atmosphere is not an effect placed over use, but the perceptible form of how it is built, maintained and shared.
What survives the photograph

The most memorable interiors of this autumn are not those with the most recognisable palette. They are the ones in which atmosphere can be traced back to decisions. A shadow exists because a light source has been located with care. A calm room is calm because circulation, acoustics and storage have been resolved. An old chair remains because someone accepted the work of repair. A timber ceiling is warm because it carries load, filters air and measures daylight—not because a timber veneer was applied at the end.

That distinction separates style from authorship. Style can be copied quickly; an operating logic cannot. The six projects are not beyond criticism, and none should be treated as a universal model. Their budgets, users and regulatory conditions differ too radically. But each offers a precise proposition about what an interior can do. The room is no longer a container filled with taste. It is an environmental and social instrument, tuned through material, light, memory and use.

Autumn is often described through retreat: shorter days, enclosed rooms, heavier surfaces. These projects suggest a more useful interpretation. The season makes us notice interior conditions again. It reveals which spaces can hold changing light, which histories have been allowed to remain active, which materials promise more than an image and which forms of comfort depend on someone else’s invisibility. The rooms that matter now are not simply beautiful places to enter. They are places that make the terms of entry worth examining.
Project index and sources
Versailles pied-à-terre and Residence DNB — Archiproducts, Best Interior Design Projects of September
Eteläranta 6 / AD Museum — Studio Joanna Laajisto
Office by Nature / Tafelberg — Studio Massimo
Office by Nature — Archilovers project documentation
Hotel Kämp — Fyra
Bar Leone — BOND

Research and text by Viacheslav Munister for EPRIS Journal. The review is based on official studio documentation and published project information. Image captions identify the credited photographer where supplied by the source; Eteläranta 6 images are credited courtesy Studio Joanna Laajisto.

articles.title: Gayane Arushanian: Home Is Something You Carry
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: A Ukrainian artist of Armenian descent, now between Miami and Kyiv, on balance that is earned rather than given, a series that began as a paper game and turned out to be a factorial, and why she refuses to read her work only through war.

content.content: Gayane Arushanian is a Ukrainian multidisciplinary artist of Armenian descent. She was born in Nagorno-Karabakh and came to Ukraine as a child, when war forced her family to leave. She trained at the art school of the Children's and Youth Creativity Centre in Zaporizhzhia, then took two degrees at once: industrial architecture and economic cybernetics. Her main series are IMMERSION. Lapis Lazuli (since 2016), Equilibrium (since 2017) and Abstract Animals (since 2022).

She has had solo exhibitions in Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv and has shown in group exhibitions in Kyiv, Lviv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Dnipro and Kharkiv, in Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain and the United Kingdom, and in the United States at CONTEXT Art Miami during Miami Art Week. She founded G-ART STUDIO in Zaporizhzhia (2012) and Dnipro (2016) and the School of Experimental Art in Kyiv (2017), which she reopened in 2024 after a pause caused by the full-scale invasion. She now lives and works between Miami and Kyiv.
EPRIS Journal asked her about home, hidden order, the body's sense of balance, and what changes when a painting steps out into space.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mnbwnodcyb.jpg
content.caption: Gayane Arushanian in the studio with her works, autumn 2025. Photo: Yuliia Osipova.

content.content: I. Memory and home

You were born in Nagorno-Karabakh. In 1992 war drove your family to Ukraine, and thirty years later another war made you rebuild your life from scratch, this time in Miami. You have said you started drawing at ten as a way of healing. Is your art still an answer to the loss of home, or has it become something else?

Both wars were a litmus test for me. Cruel as it may sound, life is sometimes like that, and we know from the history of art how many artists have faced war, more than once. For me that experience became a push to create even more loudly. It was in the face of destruction that I understood how much I am an artist. That was the effect war had on me.
Crises, moments of inner crisis, made me express myself through art even more loudly. Because on the edge of war and death you feel love and the wish to live even more strongly.

Your 2025 exhibition at Mlyn Design Hub was called Where Home Begins, and your profile simply says HOME. Someone who has lost home twice has a particular right to ask where it begins. So where? In the body, the language, memory, the studio, people – or in the work you carry from country to country?
When I read this question, tears come to my eyes. I understand how deep it goes, and I remember the whole road behind it.

I would put it this way: only a person's inner truth gives birth to a place we can call home. Perhaps you could call me a cosmopolitan – that is how my life has turned out. Interestingly, it was the film Home by the French director Yann Arthus-Bertrand that inspired me. People divide absolutely everything. Yes, the world we live in doesn't exist without that either. But I understood, once and for all: home is me, and wherever I am, I carry that meaning.

It is my inner truth, from which I create this home and in which meanings are born. They are the patterns I have understood and seen, and that I pass on through the art I am constantly making. For me everything is born from the heart, from a pure love for everything that exists.
So I wouldn't want to divide it into the body, the language, memory, people or the work. All of it is part of my truth. I carry all of it with me.
But of course, my home will always be my Armenia, my Nagorno-Karabakh, to which I cannot return. And my Ukraine – the way I lived it, the way I felt it, the way I carry it inside me.

Armenian roots, a Ukrainian formation, an American present. Which of the three is most present in your work, even when you don't call on it? And has a viewer in one country ever seen something in a painting that viewers elsewhere didn't notice at all?
I can't separate the parts that make up who I am. You can't throw part of your life out of yourself. My Armenian roots influenced me greatly, and each of these cultures has its share in who I am.

But if we're talking about which is most present in my work, it is without doubt my Ukrainian formation. More than thirty years of my life were lived in Ukraine. That is where I took shape as a person and as an artist. Ukrainian reality, life in Ukraine, the opportunities I created there and keep developing beyond it – all of that formed me. So I am a Ukrainian artist of Armenian origin. And living abroad, I keep shaping my vision.

As for viewers – yes, some Armenians noticed in my Abstract Animals, especially Abstract Animal II, a resemblance to Armenian khachkars. They saw something Armenian in it. Even in fairly abstract works, a deep or bright red was read as Armenian temperament, emotion, a link to the roots.

What's interesting is that nobody – at least nobody who said it to me – has ever said, "This is something Ukrainian." But I don't create specifically Ukrainian images; there are no direct references to traditional Ukrainian motifs in my work. Ukraine formed me, and that influence shows in how I feel, see and create.

At the same time, I wouldn't say Ukraine feels very different from Armenia when it comes to colour. Maybe that's why I found myself in both. To me both peoples are warm and sincere, and both cultures are very rich in colour. So here too it's hard for me to say where one ends and the other begins in my work.

Many artists who have lived through war say they don't want their work read only through trauma: it is both true and a trap. How do you feel about curators, journalists and collectors so often starting the conversation with war – us included?

I'm calm about it, including in this interview, because I have accepted the experience of war as part of my path. I don't separate myself from it. I don't call it only trauma, because it has become part of my life. It is what formed me.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22me0kjk6x0r.jpg
content.caption: Creative chaos, studio in Kyiv, 2019.

content.content: II. Cybernetics and hidden order

You have two master's degrees – urban planning and design, and economic cybernetics, the science of control, feedback and systems. You say you look for "hidden order behind what seems to be chaos". Yet abstraction, from Kandinsky to Pollock, was often a revolt against order. Are you closer to the engineer who decodes a system, or to the artist who lets it break?
Chaos doesn't exist without order, just as white doesn't exist without black, or light without darkness.

Engineering and economic cybernetics are closely tied to physics and higher mathematics. For me they are sciences of the patterns that lie at the root of life. Still, I don't count myself an engineer. I don't build systems by strict rules. And even if I had the chance to build something, I'd be interested in breaking those rules, in making something that goes beyond them.

Your series Factorials was, in your words, a response to rupture, exploring "the inner structures of influence within a system". A factorial grows explosively: each new element multiplies all the previous ones. Did you think of the mathematical metaphor literally? Which system did you mean – family, country, self, the world – and what broke in it?

Before I started, I didn't think about a mathematical metaphor. It was pure creation. The very first object was made of paper. I was making the elements of a sculpture, tearing them, opening and closing them in my hands, watching what happened. It was like a game. I opened one element and saw that the whole picture had changed. At some point I thought: "But this is a factorial." It even reminded me of that school lesson where we were told about factorials.

I never take a mathematical formula and set out to depict it. First something is born in a creative state, and then I recognise in it something that is already part of my world. But it could be named quite differently, too. That's exactly why I adore abstraction: it has an endless number of names we can give it.

At first it was simply a visual system for me. Only as I went deeper into the series did I understand that it is about any system: a country, a family, oneself, education. And what broke in it? Nothing broke. Every small part affects the system and at the same time creates it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22msiqg924tj.jpg
content.caption: Factorial 3, 2021. Acrylic and spray paint on paper, 15 × 22.9 cm.

content.content: You call your abstractions "visual formulas" that translate emotional and spiritual experience into colour, line and composition. A formula should be reproducible. Can the same painting be painted twice? What in its "formula" stays unspeakable?

That is exactly why it is art. My abstraction depicts a system but is not a system itself. It is about those patterns, yet it can't be reproduced by formula. That's where its creative, artistic part lies.
I have never set out to paint the same picture twice. For me abstraction is creation through and through, and repeating it exactly is almost impossible.

What remains unspeakable in this visual formula is the meaning and the energy I create with – the force that drives me to do it. The emotional and spiritual experience itself: all the emotions and sensations I put into a work.
I never create just to create. I create because I live it. Everything in my art is something I have lived through. It is what I exist from.
For you colour is "vibration" and "sensory memory", not an aesthetic choice. Name one colour in your work and the memory it carries. Is there a colour you refuse to use because it remembers too much?

There is a lot of blue in my work. That deep, deep blue began for me in Zaporizhzhia. I used to go down to the Dnipro and could sit for hours looking at the water. Then it appeared to me in the blue of the sky – slightly different. And in Kyiv it gained a special depth: very deep, yet bright. All these shades of blue and azure come through in the Lapis Lazuli series. So much in my art is connected with these colours.
As for a colour I refuse to use – there isn't one. I allow myself absolutely every colour. What kind of artist would I be if I limited myself? For me art is born from freedom.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mj4lcmd8ak.jpg
content.caption: Chaos of Lazur, 2016. Mixed media on paper, 36.7 × 35 cm.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mfle8haupd.jpg
content.caption: Blue Month I, 2018. Watercolour on paper, 42 × 29.7 cm.

content.content: III. Equilibrium

Equilibrium took shape as a meditative focus on balance in unstable times. How did the word "balance" change for you after 24 February 2022? Doesn't balance now look less like calm and more like the tension of two forces that could tear each other apart at any second?
Editor's note: our original question dated the series to 2021; the artist corrected this in her answer below, and the question has been adjusted.
Let me clarify first: the Equilibrium series began to take shape in 2016–2017, especially in 2017, when I moved to Kyiv. It didn't appear in 2021.

Balance has never been absolute calm for me. It is the simultaneous existence of all forces. One doesn't exist without the other – that is the pattern. It can be the tension of two forces, or it can be their calm. For me balance is a single whole that can show itself in very different ways.

After 24 February my understanding of balance didn't change. On the contrary, to some extent it helped me live through the horror. I knew there was another side to that experience – love, an incredible desire to live and create. I'm not saying I knew when the war would end or what would come next. But I already felt that counterweight to destruction. For me that doesn't contradict balance. And at the same time it doesn't mean it is calm or easy.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mlgwdpeccf.jpg
content.caption: In the studio in Zaporizhzhia, working on the Equilibrium series, 2016–2017.

content.content: Balance is easy to paint as symmetry, but symmetry quickly goes dead. Where in your compositions is instability deliberately built in? Tell us about a work where you searched a long time for the point where everything holds.

Balance and symmetry are different things for me. If we mean absolute symmetry, complete sameness – in nature I see something else: repeating elements that change every time and together create an overall system. There is the power of nature in that chaos.
In the Balance works I deliberately created disruption – destruction, you could say. But everything holds not on a single line but on the whole pattern, which never repeats exactly.

At first I simply crumpled paper in my hands and watched how the folds appeared and how the form changed. Observation is very important to me in general; I watch everything. Later, on Tenerife, I saw a similar pattern in a rocky mountain, in the way the split stones had settled. All the elements are different, yet together they create something incredible.

Later still, in 2023, when I came to Miami for a few months and saw the extraordinarily beautiful Villa Vizcaya, I was struck by another coexistence. At the time this beauty was being created here, in another part of the world the Armenian genocide was taking place in the Ottoman Empire. And I myself, while in Miami, seemed to be living in another reality, while the war went on in Ukraine.
So destruction and creation exist at the same time. I see it in nature, in history and in my own life.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mnspkgvr0l.jpg
content.caption: Working on Balance, studio in Kyiv, spring 2025.

content.content: You paint large canvases that are physically hard to move and hang alone. Is balance felt by the body – when you work on a canvas taller than you, on the floor, with tape and a sponge? What does the body know about composition before the head does?

Of course, the body knows and feels its own laws of balance too. Look at yoga or at athletes: our body can hold its balance in very different positions. We're used to walking on our feet, but we can learn to stand on our hands. It's a skill we acquire gradually.

Working on a canvas bigger than you is physically harder. But over time the body gets used to it: you train your hand, you get used to the scale and the movements. It's like learning to hatch – at first your muscles may ache, then the movement becomes natural.
So I'd say the body adapts. It finds its balance with the material and the surface we work with.
IV. Space: sculpture and transformational objects

Your profile says "Creating transformational spaces". What has to happen to a space – and to the person in it – for you to call it transformed? How does an object that changes a room differ from an expensive interior accessory? Where is the line between art and design, and does it still exist?

For me a space should coexist with a person's inner world and transform along with it. If it doesn't match your inner state, it's like clothes in which you don't feel like yourself. Through art a collector fills a space with meanings and with the energy they want to feel in it. I'm convinced that an artist puts their energy into every work.

For me the line with design runs through function. Design usually answers a particular function. In art we can go beyond it: not fit the work to a task, but follow meanings, the questions we're looking for answers to. At the same time design can also be art. For me the objects made at the Bauhaus are an example: they have function, vision and a sense of their time. Art carries the time in which it is born.
Art can be decorative, but decoration isn't its purpose. And decoration isn't always art – it doesn't aim to be anything more than decoration.
Sometimes it seems to me that quite often it is time that decides what is art and what remains mere decoration.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mjoj0mncqw.jpg
content.caption: Installation view at Mlyn Design Hub, summer 2025.

content.content: Your first profession was urban construction and design. Your sculptures and relief objects look like an architect's return: a flat shape is cut out and gains thickness, shadow, weight. What does the third dimension give you that canvas doesn't? And what do you lose when a painting steps out into space?

The third dimension lets me feel form with my hands. Of course, you can paint with your hands too, but I want to go beyond the plane of the canvas and feel space. Through sculpture I create that space myself. I like that feeling, and I want to pass it on.
Do I lose anything? I don't feel it as a loss. For me it is one more way to create and to feel.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mm5n903gwy.png
content.caption: Studio in Kyiv, summer 2018, working on a 3D Equilibrium piece.

content.content: The language of your objects – streamlined silhouettes, cut-outs, openings, pastel and saturated planes – recalls an architectural drawing, a child's stencil and a sign all at once. Where do these forms come from? Do you draw them by hand or construct them geometrically – and has a form ever appeared "by itself" from a mistake or an offcut?
Most often a form is born at the call of the hand. I start drawing and it simply takes shape. Sometimes I let chance influence the process, but a form rarely comes from an offcut.

And sometimes an image comes to me. I say exactly that: "A picture came to me." It's like an imaginary screen in front of me on which I see something. Some images come in dreams. Sometimes, while I'm drawing, I already see the whole form in volume, its geometry, not just the plane.

I never sit down thinking, "Right, now I need to come up with something." Everything is born from within. Of course I was influenced by technical drawing, which I loved at school, and by architecture. I love architecture very much, and it is part of my vision too.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22moa1vdwfdz.jpg
content.caption: Abstract Animals I, 2022. Glazed ceramic, 19 × 23 × 6 cm.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mqznox58dr.jpg
content.caption: Abstract Animals II, 2022. Glazed ceramic, 16 × 21.5 × 6 cm.

content.content: Sculpture outlives canvas and is harder to move. Someone who has started life from zero several times suddenly makes heavy, immovable things. Is that chance – or a way of finally taking root?
I see it neither as chance nor as a wish to take root. For me it is the desire to work with space, with matter: to feel it and shape it – stone, clay. That feeling can't be replaced by anything.

Taking root may come as a result, but it isn't my aim. When I want to make something, I don't start by thinking, "This will be heavy, it'll be impossible to move." Yes, it can be physically hard. But what comes first for me is the desire to create, not the limit of how hard it is. That matters a great deal to me.
V. The market, teaching and honesty

CONTEXT Art Miami 2025 is one of the busiest fair weeks in the world: tens of thousands of visitors, thousands of works, a few seconds per piece. How does abstraction that needs long looking survive there? What did you learn about your works by watching strangers at the stand?

Those who stopped at my works were interested in them. What matters to me is precisely that dialogue between a person and what I create. And the experience showed me once again how important it is to understand your place in the art world.

When you create a work, you look at it as an artist; you live it. But when you enter the art market, you also have to see your work as an object within that system. That isn't easy. For me these are two different roles: the artist, and the person who wants more opportunities to create. That's why I go to international art fairs – to widen my possibilities and make something bigger.

Did I learn anything new about the works themselves? My feeling for them hasn't changed. What changed is my understanding of the place they occupy in the market. I realised it matters to me to be where my works are understood, where my meanings meet the meanings of my collector.

You've said abstraction was not understood in Ukraine at first, and that you came to accept that a work "doesn't have to be understood by everyone". But between "not for everyone" and "for the narrow circle that can afford to buy it" the line is thin. Who do you work for now – the collector, the viewer, or your ten-year-old self?

At the first exhibitions of the Union of Young Artists of Ukraine in 2012 my works were criticised a lot. At the same time I felt that in that very setting I was doing something new. Today I take it calmly. But even then I knew I wouldn't change my visual language just because someone didn't understand it.

I don't set out to work for anyone in particular. Inwardly I understand who my art might touch: some are close to its themes and meanings, some to its visual language, some are moved by it emotionally. But I don't make a work in order to touch someone. Where would my freedom as an artist be then?

In recent years I've come to see it like this: if I have created something, then somewhere there is my viewer – a person with whom I'll meet in these meanings. Perhaps they'll become my collector, perhaps they'll remain a viewer.
That feeling lets me create freely. I know that person exists somewhere, and I don't need to fit my art to them in advance.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22mi3vet70ll.jpg
content.caption: No Limit / Immeasurable, 2012. Acrylic on canvas, 94 × 94 cm.

content.content: You founded the School of Experimental Art in Kyiv and G-ART STUDIO in Zaporizhzhia and combined teaching with your own practice for years. What have your students taught you that no teacher did? And does teaching get in the way of the artist – the habit of explaining when the work should stay silent?

When it comes to children, I adore them. They teach life better than anything. They are pure nature. They teach you to be yourself, to be sincere – and in art, for me, that comes first. At the same time, a good teacher also teaches you to move towards your own nature, your own truth.

Being an artist and being a teacher are different roles, and combining them isn't easy. A good artist isn't always a good teacher, and a good teacher isn't always a good artist. I hope I'm a good teacher, but only my students can say.

I teach the rules and at the same time try to teach a person to follow their inner calling. That is very important. I have seen artists almost lose themselves through the habit of constantly copying, or of just painting when it no longer came from the soul, from their own calling.
So for me teaching isn't only explaining. I teach feeling – combining the two: understanding and feeling.

"The moment you stop being honest with yourself, it shows in the work," you said in one interview. Tell us about a time you saw it in your own painting. What gave the dishonesty away – colour, line, speed, a result that was too pretty? And what did you do with that work?
First of all, honesty means knowing yourself. And that is very hard: knowing what you feel, understanding yourself. Then you can sense when you're being honest with yourself and when you aren't.

So I don't have finished works in which I saw it. There were times I started something and it just wouldn't come. And I didn't finish it. I could throw something away at the very beginning, so I can't even call it a work.
What gives it away? It can start with a line, with a colour: you put down a colour and feel something is wrong. Maybe it shows in speed too, but speed alone decides nothing. It's a feeling.

Everything starts with the state. The artist's inner state shapes everything: the matter, the painting, the sculpture. If I'm not in that state, what can I create? For me – hardly anything in which I myself would feel meaning.

Inspire Me If You Can (2012–2015) was a portrait project – figurative, about specific people. Today you work almost exclusively in abstraction. What happened to the faces? Do they live somewhere inside your abstract forms?

In recent years I really have worked mostly in abstraction, but I don't call myself only an abstract painter. Abstraction is a large part of my path right now, but I've realised that I am a multidisciplinary artist. I don't want to limit myself to a style or a technique. There are patterns in everything, in portraiture too – any portraitist can tell you about them.

And the faces haven't gone anywhere. I think those portraits grew into photography. I often photograph people when they don't notice. I've shown little of it so far, but that is how Inspire Me If You Can continued for me.
People and their faces still inspire me greatly. And I have many more ideas I'd like to realise in the future.
VI. Doubts and the horizon
What is the biggest misunderstanding about your work?
I probably don't see anything as a misunderstanding of my work. I've never even thought about it that way.

At the start of my path I was very sensitive to how my abstraction was received. It's my creation, after all. Incomprehension, and sometimes hate, did hurt me. That's probably the only thing I could call a misunderstanding.

But over the years I've become much calmer about it. It no longer matters so much that everyone understands what I create. If someone didn't understand – then they didn't. Maybe they simply aren't my viewer. That's all.
What did you have to give up – a manner, a series, a city, a certainty – to arrive at what you do today?
I wouldn't say I had to give anything up. I consciously chose to leave something behind and move on, because I wanted to grow.

For example, I left portraits. It was very important to me that they were alive, especially the eyes. But at some point I wanted something else, and those studies remained as I finished them. I experimented a lot, and I still love experiment. Pure creativity is born in it; there is chance and mystery in it. It keeps inspiring me. And everything I made was my manner, even when it was a search.

The same with cities. I left Zaporizhzhia because I wanted to move to Kyiv. Going to Miami was my conscious choice as well. I didn't leave Kyiv because of the full-scale war – I very much wanted to stay there. But I always felt a pull towards something larger. The places I leave stay in my heart for ever.

What I gave up inwardly was the fear of growing – because it really is frightening to be alone in a huge city, or a huge country, or a completely new and enormous art world. Yet on the international art scene I feel confident. I have the sense that I'm where I'm meant to be. This is my world. I chose this path consciously. Where it leads next – we'll see.
If you could create just one space – a room, a pavilion, a square – for one city in the world, which city would you choose, and what should a person feel as they leave?
I dream of creating a huge garden with incredible flowers, trees and sculptures. Most likely I would choose Armenia and Ukraine for it. I really love Kyiv.
I'd want a person leaving the garden to feel what we feel when we listen to classical music: a sense of spring, a sense of beginning, a sense of eternity. I would call that feeling very close to God.
What are you working on now?
I'm working on a series for an exhibition. I know what I'd like to show, but for now I'll keep it secret. In parallel I'm working on the series Equilibrium.Net.
The question we should have asked – and your answer.
Not that you should have asked exactly this, but taking it creatively, I'd be interested to answer: "If you could meet a person from the past, who would it be?"

For me it's Leonardo da Vinci. Simply a brilliant artist, the genius of his time. I would love to live near him for at least a while and see with my own eyes how he lives, how he creates, what inspires him. Not just to meet and talk, but to observe his life. That would be incredibly interesting to me. I love watching wise, intelligent older people – there is so much life in them. Or Einstein, if da Vinci is too busy.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mv22n3s04rjsc4.jpg
content.caption: Gayane Arushanian. Shot on film. Photo: Rita Pakhlova.
